Wang Chen, courtesy name Chudao, was born in Jinyang, Taiyuan. His grandfather Wang Rou served as a lieutenant general of the Huns in the Han Dynasty, and his father Wang Ji was the prefect of Wei Dong County. Orphaned young, Wang Chen was adopted by his cousin Sikong Wang Chang, whom he served as a biological father, gaining fame for his filial piety toward his stepmother and widowed sister-in-law. He was well-read and skilled in writing. General Cao Shuang recruited him as a subordinate officer, and he gradually rose to minister under Zhongshu's family. After Cao Shuang's execution, Wang Chen was dismissed as an old official but later reappointed as censor of the book administration department and transferred to secretary supervisor. During the Zhengyuan period, he was promoted to Sanqi Changshi and Shizhong, overseeing writings. Together with Xunjie and Ruan Ji, he compiled the "Book of Wei," though he often concealed taboos and did not record events as truthfully as Chen Shou.

Duke Gaogui of Wei, eager to learn and talented, frequently invited Wang Chen and Pei Xiu to lectures and banquets in Shutang. When the Duke planned to attack Emperor Wen, he summoned Wang Chen and Wang Ye to inform them, but Wang Chen and Wang Ye quickly reported to Emperor Wen. For this, they were granted the title of Marquis of Anping with two thousand households. Wang Chen's disloyalty to his master drew public criticism. He was soon promoted to minister and sent to supervise military affairs in Yuzhou as General Fenwu and governor. Upon arrival, he issued a decree encouraging criticism and recommendations, offering rewards of grain for those who exposed corruption or proposed beneficial policies. His chief registrars, Chen Chang and Chu Bi, advised caution, fearing that rewards might deter honest people or attract greedy ones. Wang Chen initially insisted on his sincerity but eventually relented, following Chu Bi's advice. He then focused on good governance, implementing legal prohibitions established since Jia Kui and promoting education to reform declining customs.

Wang Chen was promoted to General Zhenglu and Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs north of the Yangtze River. When the fifth-class title system was established, he was granted the title of Marquis of Boling. During the pacification of Shu, Wu forces threatened the border, but Wang Chen defended well, causing the enemy to retreat. He was later transferred to General Zhennan. After Emperor Wu ascended the throne, Wang Chen became imperial censor and abided by the Shangshu order. Known for his talent and fame, he consulted with Yang Hu, Xun Xu, Pei Xiu, and Jia Chong on state affairs. For his role in the abdication, he was promoted to general of hussars and granted the title of Duke of Boling County, which he initially refused but later accepted with 1,800 households. He died in the second year of Taishi, and the emperor mourned him with lavish gifts. Posthumously, he was given the title of Sikong Gong. Wang Chen was always honest and frugal, leaving no property. His son Wang Jun succeeded him.

Wang Jun, courtesy name Peng Zu, was born to a poor mother from a common family. Initially despised by his father, he became heir at fifteen after Wang Chen's death. He served as Prince Consort and later held various military and civil posts. During the chaos of the court, he allied with Yi Di, marrying his daughters to Xianbei leaders for safety. After King Sima Lun of Zhao usurped the throne, Wang Jun led troops to wait and see. He later killed He Yan, who plotted against him, and occupied Youzhou. He built equipment and led 20,000 Hu and Jin troops against Sima Ying, defeating his general and capturing Yecheng, where his soldiers looted brutally. Wang Jun's power grew, and he was promoted to General Hussar and Commander-in-Chief of Hebei. During the Yongjia period, he fought Shi Le and Liu Kun, but his harsh rule led to defections. He planned to become emperor based on prophecies, killing those who advised against it. Shi Le pretended to surrender, and Wang Jun, trusting him, was captured and killed. Wang Jun had no sons, and his title passed to his nephew Daosu.

Xunjie, courtesy name Jingqian, was from Yingchuan and the sixth son of Wei Taiwei Xun You. Known for filial piety and extensive knowledge, he served as Zhonglang and later Sanqi Shilang. He taught the young emperor of Wei and was granted the title of Marquis of Guannei. He rescued Fu Gu from Cao Shuang's harm and advised Emperor Jing to declare benevolence after Gao Guixiang Gong's ascension. He participated in suppressing rebellions and was promoted to Marquis of Wansuiting. Under Emperor Wen, he became Shangshu and later Sikong. He was filial, resigning for his mother's funeral, and was praised nationwide. He formulated Jin etiquette and was promoted to Duke of Linhuai. He served as Crown Prince Tutor and Taiwei, settling music before dying in the tenth year of Taishi. The emperor mourned him greatly. Xunjie understood the "Three Rites" but lacked upright moral integrity, catering to Xun Xu and Jia Chong. He had no sons, and his title passed to his grandnephew Xun Hui.

Xun Xu, courtesy name Gongzeng, was from Yingyin, Yingchuan, and the great-grandson of Han Sikong Xun Shuang. Orphaned young, he was raised by his uncle. He was intelligent and wrote articles in his teens. He served under Cao Shuang and later became Zhongshu Tongshilang. After Cao Shuang's death, he alone attended the funeral, earning respect. He served as Anyang Order and later Tingweizheng, participating in Emperor Wen's military affairs. He advised against assassins and warned of Zhong Hui's rebellion. He wrote documents to Sun Hao of Wu, which were praised as better than a hundred thousand troops. After Emperor Wu's abdication, he was granted the title of Duke of Jibei County but refused, becoming a marquis. He served as Zhongshu Supervisor and jointly formulated laws with Jia Chong. He helped secure Jia Chong's daughter as crown prince's concubine, drawing criticism. He revised music rhythms and compiled classics. He opposed the attack on Wu but was overruled. He advised against sending princes to feudal states and discussed reducing officials. He praised the prince's character, leading to respect for He Jiao and disdain for him. He died in the tenth year of Taikang, with ten sons, including Xun Ji, Xun Fan, and Xun Zu. Xun Xu's descendants continued his legacy, with Xun Sui and Xun He crossing the river eastward during the chaos.

Feng You, courtesy name Shaozhou, was from Anping. He read extensively and was eloquent. He served as prefect of Wei County and later General Zuowei, favored by Emperor Wu. He befriended Jia Chong and Xun Xu, helping Jia Chong's daughter become dowager. He opposed the attack on Wu but later followed Wang Jun into Moling. He advised the emperor to send Qi King Sima You to his feudal state, leading to Sima You's death. He hated Zhang Hua and prevented his promotion. He died in the seventh year of Taikang, leaving two sons, Feng Bo and Feng Xiong. The historian comments that Wang Chen's disloyalty and Wang Jun's violence brought disaster, while Xunjie and Xun Xu, despite their talents, contributed to court strife. Feng You's flattery led to Sima You's death and Jia's rise, causing endless civil unrest.

A detailed account of the empresses, consorts, and dowagers of the Jin Dynasty, chronicling their lives, titles, deaths, and roles in court politics. Empress Xia Yuan Jing Yu, who died young before her husband became emperor, and was later posthumously honored. Her rival, Concubine Zhang, bore Emperor Ming but was hated by Empress Yu and neglected by Emperor Yuan; she was later honored by her son. Empress Ming Mu Yu, known for her virtue, served as regent for her young son, Emperor Cheng, during a rebellion, and died in distress. Empress Cheng Gong Du, from a virtuous family, died young without children, and her funeral was kept simple by imperial decree.

The text then covers Empress Kang Xian Chu, who served as regent for Emperor Mu, and later for Emperor Ai and Duke Haixi, including her role in the deposition of the latter. It notes the unusual practice of empress dowagers acting as regents, which was not an ancient custom, and reflects on the rise and fall of dynasties being tied to the influence of women.

summary:
Chen Qian, a native of Shuyang, Linhuai, was the son of Chen Jiao, a Situ of Wei. Chen Jiao, originally from the Liu family, was raised by his maternal grandfather and changed his surname. Chen Qian was known for his depth and resourcefulness. Early in his career, he advised his father during a false accusation by Liu Ye, which was later resolved. As a youth, he remained calm when insulted by Xia Houxuan, impressing him. He served as Shangshu Lang, Grand Administrator of Zhongshan and Anping, achieving remarkable success. He rose to Sima, Changshi, and Yushi Zhongcheng, then Shangshu, and was granted the title of Tinghou of Anguo. During the Shu invasion of Longyou, he led forces to victory. He also acted against the Zhuge Dan rebellion. After pacifying Shouchun, he was appointed envoy Chijie, commander of Huaibei military affairs, and General Andong, with his title promoted to Marquis of Guangling. He later governed Yuzhou and was transferred to command military affairs south of the Yangtze and in Jingzhou, becoming General of the Conquest of the South and Marquis of Tan.

When Emperor Wu accepted the abdication, Chen Qian was promoted to General of Chariots and Cavalry for his merits, granted the title of Duke of Gaoping County, and served as Shizhong, Grand General, and commander of Yangzhou military affairs. He captured Zhili in Wu and defeated Tu Zhong's forces. In the early Xianning years, he was promoted to Taiwei and then Grand Sima. He warned the emperor about Hu Lie and Qian Hong's overconfidence, but the emperor dismissed his concerns. Both later died in conflict with the Qiang Rong, leading the emperor to regret his decision. Chen Qian was magnanimous and achieved success in all positions. He surpassed colleagues like Maichong, Shi Bao, and Pei Xiu in resourcefulness. He held high office beyond retirement age and eventually retired, receiving honors and gifts from the emperor. He died at eighty-one, with the emperor attending his funeral.

Pei Xiu, courtesy name Ji Yan, was from Wenxi, Hedong. His grandfather Pei Mao and father Pei Qian were ministers. Pei Xiu was eager to learn and wrote articles at eight. His uncle Pei Hui had many guests, and Pei Xiu's mother was once humiliated by her aunt, but Pei Xiu's reputation grew. He was recommended to Cao Shuang, who recruited him. After Cao Shuang's death, he was dismissed but later served as Tingweizheng and Wei Sima, with his policies adopted. He participated in the campaign against Zhuge Dan and was promoted to Minister and Marquis of Luyang Township. He helped establish the throne and was promoted to County Marquis. In the Xianxi era, he reformed the official system, proposing the fifth-class title. He was granted the title of Marquis of Jichuan. He advised Emperor Wen on the heir, supporting Emperor Wu. After Emperor Wu's ascension, he became Shangshu Ling and Duke of Julu County. He faced accusations but was defended by the emperor. He was later made Sikong.

Pei Xiu was knowledgeable and compiled the "Yugong Regional Circle," a map with six principles: ratio, accurate observation, road, high-low, fangxie, and roundabout. He established court礼仪 and criminal laws. He died at forty-eight, and the emperor mourned deeply. His son Pei Jun died early, and his younger son Pei Dian succeeded him. Pei Dian, courtesy name Yimin, was elegant and knowledgeable. He served as crown prince's concubine and Sanqi Changshi. He advised against Yang Jun's rebellion and was promoted. He discussed the prince's education and medical standards. He wrote the "Chongyou Lun" against nihilism, arguing for the importance of existence and ritual. He was killed by Sima Lun at thirty-four. His sons Pei Song and Pei Gai were exiled but later restored.

Pei Kai, courtesy name Shuze, was Pei Hui's son. He was intelligent and famous young, proficient in "Laozi" and "Yijing." He served as Shangshu Lang and Ding Kelang. He was known as the "Jade Man" for his elegance. He advised Emperor Wu during a divination, calming him. He served as Sanqi Minister and other posts. He was generous, giving away possessions. He criticized Jia Chong's presence in court. He survived the Yang Jun rebellion by hiding. He later served as Zhongshu Ling. He died at fifty-five. His sons included Pei Yu, Pei Zan, Pei Xian, Pei Li, and Pei Xun. Pei Xian, courtesy name Jingsi, was upright and served as Yuzhou governor. He was captured by Shi Le but praised for his integrity. He later served under Shi Le and Jilong, but his sons were killed, and he was dismissed. He died in the Shi family's hands.

The Pei family was prominent in Wei and Jin, with eight members compared to the eight Wangs. The text praises Chen Qian and Pei Xiu as famous officials of the Jin Dynasty.

King Hui of Liaodong Dingguo died at the age of three.

Guangde, the war king of Guanghan, died when he was two years old.

In the past, Han Qi had a good relationship with Tian Su and was good at doing good deeds. He should definitely get a competent person.

He died in the seventh year and was succeeded by his son Sima Ji, the Shang King.
He died without a son, so King Sima Jian of Qi made his son Sima Bing the descendant of Sima Jian.
The 11,219 households in Jiyin were changed to Guangyang Kingdom, and Sima Bing was made King of Guangyang.
Sima Jian failed and King Guangyang was deposed.
King Yanzuo of Leping was named Dasi. He was seriously ill when he was young and was not qualified for the title of nobility.

Call him King Leping to give him a name to comfort my heart.

It is said that he was in an era of turmoil and separation, and lived in a period of war and struggle, but he was able to stay away from disasters, preserve himself, and enjoy great blessings. His ignorance was unmatched by others!
King Langxie is good at martial arts, gentle and respectful, King Fufeng is outstanding in literary talent and education, and is filial, so he may be a commendable person in the clan.

Later, due to his high status, he was persecuted by doubts, and his elegant literary talent was criticized for his faults. Feng Shou and Xun Xu came up with treacherous strategies like creeping grass. Emperor Wu deeply maintained his incomprehensible love for his son.
So he deprived the King of Qi of his power in the court and moved to a feudal country thousands of miles away. He died of resentment before he could prepare for the journey. What a pity!
If God granted him a long life and got rid of his political enemies, and he was ordered to be a trusted minister, accept the great trust of governing the country, and assist the succeeding emperor, and he was indeed able to manage the country's politics, then judging from the signs in the underworld, maybe there will be a period of decline and prosperity, and judging from the events in the world, the possible victory or defeat can be deduced. Praising: Some of the descendants of Emperor Wen and Emperor Xuan are wise and some are despicable.
King Fufeng left behind his love, and King Langxie restrained himself.
Sima Dan was the most flattering and cruel, and Sima Shu participated in public revenge.

Governing the country by oneself, being both civil and military.

summary:
Emperor Xuan had nine sons from various consorts. Queen Mu Zhang bore Emperor Jing, Emperor Wen, and Sima Qian (King of Pingyuan). Mrs. Fu gave birth to Sima Liang (King of Wencheng in Runan), Sima Nian (King of Langye Wu), Sima Jing (Marquis of Huiting in Qing Dynasty), and Sima Jun (King of Fufeng Wu). Mrs. Zhang bore Sima Xu (King of Liang), while Mrs. Bai bore Sima Lun (King of Zhao).

Sima Qian, King of Pingyuan, was granted the title of Anyang Tinghou in the Wei Dynasty and later became King of Pingyuan under Emperor Wu with 11,300 households. He suffered from severe illness and was allowed to remain in the capital rather than go to his feudal state. He held various official positions including Guanglu大夫 and served as a servant. Although a great feudal lord, he did not care for government affairs. His salary and goods were left to rot in the open air. He was known for eccentric behavior, such as keeping his concubines' coffins unsealed in empty rooms and opening them to look at them periodically. During the rebellion of King Zhao Sima Lun, Sima Qian was appointed as General Wei and later Taibao. When Sima Tong of Qi pacified Sima Lun, Sima Qian congratulated him with a hundred coins. He died in the fifth year of Yongjia at age eighty.

Sima Dian, King of Langye Wu, was talented and famous from an early age. He served as General Ningshuo guarding Yecheng and later as General Zhenshu guarding Xiapi, where he defended well against the Wu people. During the pacification of Wu, Sun Hao surrendered to Sima Dian, who sent troops across the Yangtze River, capturing enemy officials and securing the surrender of 50,000 to 60,000 people. His two sons were made marquises. He died in the fourth year of Taikang at age fifty-seven. His descendants included Sima Rui, who later became Emperor Yuan, and several others who successively held the title of King of Langye.

Sima Dan, King of Wulingzhuang, was jealous and harmful by nature with no filial character. He hated his brother Sima Yao and spoke ill of him to Sima Liang. During Sima Lun's rebellion, Sima Dan served as leading general. He killed two men while drunk and gave their heads to Sima Lun. His mother complained of his unfilial behavior, and he was moved to Liaosai with his family. He was later killed by Shi Le in the late Yongjia period.

Sima Yao, King of Dong'an, was resolute, authoritative, and learned, with filial piety in serving relatives. He was granted 20,000 households and held various positions. He was arbitrary in punishments and rewards, leading to his dismissal and exile to Daifang. He was later restored but killed by Sima Ying after the emperor's army was defeated.

Sima Jun, King of Fufeng Wu, was clever from childhood, able to write memorials and recite scriptures at age five or six. He was quiet, upright, and had the best reputation in the clan. He served as General of Zhenxi, guarding Guanzhong, and was skilled at appeasing rulers. He promoted agriculture and shared labor with soldiers. He suppressed Qiang rebellions and received surrenders from various tribes. He was filial to his mother and eager to learn, writing treatises on benevolence and filial piety. When he died, people wept for him and erected monuments.

Sima Xu, King of Liang, practiced quietness and was respectful and prudent. He served as General of Zhengxi guarding Guanzhong and later as Grand Administrator and Situ. During Sima Lun's usurpation, he served as prime minister. After his death, there was debate over his posthumous name, with some criticizing him for failing to take a stand during crises. He had no sons, and his title passed through various relatives.

Sima You, King of Qi Xian, was wise from youth, calm, kind, and fond of classical books. He was made heir to Emperor Jing and inherited the title of Wuyang Hou. Under Emperor Wu, he was made King of Qi and managed military affairs. He was known for his filial piety and moral conduct. He advised on agricultural policies and government administration. He was especially favored by Emperor Wen, who nearly made him crown prince. However, due to the machinations of Xun Xu and Feng Shou, Emperor Wu sent him to his feudal state. Sima You became ill from resentment and died at age thirty-six while traveling. His son Sima Tong succeeded him.

Wei Guan, courtesy name Boyu, was born in Anyi, Hedong Province.
During the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han Dynasty, the great ancestor Wei Hao was recruited by the imperial court from Dai County for his proficiency in Confucianism. He went to Anyi, Hedong, and died. The land where he died was given to him for burial, and his descendants settled there.
His father, Wei Jian, was the Minister of Wei.
Wei Guan's father passed away when he was ten years old, and his extreme filial piety exceeded that of ordinary people.
He has a quiet temperament and is good at distinguishing right from wrong, and is known for being knowledgeable and fair.
Inherited his father's title of Marquis of Yuexiang.
At the age of twenty, he became the minister of Wei.
At that time, Wei's laws were strict and detailed, and his mother Chen was worried. Wei Guan asked to be transferred to Tongshilang, and was later transferred to Zhongshulang.
At that time, the court officials were in exclusive power, and Wei Guan was among them. He had no distinction between those who were in power and those who were in power. He was highly regarded by Fu Gu, who called him Ning!
After ten years in the official position, he was known for his competence and was gradually promoted to the rank of regular attendant.
When King Chenliu came to the throne, he paid homage to his ministers and went to Hebei to express his condolences.
Because of the merits of agreeing on major events, the number of households in the fief was increased.
A few years later, he was transferred to Tingweiqing.
Wei Guan is well versed in legal principles, and every time he judges a case, he bases his judgment on reason, no matter how big or small the case is.
When Deng Ai and Zhong Hui conquered Shu, Wei Gan used his former official position to supervise the military affairs of Deng Ai and Zhong Hui, and also served as the Zhenxi Military Division, with a thousand soldiers.
After the Shu Kingdom was pacified, Deng Ai was granted the title in accordance with the emperor's will.
Zhong Hui secretly harbored rebellious intentions because Deng Ai was dictatorial and arbitrary, so he secretly reported the situation with Wei Guan.
The emperor issued an edict to send a guard to arrest Deng Ai, and Zhong Hui sent a guard to arrest Deng Ai first.
Zhong Hui believed that Deng Ai had few soldiers and wanted Deng Ai to kill Wei Guan in order to aggravate Deng Ai's crime.
Wei Guan knew that Zhong Hui wanted to harm him, but he could not refuse, so he arrived in Chengdu at night and sent a message to the generals led by Deng Ai, claiming that he had issued an imperial edict to arrest Deng Ai, and the others ignored him.
If you come to join the army, you will still be rewarded with titles; if you dare not come and join the army, the three clans will be killed.
When the cries of war broke out, they all came to defend Wei Guan. Only Deng Ai's entourage was still there.
When the doors opened at dawn, Wei Guan took the messenger's vehicle and went directly to the Chengdu Palace.
Deng Ai fell asleep before he got up, and both his father and son were captured.
Several generals under Deng Ai planned to kidnap Deng Ai back and went straight to Wei Guan's camp with weapons.
Wei Guan came out of the camp to meet them. He pretended to write a draft of the above table and was going to explain Deng Ai's affairs. The generals believed him and gave up.

As a result, the soldiers were worried about returning home, there was turmoil inside and outside, and people were worried and fearful.

Wei Guan went to the toilet and saw Hu Lie's former entourage, and asked him to inform the three armies that Zhong Hui would rebel.
Zhong Hui forced Wei Guan to make a decision and stayed up all night, each holding a knife across his knees.
The armies outside had secretly planned to attack Zhonghui, but because Wei Guan had not come out, they did not dare to take action first.
Zhong will ask Wei Guan to comfort the troops.
Wei Guan wanted to leave, so he tried to keep Zhong Hui from changing his mind, saying: "You are the commander-in-chief of the armed forces, so you should go in person."
Zhong Hui said: You are the supervisor, you go first, and I will go later.
Wei Guan went down to the palace.
Zhong Hui regretted sending Wei Guan and asked someone to recall Wei Guan.
Wei Guan refused on the grounds of dizziness and pretended to fall to the ground.
When he got out, dozens of messengers chased him.
Wei Guan went outside, drank salt soup, and vomited violently.

All armies responded to the righteous deed and attacked Zhonghui together at dawn.

Wei Quan deployed the generals and the morale of the army was in order.
The soldiers from Deng Ai's headquarters caught up with the broken carriage, rescued Deng Ai, and returned to Chengdu.

When Deng Ai entered Jiangyou, he was about to kill Tian Xu because he refused to join him, but later pardoned him.
When Wei Cui sent Tian Xu, he said to him: You can avenge Jiang You's humiliation.
After the matter was settled, the court discussed granting Wei Guan the title.

Although he used his resourcefulness, he did not take the credit for taking down the enemy flag, so he resolutely refused to accept it.

There are political achievements wherever he works.

When you arrive at your post, please set up Pingzhou, and then take charge of Pingzhou.

summary:
Wei Guan, courtesy name Boyu, was from Anyi, Hedong. His ancestor Wei Hao was recruited for his Confucian learning during the Han Dynasty, and his father Wei Jian served as a minister. Orphaned at ten, Wei Guan was known for his filial piety, quiet temperament, and fairness. He inherited his father's marquis title and began his official career at twenty. He served in various positions, including as a regular attendant, and was known for his competence and legal expertise, judging cases based on reason.

During the conquest of Shu, Wei Guan supervised the armies of Deng Ai and Zhong Hui. Zhong Hui, harboring rebellious intentions, plotted to have Deng Ai kill Wei Guan. Wei Guan, aware of the danger, arrested Deng Ai at night by issuing a false imperial edict. After Zhong Hui rebelled and was killed, Wei Guan, fearing repercussions from his involvement with Zhong Hui, ordered the assassination of Deng Ai and his son. Despite his role, Wei Guan refused credit for the conquest, attributing it to the generals. He was later appointed to high military positions, including General of Zhenxi and Governor of Qingzhou, where he achieved political successes and pacified border tribes like the Wuhuan.

Wei Guan was a strict administrator and a scholar, skilled in cursive calligraphy alongside Suo Jing. He advocated for the abolition of the nine-rank system in favor of ancient rural selection, but his proposal was not implemented. He also attempted to advise Emperor Wu against appointing the simple-minded Crown Prince, but his hints were dismissed. This led to resentment from Empress Jia. Later, due to his son's marital issues and political conflicts, Wei Guan requested retirement and was granted the title of Taibao.

After Emperor Hui ascended, Wei Guan was restored to power but clashed with Prince Sima Zhang of Chu. Empress Jia, resenting Wei Guan's integrity, falsely accused him of plotting rebellion. Sima Zhang arrested Wei Guan and his family, executing them despite his subordinates' advice to resist. Wei Guan was 72. His grandsons Wei Cao and Wei Jie escaped. Du Yu had predicted Wei Guan's downfall due to his role in Deng Ai's death.

Wei Guan's son Wei Heng, a calligrapher, wrote extensively on the history of Chinese scripts, from ancient characters to seal, clerical, and cursive styles. He was also killed in the purge. Wei Guan's other son Wei Zhan served as an official and petitioned to abolish cruel interrogation methods. Wei Jie, Wei Guan's grandson, was a renowned beauty and philosopher, known for his eloquence and admired by contemporaries. He died young at 27.

Zhang Hua, courtesy name Maoxian, was from Fangcheng. Orphaned and poor, he herded sheep but was recognized for his talent. He was learned and wrote the "Ode to the Quail," which gained him fame. He served as a key advisor to Emperor Wu, supporting the conquest of Wu and overseeing logistics. After Wu's fall, he was rewarded but later fell out of favor due to his support for Prince Sima You. He was sent to Youzhou, where he pacified border tribes and received tribute from distant states.

Recalled to court, Zhang Hua became a central figure under Emperor Hui, stabilizing the government despite Empress Jia's tyranny. He opposed the deposition of the crown prince, arguing for caution, but was overruled. He also thwarted a coup by Prince Sima Zhang of Chu. However, his refusal to join Prince Sima Lun of Zhao's rebellion led to his arrest and execution at 69, along with his family. He was known for his vast knowledge, collecting rare books, and his expertise in astronomy and strange phenomena, such as identifying dragon meat and predicting chaos from a bird feather.

Zhang Hua's son Zhang Yi was also killed. His grandson Zhang Yu survived. Liu Bian, a loyal official, warned Zhang Hua of Empress Jia's plots but was not heeded. He later died by poison to avoid execution. The text concludes with a lament for Wei Guan and Zhang Hua, praising their loyalty but noting their tragic ends in a time of chaos.

Taiwei Liu Yi has been retired for more than 20 years with his honest and simple integrity and unchanging nobility. His upright ambitions have become stronger with age.

Now Renjun returns to the mansion as a marquis, his status is above the three divisions, his salary remains the same, and he is given a cane for several cases without having to go to court and the first residence in the mansion.
I will come to consult you on major government affairs of the country and express my opinion.
He died more than a year later at the age of ninety-one. His nickname was Wu.

When one reaches a prominent position and fame, he will always advocate frugality and simplicity and not pursue magnificence.

Liu Gong then withdrew and said to Shi Chong with a smile: "I entered your inner room by mistake."

Although Liu Xiu was in a position of honor and favor, he did not have a mansion to live in. The salary he received was used to support and help relatives.
Although etiquette declined, he himself acted in the right way.

Liu Gong didn't mind if frivolous people laughed at him.
From childhood to old age, he was eager to learn and never let go of books. Even when he became an official, he never left his hands.

He has two sons, Liu Ji and Liu Xia.

Liu Xia was abandoned by the world because of corruption.
Liu Zhi's younger brother Liu Zhi, whose courtesy name is Zifang, is chaste, simple and like an elder brother.

He successively served as the official of Zhongshu Huangmen and the prefect of Yingchuan.
The Pingyuan people once said to people: My conversation with brother Liu Yingchuan made people feel refreshed and inspired, and I did not doze off even after dark.

After entering the imperial court, he served as Secretary Supervisor and concurrently as Nanyang King's Master. He was also appointed as a regular servant of Sanqi, and then moved to serve as Shizhong, Shangshu and Taichang.
The author of "An Explanation of Doubts on Mourning Clothes" contains many points of analysis and explanation.

Able to promote loyalty and good deeds, and to promote retreat.

summary:
Wei Shu, courtesy name Yangyuan, was born in Renchengfan. Orphaned young, he was raised by his maternal grandfather’s Ning family. A feng shui master predicted a noble nephew would be born, and Wei Shu’s intelligence led his grandmother to believe he fulfilled this prophecy. Tall and majestic, he was slow and simple, not valued by villagers. His uncle Wei Heng underestimated him, but Wei Shu remained unbothered. He enjoyed riding, archery, and hunting. Wang Yi of Taiyuan predicted he would become prime minister and supported him. Wei Shu once witnessed a prophecy about a boy who died at fifteen from an ax wound, which later came true. At forty, he studied for a hundred days, passed exams, and became Chief of Mianchi. He later served as Shangshu Lang, where he voluntarily resigned when incompetent officials were dismissed. He excelled in archery, surprising his superior Zhong Yu. As Prime Minister’s aide, he planned wisely on major issues. Emperor Wen valued him, and he governed Yiyang and Rongyang with a good reputation. He served as governor of Jizhou for three years, known for simplicity and benevolence. Emperor Wu rewarded him for honesty. He married three times, all wives predeceased him. In the Taikang era, he advocated for the Fengshan ceremony but was refused. He served as Zuopushe and managed the official department, proposing reforms for imperial marriage gifts. He became Situ and was known for distributing his salary to relatives, leaving no surplus. He appointed Zhou Zhen, who had been avoided due to a superstitious nickname, without disaster. He repeatedly resigned due to illness, eventually being allowed to retire as Juyangzi with honors. He died at eighty-two, posthumously named Kang. His son Wei Hun died young, and his great-nephew Wei Huang succeeded him.

Li Xi, courtesy name Jihe, was from Shangdang Tongtian. He had good conduct, studied widely, and refused recruitment by Guan Ning and others. Emperor Xuan summoned him, but he declined due to his mother’s illness. He later served as a special chariot in Bingzhou, advising Bi Gui against improper conduct. Emperor Jing appointed him as a lieutenant; when asked why he accepted, Li Xi replied he feared the law. He became censor Zhongcheng, feared for his uprightness. He recommended Sun Pu, praised for identifying talent. He was dismissed as Grand Sima but later served as governor of Liangzhou, stabilizing the region and defeating Qiang invaders without prior approval, compared to Han generals. He returned to Beijing, then governed Jizhou and became Sili Xiaowei. When Wei surrendered to Jin, he assisted in ceremonies. He was made Marquis of Qi and accused officials of occupying public rice fields, leading to punishment for Liu You. He served as crown prince’s tutor, teaching diligently. He resigned due to old age, receiving honors. He advocated attacking Liangzhou invaders but was overruled, leading to Liangzhou’s destruction. He was honest and frugal, sharing with relatives. He died, posthumously named Taibao. His son Li Zan succeeded him.

Liu Yi, courtesy name Zizhen, was from Gaotang, Pingyuan. Poor in youth, he sold cow clothes but studied diligently. He was recommended as Xiaolian but refused. He served as Shangshu Lang and Tingweizheng. He predicted Zhong Hui and Deng Ai would conquer Shu but not return, which came true. He wrote “On Chong Rang Lun” advocating humility to correct worldly competition. He argued that humility reveals talent, reduces slander, and stabilizes governance. He criticized the lack of humility in official appointments, leading to mediocrity and corruption. He proposed that officials should recommend the worthy, with selection based on collective recommendations rather than seniority. He served as Taichang and Shangshu. His son Liu Xia’s bribery led to his dismissal. He later served as crown prince’s mentor and Taibao. He resigned at ninety-one, dying soon after. He was frugal, once mistaking Shi Chong’s luxurious toilet for a bedroom. He studied the “Three Biographies” and wrote “Spring and Autumn Regulations.” His sons Liu Ji and Liu Xia were noted, with Liu Xia disgraced for corruption.

Gao Guang, courtesy name Xuan Mao, was from Chenliu. He knew law from youth, serving as Shangshu Lang and governor of Youzhou and Yingchuan. He was appointed Huangsha Yushi for legal expertise. During Sima Lun’s rebellion, he stayed loyal. He served as Tingwei and Shangshu, later following Emperor Hui to Chang'an when others fled. He became Zuopushe and young master. He died of illness, posthumously named Sikong. His son Gao Tao was corrupt and plotted against Sima Yue, leading to his execution. The historian praised Wei Shu and Liu Yi for their wisdom, Li Xi for his boldness, and Gao Guang for his integrity, noting Liu Xia’s corruption as a flaw.

Fu Xuan, whose courtesy name was Xiu Yi, was from Niyang in the north.
His grandfather Fu Xie was the prefect of Hanyang in the Han Dynasty.
His father, Fu Qian, was the governor of Fufeng in the Wei state.
Fu Xuan was lonely and poor when he was young. He was erudite, good at writing articles, and knew the rhythm of music.
He has a strong and upright character and cannot tolerate the shortcomings of others.
He was appointed as a planner in the county, and he was recommended as Xiaolian twice. He was also recruited by the Taiwei, but he did not take up the post.
He took the state examination and passed the scholar examination, and was appointed as a doctor. Due to their reputation at that time, he and Donghai Mushi were selected as writers and compiled Wei books.
Later, he learned about the military affairs of Anton and Weijun. He was transferred to the county magistrate of Wen County and promoted to the prefect of Hongnong. In charge of the post of captain of Diannong School.
He was a competent official, wrote many petitions and made many corrections.
After the establishment of the fifth-grade system, he was granted the title of Baron Quail.
When Emperor Wu Sima Yan was the king of Jin Dynasty, he appointed him as a regular attendant of Sanqi.
When Emperor Wu succeeded to the throne, he was promoted to viscount and promoted to Prince Consort and Commander-in-Chief.
As soon as Emperor Wu came to the throne, he widely adopted outspoken speech and opened up a way of speaking without taboos. Fu Xuan and Huangfu Tao, the regular servant of Sanqi, jointly took charge of the post of admonishment officer.
Fu Xuan Shangshu said: I have heard that the former king came to the world, proclaimed the great teachings, and increased etiquette, righteousness, and moral integrity. The teachings flourished in the court, public opinions became popular below, and everyone followed them together, and everyone had a heart of benevolence and righteousness.
The perished Qin Dynasty destroyed the laws of the ancestors and ruled with harsh laws, and the heart of benevolence and righteousness declined.
In modern times, Emperor Wu of the Wei Dynasty Cao Cao liked magic, so the world valued punishments; Emperor Wen of the Wei Dynasty Cao Pi admired those who knew the truth, so the world despised keeping integrity.
From then on, the imperial court was unable to govern, so empty, useless, and uninhibited discussions flooded the government and the public, so that there was no longer any fair discussion in the world, and the ills of the Qin Dynasty's demise recurred today.
His Majesty's morality is supreme, the dynasty has risen, he has inherited the throne, he has carried forward the teachings of Yao and Shun, he has opened up the path of righteous advice, he has experienced the frugality of Xia and Yu, and after considering the laws and essays of the Shang and Zhou dynasties, I can only sigh, what else am I going to say!
It's just that I didn't recommend courteous ministers with lofty ideals to uphold moral integrity; I didn't remove hypocritical and despicable villains to punish disrespectful ministers, so I still dare to say something.
The edict replied: Recommending ministers with high aspirations and etiquette is an especially important thing today.
So Fu Xuan was asked to draft an edict and present it to him.
Fu Xuan wrote again:
I heard that Shun recommended five ministers and governed without doing anything. This was because he had found the essentials in employing people.
Because there are so many official positions in the world, it is necessary to examine and find the right person.
If you don't find the right person, you will waste a lot of money in one day, not to mention the accumulated time?
"Shangshu Gao Tao Mo" said: Do not leave hundreds of officials vacant, which means that the positions cannot be abandoned for a long time.
Those who have been ill for a hundred days and have not recovered should be allowed to leave their jobs and be given generous courtesy and salary until they recover.
The ministers will not give up their positions in the government, and the country will not be burdened by idle officials. This is the top priority of the king's government.
I heard that the previous emperors managed state affairs according to the division of labor between scholars, farmers, industry and commerce. Each had its own industry and different affairs.
For the children of scholars and above, the Imperial Academy was established for them to educate them, sage teachers were selected to teach them, and they were appointed according to their respective talents.
Agriculture must ensure a bumper harvest, industry must provide sufficient equipment, and merchants must ensure the circulation of goods.
Therefore, the world is huge and there are many people, and no one is empty-handed.
The division of labor is so thorough and complete.
However, there was no fixed division of labor in the Han Dynasty and the Wei Dynasty. The children of hundreds of officials did not learn the Five Classics and Six Arts but engaged in socializing and enjoyed the imperial salary before they knew how to do things. Agricultural and industrial industries were mostly abandoned, and some left their business in pursuit of huge profits. They were in the Imperial Academy in vain, but they did not hear the teachings of the previous kings.
Now that Shengming's politics has begun, the mistakes of the Han and Wei dynasties have not changed. There are many informal officials but no schools. There are many people who are not doing their jobs but few people who are engaged in agriculture. Industrial utensils are not suitable for use.
I think it is urgent to formulate a system to uniformly plan how many people in the world will be scholars, so that they can serve as various officials; how many people will be farmers, so that they can have a year's worth of grain reserves after working for three years; how many people will be workers, so that all kinds of utensils are sufficient; how many people will be engaged in business, so that they can circulate goods.
Respecting Confucianism and Taoism and advocating academics, agriculture as the most noble, and commerce as the lowest, these are all important matters in national affairs.
Previously, Huangfu Tao made a memorial requesting that the appointment of casual officials should be reviewed and let them personally cultivate the land so that the world could enjoy the benefits of sufficient food.
Xia Yu Houji personally engaged in farming, and his blessings were passed down to later generations. Therefore, the "Mingtang" and "Yueling" chapters in the "Book of Rites" record the system of the emperor's land registration.
Yi Yin was a famous official in ancient times and farmed in Youxin; Yan Ying was a senior official in Qi State who also went to the seaside to farm in order to avoid the disaster of Duke Zhuang of Qi.
In the past, sage emperors and capable men were all engaged in agricultural production.
The emperor conferred official positions, and if those officials who were superfluous, idle and had nothing to do were urged to study, they should be allowed to farm. There was no reason to let them sit back and eat the people's food.
Nowadays, there are many civil and military officials, but there are still more who do not serve in their posts. In addition, they serve as soldiers and cannot grow crops, and they are half the number of farmers. In this way, the number of people sitting facing south and receiving salary is three times that of the previous dynasty.
Let the idle and redundant officials work on the farm and collect their taxes, and private individuals will also gain substantial benefits, and the world will not be short of food.
Every family has enough food. A son should be filial, a father should be loving, an elder brother should be friendly, and a younger brother should be filial.
If the world has enough food and clothing, then the teachings of benevolence and righteousness will be implemented without orders.
The key to government is to set up officials according to the total number of people, divide labor until people are assigned their duties, and the division of labor between scholars, farmers, industry and commerce cannot be abandoned at all times.
如果不能精确制定相应的制度，就应考核天下的文武官员，能为长官辅佐的人让他们学习，其余的都让他们务农。

As for the surplus people among the hundreds of industrial and merchant merchants, they were also allowed to engage in agriculture.
What's not enough about farming like this?
"Shang Shu Shun Dian" says: The political performance will be evaluated once every three years, and those who are inferior and promoted to outstanding people will be dismissed after three evaluations.
It can be seen that the promotion order is only after nine years.
Therefore, if you stay in an official position for a long time, you will think about establishing a good education; if you stay in an official position for a short period of time, you will strive to do something with political achievements.
The six-year period is not long enough, and neither demotion nor promotion is thorough enough.
What Huangfu Tao reported was in line with ancient etiquette.
Confucian scholarship was the first priority of Wang Zheng.
I follow Confucianism, value Confucianism, and focus on the selection of Confucian scholars, but I am still worried that education cannot be respected; now I don’t regard Confucianism as a top priority. I am afraid that it is declining day by day without noticing it. Confucius once said: People can promote Tao, but Tao cannot promote people.
In this way, those who respect Confucianism should not only respect Confucian books, but also respect Confucian people.
The so-called emphasis on Confucianism means not indiscriminately educating those who do not follow Confucianism; the so-called emphasis on the selection of Confucian scholars means not indiscriminately appointing people who do not follow Confucianism.
In this way, the school education syllabus is established.
After the book was written, the emperor issued an edict saying: The two ministers' comments are very sincere. It can be said that you want to benefit current affairs.
But those in charge mostly make decisions based on standing rules, so how can we not let you express your anger?
Some of the discussions made by the two regular servants listed out the outline but the items were not detailed. They could also let them tailor it, and then let eight officials including Wu Cao Shangshu, Er Pu She and Zong Ling jointly study it for meticulousness.
Generally speaking, any remarks related to the ruler are the most difficult for ministers to deal with.
And if the monarch cannot adopt it humbly, it will only make the loyal ministers and those who have remonstrated since ancient times be so moved that they become silent.
Every time I think about this, I sigh.
Therefore, the last edict required the ministers to speak out boldly and not to stop, which could almost inspire Hun Mo to correct his mistakes and protect the throne forever.
If there is some merit in what you say and your mood is in line with loyalty, even if there are mistakes in your words and there are gains and losses in your words, you should be forgiven and forgiven.
The ancients did not reject others' behind-the-scenes comments and criticisms, let alone their opinions which are worthy of adoption.
Recently, both Kong and Qi Wulu were convicted of contempt. The reason why I have forgiven them is to let the world know that I, the Jin Dynasty, do not need to taboo speech.
Soon Fu Xuan was promoted to the rank of Attendant.
At first, Fu Xuan recommended Huangfu Tao, but after entering the court, the two had conflicts. Fu Xuan had a dispute with Huangfu Tao over political affairs.
In the fourth year of Taishi's reign, he was appointed as Yushi Zhongcheng.
At that time, there were many floods and droughts. Fu Xuan wrote in another book:
I heard that Emperor Shengming inherited the destiny of heaven, and the weather was not necessarily without disasters. Therefore, Yao had floods for nine years, and Shang Tang had droughts for seven years. They could only use people to relieve them.
Therefore, the floods can be overwhelming and the sky will not be submerged, and the ground will not grow grass but will not be sleepy.
I believe that your majesty has a sage moral character. At present, there are minor floods and droughts, and the people are not suffering from major famines. You issue edicts to respect the destiny of heaven and seek opinions that are in line with the will of heaven. You are as strict with yourself as Xia Yu and Shang Tang. You are as cautious as King Wen of Zhou and do not dare to neglect.
I'm so happy that Shang Shu stated the five things that should be done:
The first thing is: Nowadays, people cultivating are trying to grow a variety of crops, but they cannot mature due to drought, thus wasting their labor and yielding no harvest.
In addition, in the past, when soldiers used the government's cattle, the government would get six-tenths of the harvest, and soldiers would get four-tenths of the harvest. If they used private cattle, they would share it equally with the government. This has been implemented for a long time, and everyone has peace of mind.
Now once the share ratio of government cattle is reduced, the government will get eight-tenths, and the soldiers will get two-tenths. If private cattle are used or there are no cattle, the government will get seven-tenths, and the soldiers will get three-tenths. Everyone will lose what they have gained, and they will definitely be unhappy.
I thought that when a hired soldier would give him four-tenths of the government's cattle and use private cattle to share it equally with the government, then the soldiers all over the world would be happy and cherish the food, and there would be no worries about ruining agriculture and abandoning industry.
The second thing is that although officials with a salary of two thousand dan obeyed the edict to devote themselves to agriculture, they still did not do their duty to benefit from the land.
In the past, the Han Dynasty was not pragmatic in cultivating farmland. After verification, officials with a salary of two thousand dan were killed, and the calculation was calculated by ten.
I think we should reiterate the old laws of the Han Dynasty to warn the counties and counties all over the world and urge them to use the death penalty.
The third thing is: since the Wei Dynasty, no attention has been paid to the construction of water conservancy. The late emperor commanded hundreds of officials and divided those in charge of the river embankments into four divisions. Together with the headquarters, there were five river embankment ministers. Because water conservancy was of great importance, it was not something that one person could consider comprehensively when it was established together with farming.
Now there is only one person in charge of the river bank, who manages water conservancy all over the world and cannot take everything into consideration.

It can be divided into five divisions so that each of them is proficient in the respective ministries.

Recently, the tax on acres of land has been increasing day by day, and the soldiers who farm the fields have become even more powerful. The labor force cannot be rested, and even more than one acre is used, and some are not enough to repay the cost.
It is not that the world is different from the previous one and suffers from disasters. Its shortcomings are precisely due to the lack of rest in labor in order to increase the number of acres.
I privately saw that Shi Hui, the embankment visitor, was very good at water conservancy and farmland, and knew the pros and cons. I asked Zhongshu to summon Shi Hui to carefully inquire about the gains and losses of agricultural water conservancy, which would definitely help.

It is best to consider that these two counties and the established counties belong to Qinzhou, so that Hu Lie can take charge of border affairs.

This is indeed a fundamental matter of governing the country and an urgent task today."
