In the early morning, the troops gathered at Simamen. Emperor Jing was calm both inside and outside, and the arrangements were very strict.
Emperor Xuan said: This son is really good after all.
At the beginning, Emperor Jing secretly took in three thousand scholars who were not afraid of death and scattered them among the people. When they arrived, they gathered them together in one morning. No one knew where these people came from.
After the incident subsided, because of his meritorious service, he was granted the title of Marquis of Changping Township, with a population of 1,000 households, and was later granted the title of General of Wei.
When Emperor Xuan died, people who discussed politics said: Yi Yin is dead, and Yi Zhi will inherit the business. The emperor appointed Emperor Jing as the general of the Fu army to assist in government affairs.
In the spring and first month of the fourth year of Wei Jiaping's reign, he was promoted to general and granted the title of Shizhong. He held the title of Commander-in-Chief, commanded all the Chinese and foreign armies, and recorded affairs of the Shangshu.
Order the officials to recommend talents, clarify the hierarchy between the young and the elderly, sympathize with the poor and lonely, and clean up those who have been abandoned.
Zhuge Dan, Mu Qiujian, Wang Chang, Chen Tai, and Hu Zun were appointed governors of the four directions; Wang Ji, Zhou Tai, Deng Ai, and Shi Bao were in charge of the prefectures and counties; Lu Yu and Li Feng were in charge of elections; Fu Gu and Yu Song participated in making plans; Zhong Hui, Xia Houxuan, Wang Su, Chen Ben, Meng Kang, Tan Feng, and Zhang Ji participated in the court meetings. They were admired by all the people and respected inside and outside the court.
Occasionally, there were people who asked for changes in the system. Emperor Jing said: "As if you don't know anything, you obey the laws of God and do it. This is what the poet praises."
The rules and regulations of three generations of ancestors should be observed; unless there is a war, they cannot be changed at will.
In the summer and May of the fifth year, Zhuge Ke, the Taifu of Wu State, besieged Xincheng. The court was worried that he would divide his troops to invade Huaisi and planned to guard various waterway ports.
Emperor Jing said: Zhuge Ke had recently gained power in Wu State, and wanted to seek temporary benefits. He gathered his troops in Hefei, hoping that he would succeed by luck and had no energy to cause trouble in Qingxu.
Besides, there is not one waterway port. If there are more guards, more troops will be needed. If there are fewer guards, it will not be enough to defend against the enemy.

Emperor Jing sent General Guanqiu Jian, the general of Zhendong, Sai Zhen, the governor of Nuosu, and others to resist the enemy.
Dan Qiu Jian and Sai Zhen requested to go out to fight. Emperor Jing said: Zhuge Ke went all out to penetrate our side and put the army in danger. Their sharp edge was difficult to withstand.
Besides, the new city is small and strong, making it difficult for enemy troops to attack.
So he ordered the generals to build high forts to defend.
After several months of stalemate, Zhuge Ke's siege force was exhausted, and more than half of his troops were killed or injured.
Emperor Jing ordered Governor Wen Lian to lead his elite troops to Heyu to intercept the enemy's retreat, and Wu Danjun led the generals as his successors.
Jiang prisoner fled out of fear. Sai Xun went up to attack and defeated the enemy army, killing more than 10,000 enemies.
In the spring and first month of the first year of the fifth year, the emperor and Zhongshu Ling Li Feng, the Queen's father Guanglu doctor Zhang Ji, Huangmen Supervisor Su Shuo, Yongning Department Ling Leqian, red servant Liu Zhili and others planned to use Taichang Xing Lou Sai to replace Emperor Jing to assist the government.

Emperor Jing was angry and sent warriors to beat him to death with sword-tipped darts.
The arrest of Xia Houxuan, Zhang Ji and others reduced the number of three clans.

The general inspector worshiped the laws of heaven and put them under the criminal law.
Zhou Bo surrendered to the Lu family, and Huo Guang captured Shangxuan's achievements, which are difficult to surpass.
9,000 additional households were added to the general's food estates, adding to the previous total of 40,000 households.
Emperor Jing declined and refused to accept.
The emperor felt deeply unsafe because Xia Houxuan and Zhang Ji were executed.
Liangcha was also worried about causing disaster and secretly planned to depose and re-establish the emperor, so he secretly advised the Empress Dowager Wei Yongning in a polite way.
In Jiaxu, the ninth month of autumn, the Empress Dowager issued an order: The emperor was too old to manage the complicated government affairs himself. He indulged in favors from the inner palace, indulged in lewdness, approached actors and actresses every day, indulged their ugly behavior, welcomed the concubine's family to stay in the inner palace, destroyed the morality between people, and disturbed the moral integrity of men and women.
He was coerced by a group of villains and was about to endanger the country, so he could not continue to worship the ancestral temple.
Emperor Jing convened a gathering of ministers for discussion, and said with tears: "The Queen Mother's order is this, what should we do with the royal family?"
The ministers all said: Yi Yin exiled Taijia to bring peace to Yin, Huo Guang deposed the king of Changyi to bring peace to Mo, weighed the priorities, stabilized the country, and brought peace to the world.
The Yin and Han dynasties did this in ancient times, and Ming Gong should do the same today. All matters today must be obeyed by Ming Gong's orders.
Emperor Jing said: Everyone has high expectations for me, how can I dare to evade them?
So he and all the ministers reported to the Queen Mother: "I heard that the emperor rescues and nourishes the people and makes the world stable for a long time."
The emperor was too old to manage the complicated government affairs himself, so he asked the young actors Guo Huai, Yuan Xin and others to expose their bodies and play lewd games every day.
She also dressed up as a coquettish woman from Liaodong under the watchful eye, and passers-by covered their eyes.
Linghu Jing, the merchant of the Qing Dynasty, admonished the emperor, but the emperor burned him with iron.
When the Queen Mother encountered the funeral of Lord Heyang, the Emperor laughed and entertained as usual.
Pang Xi, the Shang Cheng of the Qing Dynasty, advised the emperor, but the emperor did not listen.
The Queen Mother returned to the North Palace and killed Zhang Meiren. The Emperor was very resentful.
Pang Xi remonstrated, but the emperor was angry and shot Pang Xi with a slingshot.
Whenever documents were delivered, the emperor would not read them.
The Queen Mother ordered the Emperor to give lectures in Shiqian Hall, but the Emperor refused to comply.
He cannot carry on the royal line.
The minister requested that the emperor's seal be taken back according to the practice of Huo Guang in the Han Dynasty, and let him return to his fiefdom as the king of Qi.
The Empress Dowager accurately reported that the relevant officials used cattle, sheep, and pigs as sacrifices to write simple policies and report to the ancestral temple. King Qi boarded the royal attendant's car, and the ministers followed him to Xiyemen.
Emperor Jing cried and said: My ancestors have received special treatment from past dynasties. When the late emperor was dying, he sent Shao to support him. I feel ashamed of my heavy responsibility and cannot teach people to do good or correct their mistakes.
Dear ministers, if you want to use ancient laws and consider the long-term interests of the country, you would rather betray the emperor himself and sacrifice the royal ancestral temple.
So he sent envoys holding talismans to escort him, and lived in Chongmen, Hanoi, to kill Guo Huai, Yuan Xin and others.
On the same day, he discussed with the ministers how to establish a new king.
Emperor Jing said: There is no peace in the world today, and two enemy countries are vying for victory. The monarchs of the four seas must be wise and sage people.
Cao Ju, King of Pengcheng, was the son of Taizu. In terms of wisdom, he was benevolent, sage, and fair. In terms of age, he was the eldest brother in the royal family.

King Shuhai Ding, the younger brother of Emperor Ming, planned to make his son Cao Mao, the Duke of Gaogui Township.
Emperor Jing persisted in arguing but failed, so he followed the Queen Mother's order and sent people to Yuancheng to welcome Gaogui Xiang Gong as the emperor, and changed his reign to Zhengyuan.
When the emperor accepted the seal, he was lazy and raised his feet very high. Emperor Jing was worried when he heard about it.
When the great court meeting was about to be held, Emperor Jing taught the emperor: A wise king values ​​the beginning and respects the beginning with integrity. This is what the ancients were cautious about.
Tomorrow, facing the great court meeting, everyone will look at the emperor's dignified appearance, and the minister will listen to the sweet voice.
The Book of Songs says: What is shown to people is not frivolous and can be imitated.
"Book of Changes" says: If you say something good, someone thousands of miles away will respond.
Although the etiquette is thorough and complete, it should also be treated with respect and caution in order to be in line with the expectations of the world.
Guisi, the emperor issued an edict saying: I heard that a monarch who establishes a foundation must have capable ministers; an emperor who abides by established laws must also rely on ministers who can correct and assist.

Think deeply about grand discussions, first establish wise strategies, weigh the priorities, stabilize the country, and help me ascend to the throne, the ancestral temple will be peaceful, and all people will be happy and dependent.

The prosperous age when criminal law was put aside actually came from this.
We should follow the spirit of the ancestors who were not ashamed to ask questions, so that lectures and poems can be heard frequently, and the words of the classics can be stated around them every day.
At that time, the emperor loved luxury and extravagance, and Emperor Jing advised him: "When you first get involved in government affairs, you should advocate simplicity."

Ordered to send elite troops to pursue Wen Qin.

Order the ministers to discuss the funeral arrangements.
Relevant officials discussed that Emperor Jing's loyalty had stabilized the country and his achievements had saved the world, so Huo Guang's precedent should be followed. Cao Shuang and others led their troops to retreat, and as expected, Fei Zhang led his troops to pursue them straight to the Three Ridges. After a battle and many obstacles, the Wei army was able to pass.

Emperor Wen was promoted to the general of Anxi and held a festival, and he stationed troops in Guanzhong to control the military affairs.
Guo Huai attacked Jiang Wei's deputy general Ju'an in Qudi, and the outcome was indecisive for a long time.
Emperor Wen then marched to occupy the Great Wall and ran south to Luo Valley to confuse the enemy.

Emperor Wen was transferred to General Anshu and Chijie to guard Xuchang.

Emperor Wen was sent to temporarily serve as General of the Expedition to the West and stationed in Chang'an.
Chen Tai, the governor of Yongzhou, planned to occupy Didao before the enemy came. Just when the Qiang and Hu tribes in Xinping rebelled, Emperor Wen defeated them and showed off his troops in Lingzhou. The enemies in the north were shocked and frightened, and the rebels surrendered.
Because of his meritorious service, he was again granted the title of Xincheng Rural Marquis.
When Gaogui Township was established as the king, because Saitong participated in the formulation of the strategy, he was granted the title of Gaodu Marquis and was granted the title of two additional households in the city.
When Tan Qiujian and Wen Qin rebelled, the army marched eastward. Emperor Wen served as the leader of the army and stayed behind to guard Luoyang.
When Emperor Jing became seriously ill, Emperor Wen went to visit him from Kyoto and was appointed General of the Guard.
After Emperor Jing died, the emperor ordered Emperor Wen to guard Xuchang, and Shangshu Su led the Sixth Army back to the capital.
Saitong adopted the strategy of attacking the bell box and led his army back.
When he arrived in Luoyang, he was promoted to the rank of general, and was added to the rank of attendant. He was in charge of all the Chinese and foreign armies, recorded the affairs of the ministers, assisted in the affairs of the court, and went to the palace wearing swords and shoes.
Emperor Wen resolutely refused to accept it.
In the first month of spring of the first year of Ju Ling's reign, he was granted the title of Grand Governor, and there was no need to give his name when performing duties.
In the sixth month of summer, he was granted the title of Duke of Gaodu, with a circumference of seven hundred miles, plus nine tins, an ax and cymbals, and the title of Grand Governor. He wore a sword and wore shoes to go to the palace.
And he firmly refused to accept it.
In autumn and August, Geng Shen added fake yellow iron and enfeoffed three more counties.

We should work together with all parties to defeat Zhuge Dan with complete victory.

Your Majesty should temporarily visit the battlefield in person so that the soldiers can rely on the emperor's reputation.

So he ordered the encirclement to be closed, and sent the sick and weak in batches to Huaibei to obtain supplies. They opened a warehouse and distributed soybeans to the sergeants, three liters per person.

He refused high honors but was eventually made Duke of Gaodu with nine tins.

He defeated Wu reinforcements, and after a long siege, Zhuge Dan was killed. He was made Duke of Jin with nine tins, but resigned nine times. Zhong Hui rebelled but was killed. Emperor Wen was made King of Jin, with twenty counties. He established five-class titles and sent envoys to Wu. He died at age 55, posthumously named King Wen, later Emperor Wen. His achievements included pacifying rebellions, conquering Shu, and stabilizing the realm, though he was criticized for regicide.

summary:
Emperor Mu, named Sima Dan, became emperor at age two after his father Emperor Kang's death. His mother, the Empress Dowager, served as regent. During his reign, there were numerous military campaigns, rebellions, and natural disasters. Key events included Huan Wen's successful attack on Shu, the rebellion of Fan Wen, and the deaths of various generals and officials. The state of Zhao under Shi Jilong and later his sons experienced internal turmoil, while Murong Huang and his son Murong Jun established the state of Yan. There were also conflicts with Fu Jian, who later proclaimed himself emperor of Qin. The text records a series of battles, surrenders, and changes in leadership across various regions, including Liangzhou and Yizhou. Emperor Mu died at age nineteen and was buried in Yongping Mausoleum.

Emperor Ai, named Sima Pi, succeeded Emperor Mu. He was the eldest son of Emperor Cheng. The Empress Dowager declared him the rightful heir due to Emperor Mu's lack of an heir. His reign was marked by continued conflicts with Murong Wei's forces, who captured Luoyang, and the ongoing influence of Huan Wen. Emperor Ai was known for his interest in immortality, consuming elixirs that poisoned him and rendered him unable to govern, leading the Empress Dowager to resume regency. He died at age twenty-five and was buried in Anping Mausoleum.

The Deposed Emperor, Sima Yi, was the half-brother of Emperor Ai. He ascended the throne after Emperor Ai's death without an heir, as decreed by the Empress Dowager. His reign saw further wars with Murong Wei and Fu Jian. Huan Wen, seeking to increase his power after a failed military campaign, deposed the emperor. Huan Wen spread rumors about the emperor's impotence and illicit affairs to justify the deposition. The emperor was deposed as the King of Donghai and later granted the title of Duke of Haixi County. He was moved to Wu County, where he lived in fear, avoiding political involvement and indulging in pleasure to preserve his life. He died at age forty-five. The text concludes with a historical commentary praising Emperor Mu's stable early reign, Emperor Ai's generosity, and the deposed emperor's wisdom in refusing a plot to restore him to the throne.

summary:
Emperor Yuan, named Sima Rui, was born in Luoyang in 276 CE with auspicious signs. He succeeded as King of Langya at fifteen and maintained a cautious, thrifty demeanor during the political turmoil of Emperor Hui's reign, avoiding disaster. Initially unrecognized for his talents, only servant Ji Shao perceived his extraordinary nature. He held various military posts, including General of the Left and General of the Auxiliary State, and participated in campaigns against Sima Ying. After a failed battle, he narrowly escaped capture during a thunderstorm. Following Sima Yue's westward march, Emperor Yuan adopted Wang Dao's strategy and established his base in Jianye, winning the loyalty of Jiangdong's elite through respectful governance.

After Emperor Huai was captured, Emperor Yuan was recommended as alliance leader and later appointed Prime Minister Zuo. He pacified Jiangdong, defeating rebels like Sun Bi and Du Zeng. When Chang'an fell, he mobilized troops and received auspicious signs, including a jade seal reading "Longevity for Ten Thousand Years." In 318 CE, Emperor Min's edict authorized him to govern, and after mourning, he accepted the title of King of Jin. He ascended the throne on the ninth day of the third month, implementing a general amnesty and establishing a bureaucracy in Jiankang. He rejected auspicious omens, stating his focus on self-blame for state failures.

Emperor Yuan's reign faced challenges from Shi Le's invasions, repelled by General Zu Ti. He issued proclamations offering rewards for Shi Jilong's head. He mourned ministers Zhu Song and Gu Qiu despite protocol, emphasizing the need for special rites during national decline. In 319 CE, after Emperor Min's death, he assumed the imperial title, issuing edicts on governance, frugality, and moral conduct. He banned extravagant gifts and promoted merit-based evaluations. Natural disasters like droughts and earthquakes prompted personal prayers and relief efforts. He dealt with rebellions, including those by Zhou Fu and Xu Gong, and faced military defeats against Shi Le's forces.

In 322 CE, Wang Dun rebelled, capturing Stone City and defeating imperial forces. Emperor Yuan offered to abdicate, but Wang Dun assumed dictatorial powers, killing officials like Dai Ruosi and Zhou Qiye. Emperor Yuan died in the inner hall at age forty-seven, buried in Jianping Mausoleum with the temple name Zhongzong. He was known for simplicity and frugality, once pouring away wine after Wang Dao's admonition and using plain curtains instead of expensive ones. He refused costly gifts for his concubine and discouraged excessive construction. However, his reign was plagued by weak military control and internal strife, leading to his death from sorrow and anger.

Historical accounts note prophecies of imperial destiny in Jinling, fulfilled when Emperor Yuan crossed the Yangtze River 526 years after Qin Shihuang. A nursery rhyme about five horses crossing the river symbolized the southern migration of kings, with Emperor Yuan becoming the dragon. Rumors suggested his birth resulted from an affair, fulfilling the "ox succeeds the horse" prophecy. Despite initial successes, the state's reliance on powerful generals led to internal conflicts, and Emperor Yuan's efforts to restore order ultimately failed, with later historians attributing the dynasty's decline to fate and flawed succession.

summary:
Emperor An, named Dezong, was the eldest son of Emperor Xiaowu. He was established as crown prince in 387 and ascended the throne in 396 after his father's death, granting amnesty to the empire. He appointed Prince Daozi of Kuaiji as regent. During his reign, numerous rebellions and military conflicts occurred across the realm. Various warlords declared themselves rulers, including Wu Gu who founded Southern Liang, and Duan Ye who proclaimed himself Liangzhou Mu. Wang Gong and Yu Kai raised troops against officials Wang Guobao and Wang Xu, leading to their executions to appease the rebels.

The following years saw continued turmoil. Murong Xiang and Murong Lin successively claimed imperial titles. Wang Gong, Yu Kai, Yin Zhongkan, Huan Xuan, and Yang Quanqi rebelled. Huan Xuan defeated imperial forces at Baishi. The court sent Yuan Xian, Wang Shi, and Xie Yan to attack Huan Xuan and others. Liu Laozhi's son defeated Wang Gong, who was captured and beheaded. Huan Xuan became alliance leader. Tuoba Gui of Wei ascended the throne as Tianxing. Sun En, a demon thief, captured Kuaiji, killing several officials. The court sent Xie Yan and Liu Laozhi to repel him.

In 402, Huan Xuan defeated the imperial army at Gushu. Liu Laozhi betrayed and surrendered to Huan Xuan. The imperial army was defeated at Xinting, with Prince Yuanxian of Kuaiji and others killed. Huan Xuan appointed himself to various high positions and moved Prince Daozi to Ancheng. In 403, Huan Xuan usurped the throne, making the emperor a prisoner in Xunyang. In 404, Liu Yu raised troops against Huan Xuan, defeating his forces. Huan Xuan fled with Emperor An but was eventually beheaded. The emperor returned to the capital.

Emperor An was described as unintelligent, unable to speak from childhood, incapable of distinguishing seasons or caring for himself. This explains why Huan Xuan did not kill him during the usurpation. A prophecy stated there would be two emperors after the Ming Dynasty. Liu Yu, wanting to claim the throne, secretly had Emperor An strangled in 418 at age thirty-seven, establishing Emperor Gong to fulfill the prophecy.

Emperor Gong, named Dewen, was Emperor An's half-brother. He had been enfeoffed as King of Langxie and held various positions including General of the Central Army and Grand Sima. After Huan Xuan's defeat, he returned to his former position. In 419, following Emperor An's death, Liu Yu issued a false edict proclaiming Emperor Gong's succession. In 420, following Liu Yu's instructions, Fu Liang persuaded Emperor Gong to abdicate. The emperor willingly complied, stating the Jin family had long lost the empire. He wrote the abdication edict on red paper. Liu Yu made him King of Lingling. In 422, Liu Yu sent soldiers who killed Emperor Gong in his inner chamber at age thirty-six.

As a youth, Emperor Gong had been cruel and impetuous, once shooting horses for sport until someone noted that "Ma" (horse) was the imperial surname, making such killing unlucky. He then regretted his actions and became a devout Buddhist, casting a bronze statue and personally escorting it to Waguan Temple. He was known for his courtesy in serving his brother Emperor An, caring for his daily needs.

Emperor Hui Ji, named Zhong and styled Zhengdu, was the second son of Emperor Wu. He was made crown prince at age nine in the third year of Taishi and ascended the throne on April 20, the first year of Taixi, upon Emperor Wu's death. He granted amnesty, changed the reign name to Yongxi, honored Empress Yang as empress dowager, and established Crown Prince Jia as empress. Emperor Wu was buried in Junyang Mausoleum on May 13. Officials and participants in the funeral received rank promotions, taxes were exempted for a year, and high-ranking officials were granted titles. Taiwei Yang Jun was appointed Taifu to assist in governance.

In the eighth month, Sima Wei, King of Guangling, was made crown prince, with He Shao, Wang Rong, and Yang Ji as his tutors. Generals were sent to garrison various regions. In winter, Sikong Shijian became Taiwei, and Sima Tai, King of Longxi, became Sikong. In the first year of Yongping, Emperor Hui issued an edict expressing his humility and fear, changing the reign name from Yongxi to Yongping. He forbade officials from visiting the mausoleum, and the crown prince came of age and was crowned. In the second month, silks were given to the prince, and Sima Wei and Sima Yun visited. In the third month, Grand Tutor Yang Jun and others were killed, and their clans were exterminated. Empress Jia deposed the empress dowager and killed her mother. Sima Liang, King of Runan, was made Dazai to assist in government, and other nobles received appointments. Over a thousand people were ennobled, but Sima Yao and Sima Mao were later dismissed.

In the fourth month, Sima Xu, King of Liang, was appointed general, and Ruan Tan became governor. In the fifth month, Sima Gui, King of Piling, died, and taxes were exempted for the elderly and widowed. In the sixth month, Empress Jia ordered Sima Wei to kill Sima Liang and Sima Wei, then executed Sima Wei for unauthorized killings. In the seventh month, ten counties were divided into Jiangzhou. In the eighth month, Sima Lun, King of Zhao, and Sima Yong, King of Hejian, received military commands. Sima Kui moved to Changshan, and Ma Fan and Sima Yue were made kings. In the ninth month, Sima Jian, King of Qin, died. In the twelfth month, an earthquake struck the capital. That year, seventeen Dongyi countries and twenty-four Nanyi tribes made contact.

In the second year, Empress Jia killed the empress dowager. In the eighth month, a general amnesty was declared. In the ninth month, Sima Dan, King of Zhongshan, died. In the eleventh month, a great plague occurred. Hail destroyed crops in Pei. In the third year, hail fell in Xingyang and Hongnong. In the fourth year, Shi Jian died, and natural disasters struck Shu and Shouchun. The Xiongnu Hao San rebelled but later surrendered and was killed. Earthquakes and landslides caused casualties and famine. In the fifth year, a comet appeared, and earthquakes, hail, and strong winds caused damage. A fire destroyed the arsenal. Floods struck several provinces, and the emperor sent censors to provide relief. In the sixth year, amnesty was declared, and officials died or were appointed. Earthquakes, frost, and blood on the ground occurred. Floods and rebellions by the Xiongnu and Di peoples led to battles and sieges. Famine and plague struck Guanzhong. In the seventh year, Zhou Chu died in battle, and hail, plague, drought, and famine continued. The emperor allowed the sale of children. summary:
In the past, sages used the xuanji to simulate the North Star's movement, observing the sky to measure the sun's shadow and the motions of the sun, moon, and five planets. They divided celestial areas on earth, established calendars, taught agricultural seasons, and promoted prosperity, linking yin and yang harmony with governance. Observing celestial phenomena to form hexagrams and adding leap months to describe seasonal changes became the essence of calendrical science. Emperor Yan distinguished eight seasons for agriculture, Xuanyuan established principles for writing, and appointed Xihe to count the sun, Chang Yi to track the moon, and astrological Qi in specific regions. Rong Cheng synthesized these methods, examined solar terms and celestial phenomena, established the five elements, studied solar and lunar movements, and wrote "Adjusting the Calendar." During the Shaowu period, Fengniao managed the calendar; in Zhuanxu's time, Nanzheng oversaw astronomy; in the Tao and Tang Dynasties, Xi Yuhe was in charge; and in Yao's era, Yu and Shun inherited the calendar. By the Xia, Shang, and Zhou dynasties, their Zhengshuo and calendars differed. The "Biography" notes that when the big Mars appears, it is March in Xia, April in Shang, and May in Zhou. Emperors set sun officials, and princes set sun emperors to harmonize nations and coordinate celestial bodies, ensuring cold and heat, yin and yang cycles, and solar terms aligned with the sun's position without error.

With the Zhou Dynasty's decline, historians failed in their duties, and astronomical personnel dispersed, leaving good and bad omens unmonitored. The Qin State annexed the world, respected the five elements' mutual interdependence, believed in water virtue's auspicious response, and took October as the first month. The Han family followed the Qin calendar for over a hundred years until Emperor Wu ordered Sima Qian and others to create the "Han Calendar," adopting Xia Zheng. Later, Liu Xin created the "Santong Li" to explain the "Zuo Zhuan," but his explanations were untrue, and Ban Gu was misled. Emperor Guangwu established Shuhan, and Zhu Fu repeatedly noted calendar errors, but the world's instability prevented detailed examination. In the late Yongping period, the "Four Point Calendar" was used, completed over seventy years later. During the Guanghe period, Liu Hong and Cai Yong revised the legal calendar, and Sima Biao compiled the "Book of the Later Han Dynasty" based on their work. Liu Hong studied ancient calendars, investigated solar, lunar, and planetary movements, and found the "Four Points Calendar" inaccurate due to too many points. He used 589 as the rule and 145 as fighting points, writing the "Qian Xiang Method," which aligned with ancient records and current observations. He created techniques for delayed solar movement and examined lunar motion, with the white path intersecting the ecliptic, achieving greater precision than previous calendars.

In the first year of Jian'an, Zheng Xuan studied Liu Hong's calendar and annotated it. During the Huangchu period, Gao Tanglong discussed the calendar, and Han Yi believed the "Qianxiang Calendar" reduced too many dou points, creating the "Huang Chu Li" with 4,883 as the rule and 1,205 as dou points. Chen Qun submitted a report noting the calendar's complexity and debates among Confucian scholars. In the first year of Huangchu, the "Four Points Calendar" was replaced due to errors, and Han Yi compared his calendar with the "Qianxiang Calendar" for three years, studying solar and lunar motions but unable to decide differences. The emperor ordered astronomical instruments to test accuracy over a year. Xu Zhi believed Liu Hong's lunar motion method had been used for over 40 years with errors exceeding an hour. Sun Qin noted that Sima Qian's Taichu Calendar was rough, and Liu Xin created the Santong Calendar. The "Four Points Calendar" often erred, with eclipses differing by half a day. Liu Hong's Qianxiang Calendar calculated lunar and planetary motions consistently with actual phenomena. Dong Ba stated that sages used sundial shadows, strings, and angles to test calendars, with Xian, Wang, Jian, and Fu as key points. Xu Yue noted that Liu Xuan researched for over 20 years, referencing Han calendars and using Liangyi Guojian to examine moon phases. The moon runs for nine years with an end called the Nine Paths; nine chapters include 171 years, and nine-nine 81 chapters with 567 divided into nine endings, advancing and retreating four degrees and five minutes in front of the Ox constellation. To align with the "Four Points Calendar," subtract one sixty-three points. Examining Xian and Wang requires measuring the moon's position at dawn and dusk.

The key to testing the calendar lies in solar eclipses. During the Xiping period, Liu Hong predicted a solar eclipse at Chen hour, eclipsing two-thirds from bottom to top, which proved accurate, making him famous. Five solar and lunar eclipses were tested: four in the "Qian Xiang Calendar" and one in the "Huang Chu Li." Han Yi challenged Xu Yue, who replied that the "Qianxiang Calendar" had a unique message correction method. Jupiter, Saturn, Venus, and Mercury appearances and concealments were tested 15 times, with the "Qian Xiang Calendar" close to the sky seven times and the "Huang Chu Li" five times. Li En noted differences in celestial degrees and lunar eclipses. Dong Ba recalled that Fuxi created the Bagua, Huangdi wrote "Calendar Calendar," and after 11 generations and 5,000 years, seven calendars were used. Zhuanxu used Mengchun as the calendar year, while Tang's "Yin Calendar" used the winter solstice. Xia inherited Yao and Shun's methods. Yang Wei argued that within 60 days, calendar precision can be known without waiting ten years, but without following calendar laws, it is like using no rules or scales. Han Yi formulated his calendar based on Liu Hong's method but abandoned his theories, preventing Liu Hong's wonders from being passed down. The verification proposal was not finalized due to the emperor's death.

In the first year of Jingchu, Yang Wei formulated the "Jingchu Calendar," which was implemented with Chou month as the first month. After the emperor's death, Xia Zheng was reinstated. The Liu family in Shu used the "Four Points Calendar," while Wu used the "Qianxiang Calendar" until its fall. Emperor Wu of Jin followed the "Jingchu Li," renaming it "Taishi Li." Yang Wei's calendar was inaccurate for the five planets, so the Jin replaced its calculation method with the "Qianxiang Calendar." All subsequent calendars referred to the "Qianxiang Calendar," adding or subtracting basic data. Liu Hong's calendar technique became the model for later generations. The text then details the Shangyuan era, various constants (e.g., Qianfa 1,178, Huitong 7,171, Jifa 589), and methods for calculating years, months, days, solar terms, leap months, lunar phases, eclipses, and planetary positions. It includes formulas for determining the winter solstice, twenty-four Qi, leap months, and the positions of the sun, moon, and five planets (Jupiter, Mars, Saturn, Venus, Mercury). The methods involve multiplying and dividing specific constants to find degrees, remainders, and celestial positions, with adjustments for retrograde motion, conjunctions, and eclipses. The text concludes with detailed steps for calculating planetary appearances, conjunctions, and movements, including direct and retrograde motion, with specific numbers for each planet's cycles and degrees.

The evolution of ritual and ceremonial systems in ancient China, emphasizing their role in maintaining social order and moral conduct. Humans possess spiritual energy and emotions, and sages established rituals to control arrogance, worship heaven and earth, and define social hierarchies, thereby ensuring good governance. The text references the concept that self-restraint and a return to ritual can lead to universal benevolence.

Historically, early practices were simple, with modest ambitions and frugal customs. Over time, rulers like Xuanyuan, Zhuanxu, Yao, and Shun developed systems, which were perfected during the Zhou dynasty with detailed regulations and rituals. However, by the end of the Zhou, social customs declined, and the king's rule weakened, leading to a loss of proper etiquette. Confucius later studied ancient models but could not implement his ideas due to a lack of a wise ruler.

The text then discusses the Han dynasty's efforts to revive rituals, noting that Emperor Wen abolished the two-year mourning period, and Emperor Guangwu combined suburban sacrifices. During the Yuanding and Yongping eras, education and Confucianism were promoted. However, later periods saw a decline in ritual and music systems, with a focus on glitz, though sacrificial rites were generally preserved. The Cao and Wei dynasties saw improvements, with scholars like Wang Sheng and Gao Tanglong studying ancient texts.

During the Wei and Jin dynasties, there were debates and reforms in sacrificial practices. For example, in the first year of Jingchu, a round mound was built for sacrifices, and Emperor Wu of Jin sought to promote etiquette. The text details various rituals, including suburban sacrifices, Mingtang ceremonies, and the worship of the Five Emperors. It also discusses the establishment of the northern suburbs and the integration of various gods into the sacrificial system.

The text delves into specific debates, such as the correct duration of mourning (twenty-seven months according to Zheng Xuan, twenty-five according to Wang Su) and the proper rituals for mourning different relatives. It highlights the confusion and differing interpretations of mourning rites, emphasizing the need for clear regulations. The text also covers the rituals for solar eclipses, including the use of red scarves and drums to save the sun, and the debates over whether to cancel court meetings during eclipses.

The text discusses the establishment of temples and sacrifices for ancestors, including the seven-temple system and the placement of divine tablets. It notes that during the Jin dynasty, the ancestral temple was rebuilt, and the system of moving divine tablets based on generational ties was implemented. The text also covers the rituals for the queen's silkworm ceremony and the emperor's plowing ceremony, which were meant to promote agriculture and filial piety.

Finally, the text addresses the sacrifices to various gods, including the Six Sects, the Five Mountains, and the Four Rivers. It notes that during the Eastern Jin dynasty, many rituals were abandoned or simplified due to political turmoil. The text concludes with a discussion of the proper rituals for mourning and the importance of adhering to ancient customs while adapting to contemporary circumstances.

The Wei and Jin dynasties saw further legal codification, with the Wei Code creating 18 chapters and the Jin Code expanding to 21 chapters, aiming to simplify and standardize laws.

summary:
Celestial bodies and their movements as omens reflecting the state of human affairs, particularly the ruler's virtue and the kingdom's stability. The sun, as strong yang energy, symbolizes the king. Its brightness or dimness, color changes, and phenomena like sunspots, eclipses, or multiple suns indicate the ruler's virtue, ministerial loyalty, or impending disaster. A bright sun signifies a prosperous country; a dim or red sun without light warns of unvirtuous rulers and chaotic ministers. Solar eclipses represent yin (ministers) invading yang (the ruler), foretelling national ruin. The moon, as lunar essence and symbol of the heroine (queen or empress), reflects the conduct of ministers and women in power. Its abnormal color, brightness during the day, or multiple moons signify treachery, power struggles, war, and famine.

The text then details the five planets—Year Star (Jupiter), Sparkling Deluder (Mars), Quelling Star (Saturn), Grand White (Venus), and Chronogram (Mercury)—each associated with a season, element, virtue, and aspect of governance. Their positions, movements, colors, and conjunctions predict the rise and fall of states, agricultural yields, war, and the fate of rulers and ministers. For example, Jupiter governs benevolence and agriculture; its proper movement brings harvests, while deviation causes trouble. Mars governs propriety and war; its abnormal appearance signals military chaos, banditry, and death. Saturn represents integrity and the emperor; its movement indicates the ruler's virtue or lack thereof. Venus governs morality and speech; its advance and retreat predict war outcomes. Mercury governs wisdom and punishment; its untimely appearance brings famine and military revolt. Conjunctions of planets, such as Jupiter and Saturn meeting, foretell civil strife and famine, while Venus and Mars meeting indicate war and mourning.

The text also covers comets, guest stars, meteors, and various atmospheric phenomena (clouds, rainbows, halos) as omens. Comets, or "broom stars," signify sweeping away the old and ushering in the new, often bringing war and floods. Specific comets like the "Red You Flag" or "Heavenly Spear" portend rebellion, military defeat, or the death of a ruler. Guest stars like the "Old Man Star" or "Zhou Bo Star" indicate famine or prosperity. Meteors, as "angels," foretell events based on their size, speed, and direction; their fall marks war or the death of a general. Atmospheric qi, such as the "Emperor's Qi" (red inside, yellow outside) or the "Qi of a Fierce General" (like a dragon or beast), signal the rise of a king or a military leader. Cloud formations, like "formation clouds" or "hook clouds," predict war, and their colors (white for mourning, red for war, etc.) determine the nature of the event.

**Qingzhou** is recorded in the "Yu Gong" as one of twelve pastoralist areas between Shuhai and Mount Tai. It was named for its eastern polar location and green color. Emperor Wu of Han established it as one of thirteen states, a designation that continued through the Jin Dynasty. The province governed six counties, 37 counties, and 53,000 households. Its history includes periods under the Shi family, occupation by Duan Chong, and control by Murong Ke and Fu's forces. After the Yongjia Rebellion, the imperial court established Youzhou here. Later, Murong De made it the capital of Nanyan, and Liu Yu eventually eliminated Murong Chao, leaving Chang Shi Yangmuzhi as governor. After the Yuan Emperor crossed the Yangtze, Qingzhou was established in Guangling, and later a Northern Qingzhou was created, with the overseas Chinese establishing a Southern Qingzhou. Eventually, Southern Qingzhou was abolished, and Northern Qingzhou was simply called Qingzhou.

**Xuzhou**, also from the "Yu Gong," was one of the twelve pastoralist areas. Its name is said to mean "soothing." The Han Dynasty divided Shuhai County and established various commanderies and states here. When the Thirteen Prefectures were established, Xuzhou governed Chu State and four counties. The whole state governed seven counties, 61 counties, and 81,021 households. During the Yongjia Rebellion, parts of Xuzhou fell to the Shi family. After Emperor Yuan crossed the river, Xuzhou only gained half its territory, leading to the establishment of overseas counties. Emperor Ming also established several southern commanderies. During the reign of Emperor Mu, seven counties in the South East China Sea were assigned to Jingkou. In the seventh year of Yixi, Huaibei was divided into North Xuzhou, and Huainan was only called Xuzhou.

**Jingzhou**, recorded in the "Yu Gong," was one of the twelve pastoral areas. Its name means "strong" or "police," referring to the spirit of the region or the need to guard against southern barbarians. During the Six Kingdoms period, it was Chu territory. The Qin and Han Dynasties established various commanderies here. When the Thirteen Prefectures were established, Jingzhou governed seven counties. After the Battle of Chibi, Wu and Shu divided Jingzhou, leading to a northern and southern Jingzhou. After the Jin pacified Wu, the whole state governed 22 counties, 169 counties, and 357,548 households. Emperor Hui divided some counties into Jiangzhou and Liangzhou. Emperor Huai divided nine counties into Xiangzhou. After Emperor Yuan crossed the river, he established new counties. During the reign of Emperor Mu, Lingling was divided into Yingyang County. In the thirteenth year of Yixi, Xiangzhou was abolished and its counties were assigned to Jingzhou.

**Yangzhou**, from the "Yu Gong," was one of the twelve pastoral areas. Its name is believed to refer to the restless energy of Jiangnan or the strong water waves. In ancient times, it was the most remote region from Wang Ji. After the Qin unified the world, it established three counties. The Han Dynasty created various kingdoms and commanderies. When the Thirteen Prefectures were established, Yangzhou governed six counties. After the Jin pacified Wu, the whole state governed 18 counties, 173 counties, and 311,400 households. Emperor Hui divided parts of Yangzhou and Jingzhou to establish Jiangzhou. After Emperor Yuan crossed the river and established his capital in Yangzhou, the Si, Ji, Yong, Liang, Qing, Bing, Yan, Yu, You, and Ping prefectures were all occupied. During the Yuanfeng period, Dan'er and Zhuya counties were established. Emperor Shun established the area as a state. The province governs seven counties, 53 counties, and 25,600 households. The sage observed seasonal changes to create a standard watch and understood the five elements to make bells, aligning music with state affairs. Shen Gu used bamboo to standardize pitch, establishing the twelve laws (Huang Zhong, Gu Xi, Yi Ze, etc.) as an embodiment of natural laws. The sundial shadow and rhythm tube were used to harmonize yin and yang, with the rhythm pipe producing a sound of harmony between heaven and earth, standardizing measurements as stated in "Yu Shu." Virtuous music, grand and harmonious, could move heaven, earth, ghosts, and gods, guiding emotions and customs. Ye Shi noted that aspirations are expressed in chanting, and a gentleman listens to sound to choose music, then to grasp music, and finally to examine political affairs.

Tai Shigong's "Lvshu" states that kings follow the six laws as the foundation of all things, especially in war. Observing the enemy's situation and listening to music can predict outcomes. After Qin Shihuang burned books, these laws declined. During the Han Dynasty, Prime Minister Zhang Cang examined music and temperament but failed to complete the assessment. Emperor Xiaowu set up an official position for coordinating music, and Sima Qian investigated the order of music and rhythm. Wang Mang also studied musical rhythm, with Liu Xin presenting five items: complete mathematics, harmony of five tones, high and low pitch, length and shortness, and capacity of round and square. Ban Gu compiled these into "Lü Li Zhi." Cai Yong recorded later scholars' work in "Xu Hanshu." During the end of Mo, musicians fled, and laws were destroyed. Emperor Wu of Wei acquired musician Du Kui to test musical instruments, and Du Kui balanced the legal system. After Emperor Wu of Jin founded the country, the system remained unchanged until Xun Kan rebuilt new standards in the tenth year of Jin. During Yuankang, Xun Xun's son Yingpeng continued the work, but the Yongtai Rebellion caused the loss of rituals and music to Shi Le. When Emperor Jin and Yuan moved to Jiankang, ceremonial utensils and musical instruments were scarce.

The text records that the twelve laws were produced during the Huangdi era. Linglun cut bamboo from a valley west of Daxia and north of Kunlun, selecting a tube three inches and nine minutes long, naming the sound Huang Zhong's Palace, called Han Shao. Twelve bamboo tubes were made to imitate the phoenix's cry, with six sounds of the phoenix and six of the phoenix, all from the Yellow Bell Palace rhythm, forming the twelve rhythms. Bamboo tubes were used initially due to their naturally formed cavity size. Huangdi also used jade to make rhythm tubes, one foot long with six holes, one for each month. During Shun's reign, the king of the West presented Zhaohua's lüguan made of jade. During Emperor Mozhang's reign, Xi Jing unearthed a white jade rhythm tube under the Shun Temple. In the first year of Emperor Wu's reign, a jade rule was obtained from the tomb of King Xiang of Wei. Jade was used for its clear and moist tube body. During Emperor Moping's reign, Wang Ling used copper to make musical instruments, symbolizing unity and stability, as copper does not deform with dryness, moisture, cold, or heat.

"The Rites of Zhou" records that the Taishi is in charge of the six laws and six lu, coordinating yin and yang sounds. The six rhythms (Huangzhong, Taigu, Guxi, Ruibin, Yize, Wushe) are yang sounds, while the six lu (Dalu, Yingzhong, Nanlu, Linzhong, Zhonglv, Jiazhong) are yin sounds. The imperial master used twelve laws to predict military affairs and good or bad luck. Dian Tong was in charge of the sum of six rhythms and six lu to analyze yin and yang sounds and make musical instruments, using the twelve rhythms as length standards and twelve tones as test standards. King Zhou Jing wanted to make a Wushe bell and asked about the rhythm. Shi Xi explained that the yellow bell corresponds to earth, and from it, the second rhythm of Tai Cun assists Yang Qi. The third law, Guxi, is used for worship. The fourth, Ruibin, is used in the ancestral temple. The fifth, Yi Ze, sings the virtues of the Nine Gongs. The sixth, Wushe, declares the virtues of philosophers. There are also six rooms: Da Lu assists the Yang Law, Jia Zhong harmonizes the four seasons, Zhonglu nourishes neutrality, Lin Zhong brings peace, Nanlu assists formation, and Yingzhong restores utensils to their normal state.

The First Emperor of Qin burned books, scattering classics. Lu Buwei's "Spring and Autumn Annals" stated that Huangzhong Palace is the foundation of the law, with Lin Zhong born under it, Tai Cun above Lin Zhong, and so on, following the rule of three-thirds increase or decrease. After the Han Dynasty, Zhang Cang studied the legal calendar but it was incomplete. Emperor Xiaowu set up the official position of Xielu, standardizing pitch, but the number of notes remained five. King Liu An of Huainan invited scholars to study Lu Lu, stating that Huang Zhong's rhythm is nine inches, with the palace sound determined. The twelve laws correspond to the twenty-four seasonal changes, with Jiazi corresponding to Zhonglu, Bingzi to the bell's feather, Wuzi to Huangzhong's palace, Gengzi to Wushe's quotient, and Renzi to Yize's corner. The twelve laws produce sixty tones, and three hundred and sixty tones correspond to the number of days in a year.

Sima Qian's "Eight Books" discussed Lu Lu, stating that the most primitive chaotic energy contains the three qi of heaven, earth, and humans, activated in Zi. The twelve laws' mutual generation originates from here. The calculation method uses the nine-inch length of the Huang Zhong rule, with lower rules multiplying two by nine and dividing by three, and upper rules multiplying the lower rule by four and dividing by three. The law corresponds to the twelve celestial beings, with six laws as yang and six lu as yin. Sima Qian noted that if the length of the twelve laws is calculated according to "Huainanzi," Ruibin is a repeated ascendant. In the first year of the Yuan Dynasty, Wang Mang recruited scholars to examine music and rhythm, with Liu Xin sorting out the memorials. Ban Gu's "Book of Han" compiled these into annals, with the order of gain and loss based on the nine-inch yellow bell. During Emperor Yuan's reign, Jingfang was proficient in five tones and sixty temperaments. He explained that the method of mutual generation of sixty laws uses the upper law to produce the lower law with a ratio of two-thirds, and the lower law to produce the upper law with a ratio of three-fourths. The twelve laws change into the sixty laws, like the eight trigrams change into the sixty-four hexagrams. Jingfang added that a precision instrument, shaped like a zither with thirteen strings, is used to determine temperament data. The pitch of the pitch instrument is clear, but the pitch deviation caused by string tension is difficult to standardize without a temperament to calibrate.

In the first year of Yuanhe, Emperor Zhang of Han, Yin Xi reported that no one in the court knew how to use accurate instruments to adjust the sixty rhythms. Shao Yanchong taught his son Yan Xuan, but when tested, Yan Xuan could only identify two of the twelve laws accurately, so he could not be appointed. From then on, lawyers could no longer adjust the instrument. In the sixth year of Xiping, Emperor Ling summoned Zhang Guang and others, but they did not know the meaning of the accurate instrument. The problem of music could not be summarized, and there were no people in the palace who could distinguish pitch. At the end of the Han Dynasty, wars caused the loss of Yale San. During Emperor Wu of Wei's reign, Du Kui was proficient in music and cast bells, but the pitch was often off. King Wu of Wei checked and found Du Kui's opinion accurate. In the tenth year of Taishi, Zhongshu supervisor Gou Xu and Zhongshu ordered Zhang Hua to produce twenty-five copper and bamboo flutes. Three were consistent with Du Kui's laws, while the others were flute flutes. Liehe explained that the flute was used for practice, and the whole group could play in tune if the names and dimensions were known. Xun Xu and others reported that the flute making was not standardized, and they proposed making twelve flutes according to the twelve laws, with each hole tuned to the same tune. The emperor agreed, and Gou Xu asked Liehe about the method. Liehe replied that the flute length should be based on the rhythm, and the holes should correspond to the rhythms. The flute workers made the flutes, and the rhythmists adjusted their temperament, resulting in standardized instruments and harmonious sounds.

The text describes the construction of twelve flutes, each with a specific length and fingering method. For example, the Huang Zhong flute is two feet eight inches long, with the upright tone corresponding to Huang Zhong and the lower tone to Lin Zhong. The fingering method for the upright tone uses Huang Zhong as the palace, and the flute's holes are positioned according to the mutual generation of the laws. The lower Zheng tone uses Lin Zhong as the palace, and the Qingjiao tone uses Guxi as the palace. The flute's length is determined by the angular rhythm, with longer flutes being eight times the angle rhythm and shorter flutes four times. The flute tube's volume is ten times its angular volume. The text also discusses the three palaces (positive tone, downward sign, and clear angle) with twenty-one changes, each palace having seven tones. The four fu holes are used to change pitch but are not actually opened, only sized to meet the needs of pronunciation.

The text explains the correspondence between musical sounds and the five elements: earth sound is the palace (number 81), fire sound is the sign (number 54), gold sound is the quotient (number 72), water sound is the feather (number 48), and wood sound is the horn (number 64). Each sound is associated with a season and a symbol (monarch, things, ministers, etc.). The twelve laws correspond to the months, with Huang Zhong in November, Da Lu in December, Tai Cun in January, etc. The text also discusses the method of weathering, where a triple secret room is built, and rhythm tubes are placed on wooden cases to wait for the Qi to arrive. The correct length standard is described in "Mozhi," and Xun Xu made a new ruler based on ancient standards, which was consistent with ancient artifacts. The new clock rhythm was praised, but some criticized it for being too high. The text concludes with a discussion of weighing and capacity units, referencing "Zhou Li" and "Spring and Autumn Annals," and noting the changes in systems over time.

Among the five types of etiquette, the third pertains to guest rituals, including meetings with emperors and gatherings of princes. Since the Zhou Dynasty, the etiquette system for sending envoys became increasingly complex. After the Qin Dynasty's book burning and harassment of Confucian scholars, laws and regulations from past dynasties were incomplete. With the rise of the Han Dynasty, Shusun Tong began formulating etiquette, referencing previous generations but often making changes. A formal ceremony was held on the first day of the first lunar month, where bells rang to accept gifts, dukes and princes stood with offerings, and officials shouted long live before music and feasting. Emperor Wu of Wei held a similar ceremony in Wenchang Hall, using Han Dynasty etiquette and setting up hundreds of lanterns. The Jin Dynasty revised this ceremony, as documented in the "Xianning Notes" and Fu Xuan's "Yuan Hui Li," which integrated rituals from Xia, Yin, Shang, Zhou, Qin, and Han dynasties.

The "Xianning Note" details the ceremony: on the day before the first day of the first lunar month, officials gathered, torches were lit, and they entered the court to congratulate the queen. At less than seven quarters of the night, officials stood in order, and the emperor arrived with bells and drums. Officials knelt and worshipped, and the emperor ascended the throne. The master of ceremonies sang praises, and vassal kings presented jade, bowing twice. The emperor stood and bowed, then sat and bowed again. After the ceremony, the king returned to his seat. The emperor then invited the Taiwei and others, who presented jade, fur, silk, and animals, bowing twice. The ceremony continued with gifts distributed, music played, and the emperor entering a chariot. Guests from various ethnic groups entered, bowed, and sat. The visitor guided the king to pour longevity wine, and music played as ministers bowed. After drinking, they bowed again. The ceremony included distributing wine, playing songs, and serving meals. After the banquet, the ministers left the palace.

The Yangtze River region was unsettled, so morning greetings ceased. The crown prince met with descendants of previous dynasties and nobles. During New Year's gatherings, a white tiger bottle was set up for those who dared to speak out. Under the Wei Dynasty, vassal kings could not meet the emperor, except during Emperor Wei Ming's reign. During the Taishi period, officials reported that princes and nobles should pay court visits every three years, with temporary meetings allowed. The etiquette for court meetings involved holding jade, similar to the old system. In years without court visits, ministers were sent to pay respects. The emperor approved this. However, princes east of the Yangtze River did not return to their own countries, and some accepted appointments elsewhere, rendering this etiquette invalid.

In the Han Dynasty, October was tentatively set as the beginning of the year due to Emperor Gao's pacification of Qin. Emperor Wu later adopted the first month as the beginning of the year but still held banquets on the first day of October and the first day of each month. The banquet etiquette involved receiving congratulations and gifts at night, with princes presenting jade and officials presenting animals. The third prince offered jade to the throne, and the emperor stood for them. Officials congratulated, and those with high salaries shouted long live and raised glasses. Music played during meals, similar to the first day of the first lunar month. Wei and Jin held small court gatherings on the winter solstice, second in scale to New Year's Day.

Ancient emperors patrolled their territories, but during Emperor Wei Wen's reign, border wars prevented this. Emperor Ming visited the east three times, providing relief to the poor and rewarding the elderly. In the first year of his reign, he visited Luoyang County and gave rewards. In the fourth year of Emperor Wu's reign, he issued an edict to officials, emphasizing the importance of inspections and sending envoys to investigate political affairs and the people's sufferings. The new etiquette for patrolling mountains, offering sacrifices, and reporting on palace construction remained the same as in the past. When princes met the emperor, they set up flags to distinguish their ranks, as per the ancient ritual. However, this etiquette was not implemented until the end of the Jin Dynasty.

The ritual system included sacrifices to heaven and earth. The emperor patrolled famous mountains, burned firewood to worship heaven, and reported success. During the Taihe period of Emperor Wei Ming, Jiang Ji reported that the emperor's grand ceremonies prioritized patrols and sacrifices. He argued that since ancient times, dynastic changes involved climbing Mount Tai and writing down names. He urged the emperor to perform the sealing ceremony, but the emperor declined, citing humility and the need to unify the world. Later, Emperor Wu pacified Wu and unified the country. Officials urged him to perform the sealing ceremony, but he repeatedly declined, citing the need for peace and stability. After several memorials, the emperor finally refused, stating that the time was not right.

Emperor Ai wanted to honor Princess Zhang, but officials debated the etiquette. Some argued that a son should not knight his father, while others cited historical precedents. The discussion concluded that the emperor should not confer titles on his mother, as it would violate the order of human relations. The emperor eventually issued an edict to worship the imperial concubine, granting her the same status as the Queen Mother. Further debates arose about the etiquette for the crown prince, with some arguing that he should call himself a minister, while others disagreed. The emperor ultimately decided to follow the old system.

The fourth type of etiquette is military, used to achieve peace abroad and tranquility at home. In the Han Dynasty, military exercises were held on the day of the Beginning of Autumn, with the emperor personally shooting sacrifices. The ceremony included training in battle formations and beheading sacrifices. In the 21st year of Emperor Xian's reign, Wei officials proposed a military parade in autumn, which was approved. During the Wei Dynasty, military parades were held, but after Emperor Hui, this etiquette was abandoned. Later, local governors conducted military parades, but the imperial court no longer did so.

The fifth type of etiquette is Jia, covering banquets, crown ceremonies, and weddings. At the end of the Zhou Dynasty, these rituals were rarely practiced. The crown ceremony for emperors was not recorded in the "Zhou Rites," but it was performed for princes. The emperor's crown ceremony involved three crowns, while the crown prince was crowned twice. The ceremony was held in the ancestral temple, and the emperor personally attended. The wedding etiquette for emperors included gifts of black coins, silk, and horses. The ceremony involved sending envoys to marry the queen, with various rituals such as asking for names, accepting gifts, and personal greetings. The emperor's wedding did not include music or congratulations, as per the rites. The crown prince's wedding also followed specific protocols, with gifts and ceremonies similar to those of the emperor.

Various calamities and portents, linking them to failures in the five behaviors of a ruler: appearance, speech, sight, hearing, and thought. A failure in hearing, described as "hearing but not hearing," is called "not planning." This occurs when a superior's will is blocked from subordinates, leading to impatience. The punishment for this is continuous cold, which prevents grain growth and results in poverty. Associated portents include drum monsters, fish evils, pig troubles, ear diseases, and black disasters. The text explains that cold air causes fish evils, and pigs, associated with water in the "Yi," suffer when the spirit of hearing is damaged. The color of water is black, hence black disasters. This condition is described as fire overcoming water.

A failure in thought, described as "the mind and heart not allowing," is called "unholiness." This means a ruler is not tolerant, preventing subordinates from holding virtuous positions. The disaster is dark weather, and the punishment is continuous wind, which harms all things and leads to early death. Associated portents include the demon of fat night, flower evils, cow troubles, strange illnesses among close friends, and yellow disasters. The text notes that cows have large hearts but cannot think, so they suffer when heart energy is damaged. The color of earth is yellow, hence yellow disasters. This condition is described as metal, wood, water, and fire overcoming earth.

A failure in speech and action, described as "words and deeds being inappropriate," is called "being unable to achieve success." The punishment is a long period of cloudy weather, and in the extreme, the country becomes weak. Associated portents include shooting demons, monsters like dragons and snakes, horse troubles, and the disadvantage of subordinates attacking superiors. The text explains that if the upper level is weak, the lower level will be alarmed, causing shooting demons. Yin Qi moving causes dragon and snake evils. The horse, associated with the king in the "Yi," suffers when the monarch's spirit is damaged. The text states that when the ruler's way is damaged, the sun and moon move out of order and stars go retrograde.

The text provides numerous historical examples of these portents. For continuous cold, it cites heavy snow, unseasonable frost, and hail, linking them to harsh punishments, framing of loyal officials, and unjust killings. Examples include frost damaging grains in the third year of Jiahe of Wu Sun Quan, and heavy snow in the fourth year of Chiwu. For continuous wind, it records strong winds overturning houses and breaking trees, linking them to ignorant and arbitrary rule, as during the reign of King Zhengshi of Wei Qi. Earthquakes are extensively documented, attributed to the power of subordinates and the disorder of yin and yang, with examples from the reigns of Sun Quan, Emperor Wu of Jin, and Emperor Hui.

The text also records instances of fish falling on arsenal roofs, interpreted as a sign of war, and locust plagues, linked to the lord's greed and harshness. Pig disasters, such as wild boars entering military camps, are seen as portents of failure and emptiness. Black and yellow mists are recorded as signs of impending doom or usurpation. summary:
The history of music and ritual in China from ancient times to the Jin Dynasty, emphasizing their spiritual and emotional significance. Spirituality and emotion are expressed through chanting and physical movement, with the heart's essence called Tao and its reflection in images called Yong. Music is used to spread sound, praise peace, and mourn chaos. Ancient sages like Shennong and Fuxi created instruments such as harps, bells, and chimes to express the soul and imitate nature. The Yin Shang Dynasty saw a decline in elegant music due to obscene influences, leading to the loss of works like "Five Heroes" and "Six Stems." Confucius remarked that people can promote Tao, but Tao cannot promote people.

From the Zhou Dynasty onward, various rulers composed music, including the Yellow Emperor's "Yunmen," Yao's "Xianchi," and others. The text describes how music and ritual were used to educate and govern, with the "Shang Shu" and "Zhou Guan" referencing the teaching of music to noble children. However, during the reign of King Ping, etiquette was destroyed, and elegant music was lost. Yanling Jizi noted that the Zhou Dynasty's decline still retained the legacy of previous kings. As nations rose, they created their own music, leading to a gradual decline in the way of kings. The Qin Dynasty unified the world but destroyed all musical works and instruments. The Han Dynasty revived music and ritual under Emperors Gaozu, Wen, and Wu, though Confucianism was abandoned. Emperor Ming of the Han Dynasty further promoted rituals and music, establishing a pagoda market and performing ceremonies in the Mingtang.

The text details various types of music, including great music for the world, sacrificial music for ancestral temples, and ceremonial music for different occasions. It explains the five tones (palace, shang, jiao, zheng, yu) and their associations with virtues and emotions, as well as the eight sounds (stone, leather, bamboo, wood, silk, earth, metal) and their corresponding winds. The twelve pitches (six yang and six yin) are linked to the twelve months and their characteristics. After the Han Dynasty's chaos, music was scattered. Emperor Wu of Wei appointed Du Kui to create Yale, but new music later changed its charm. Emperor Wu of Jin initially based rituals on the Wei Dynasty, with Fu Xuan composing lyrics for various sacrifices, including songs for heaven and earth, the five suburbs, and ancestral temples.

The text includes numerous songs and poems used in rituals, such as those for the first day of the first lunar month, sacrifices to heaven and earth, and ancestral temple ceremonies. It describes the evolution of music under different rulers, including the adaptation of old melodies by Zuo Yannian and the creation of new songs by Xun Xu and Zhang Hua. Xun Xu developed new rhythmic flutes and adjusted the pitch, though Ruan Xian criticized the high tone as sorrowful. The text concludes with the history of the "Bayu Dance," which originated from the Banshun people and was adapted by Wang Can during the Wei Dynasty. In the Jin Dynasty, it was renamed "Xuanwu Dance" and later replaced by "Zhengde" and "Dayu" dances.

A detailed historical account of chariots, clothing, and ceremonial regalia from ancient times through the Jin Dynasty, emphasizing their symbolic and functional roles in governance, ritual, and social hierarchy. Since antiquity, gods and ancestors used specific vehicles and attire, such as the Yellow Emperor’s black top and light red lower clothes, and Fang Xun’s vermilion chariot with white horses, aligning with calendrical systems. The "Moon Order" describes women dyeing satin in regulated shades, while flags bearing sun and moon images and jade-adorned garments were meant to inspire awe and suppress evil. The text cites classical texts like "Shangshu" and "Book of Rites" to justify rewarding merit with chariots and clothing, and notes that saints derived designs from nature, such as birds and plants, for garments and wheels.

The narrative traces the evolution of these systems through dynasties. During the Zhou and Yin periods, creative designs emerged, but later, as ritual order declined, princes violated norms, leading to confusion like purple garments in Qi and long tassels in Zou. Confucius advocated for clothing matching status. The Qin Dynasty unified practices, collecting furs and decorating chariots, but burned texts and simplified regalia. Emperor Gaozu followed Qin systems, while Emperor Shizong expanded ceremonies with grand processions. However, later rulers like Emperor Sheng favored concubines, and the Wang family’s dominance led to war and destruction of artifacts. After the Chimei Rebellion, Emperor Ming restored costumes based on "Zhou Guan" and "Book of Rites," and Emperor Wei Ming reduced lavish furs. Gao Tanglong advised changing Zhengshuo to align with gods, leading to yellow as the dominant color in the Jingchu era.

The text details specific chariot types, such as the "five chariots" (jade, gold, elephant, leather, wood), each with distinct decorations and uses. The jade chariot, most noble, featured a Taichang flag with twelve strands for sky worship. The golden chariot had nine strands for guests, the elephant chariot was plain red for court, the leather chariot was for military campaigns, and the wood chariot for hunting. Chariots were drawn by horses with elaborate trappings, including gold ornaments, bells, and jade fittings. The emperor’s ceremonial procession included various vehicles like the Sinan chariot (a compass guide), drum cart (measuring distance), and sheep cart, each with specific functions. The text also describes the Five Oxen Flag, plowing cart, and hunting cart, noting changes in color and flags under different rulers, such as Wei Jingchu’s shift to yellow and white.

The account continues with the emperor’s travel sequence, listing dozens of vehicles and officials in a strict order, from the elephant chariot and drummers to the golden root chariot and imperial guards. This procession included multiple ranks of officials, cavalry, and ceremonial items like flags, halberds, and drums. The text notes that after the Liao Dynasty, many old regulations were lost, and by the Yuantong era, only a few chariots remained, with temporary decorations for sacrifices. The compass and other chariots were rediscovered later, such as Liu Yu finding the Sinan chariot in the 13th year of Yixi. The crown prince’s chariot and the empress dowager’s golden root chariot are also described, with specific rules for women’s vehicles, such as the queen’s mica chariot for silkworm worship.

The second half focuses on clothing and headwear. The emperor’s ceremonial attire included a black frame crown with white jade beads, twelve tassels, and a robe with twelve chapters (e.g., sun, moon, dragons). Different occasions required specific garments, such as a soap-colored robe for ancestral sacrifices or a crimson robe for court. Crowns varied by rank: the Tongtian Crown for the emperor, Pingmian for princes, and Jinxian Crown for scholars, with beams indicating status (e.g., three beams for princes, one beam for low officials). Other crowns like the Wu Guan (martial), Alpine Crown (for envoys), and Dharma Crown (for law officials) had distinct shapes and origins, often linked to historical figures or legends. The text also describes caps, scarves, and hats, noting that the clam (a type of headgear) evolved from ancient practices and was used by all classes.

The text concludes with accessories and women’s attire. Swords were once universal but later limited to court, with wooden swords replacing metal. The emperor’s six seals, including the legendary Imperial Seal, were passed down, though the sword of the white snake was lost. Belts, pouches, and wats (tablets) were used for official duties, with specific colors and materials for ranks. Women’s clothing, such as the queen’s soap-colored top for temple visits or cyan for weddings, included elaborate headdresses with golden flowers, jade ornaments, and step decorations. Noble ladies and concubines had graded seals, ribbons, and jade, with specific attire for silkworm ceremonies. The text emphasizes that these systems were meant to reflect virtue and status, but many were lost or simplified over time, especially after the Eastern Jin Dynasty.

It then traces the development of civilization through legendary figures: Suirenshi who drilled wood for fire, Paoxishi who created the eight trigrams, Nüwa who repaired the heavens, and Shennong who developed agriculture and divided territories. The Yellow Emperor traveled extensively, reaching the eastern seaside, the Yangtze River in the south, and Mount Daiyue. Yu Shun formulated calendars, divided star districts, and established provinces including Bingzhou, Youzhou, and Yingzhou.

The text details the evolution of administrative divisions through successive dynasties. During the Xia and Shang dynasties, territorial systems were established and maintained. King Wu of Zhou moved the capital from Feng to Haojing. Under King Cheng of Zhou, the "Yu Gong" was revised, merging some provinces and dividing others. Officials were appointed to manage lands and observe astronomy, distinguishing the nine provinces with their corresponding star regions. The southeast was Yangzhou, due south was Jingzhou, Henan was Yuzhou, due east was Qingzhou, east of Hedong was Yanzhou, due west was Yongzhou, northeast was Youzhou, north of the Yellow River was Jizhou, and due north was Bingzhou.

When Qin Shihuang unified the world, he abolished the feudal princes and divided the empire into thirty-six counties, including Sanchuan, Hedong, Nanyang, Nanjun, Jiujiang, and others. The Qin territory extended to Dianfeng in the west, the desert in the north, and the sea in the east. After the Qin dynasty fell, the Han dynasty established new administrative systems. Emperor Gaozu of Han added twenty-three counties, while Emperor Wu established seventeen counties after conquering Vietnam and the Hu lands, and six more after pacifying the southwestern barbarians. By the second year of Emperor Ping's Yuanshi period, there were 111 counties total, divided into thirteen divisions including Liang, Yi, Jing, Yang, Qing, Yu, Yan, Xu, You, Bing, Ji, Jiaozhi, and Shuofang.

The text describes how later dynasties continued to modify territorial divisions. During the Later Han, Emperor Guangwu merged eight counties due to population decline. Subsequent emperors added or changed various counties. During the Three Kingdoms period, Wei, Shu, and Wu each established new counties. By the first year of Taikang under Emperor Wu of Jin, after pacifying the Wu state, twenty-three additional counties were established, bringing the total to 173 counties across nineteen provinces. The text notes that this represented a great civilized country owning all territories of Yin and Zhou.

The document provides extensive detail on the geographical measurements and cosmological understanding of the ancient world. It describes the eight poles (Baji) as being 203,1300 miles from east to west and the same from north to south. The distance from earth to heaven was half the width of the eight poles. The text explains that there are seven stars in the Big Dipper and seven layers of earth, with four corners in the sky and four great rivers flowing eastward into the sea. The terrain becomes lower in the southeast while the sky tilts toward the northwest.

The text extensively describes the feudal system established by various dynasties. Under the Xia dynasty, the territory was divided into five service zones (five fu) extending 5000 miles in radius. The system included Dianfu (imperial domain), Houfu (marquis domain), Suifu (submission domain), Yaofu (essential domain), and Huangfu (wilderness domain), each with specific tax and service requirements. The Zhou dynasty established five ranks of nobility—Duke, Marquis, Earl, Viscount, and Baron—with specific land allocations. The emperor's field was 1000 li in circumference, while dukes received 100 li, earls 70 li, and viscounts 50 li. The text notes that during the Zhou dynasty's peak, there were 13,714,933 people and no crimes were committed.

The document traces the decline of the Zhou royal family and the rise of the Spring and Autumn period, when 36 monarchs were killed and 52 countries perished over 242 years. It lists 139 known countries including Lu, Zhu, Zheng, Song, Ji, Wei, and others, plus 31 countries that disappeared. The five hegemons emerged, followed by the seven warring states of Han, Wei, Zhao, Yan, Qi, Qin, and Chu. The text describes the well-field system in detail, where land was divided into nine squares of 100 mu each, with eight families jointly cultivating the central public field.

The text concludes by describing the administrative systems of the Qin and Han dynasties. After Qin Shihuang abolished the five-rank nobility system, the Han dynasty established second-class titles, granting fiefs to meritorious officials. By Emperor Ping's reign, there were 12,233,062 households and 59,594,978 people, with territory extending 9,302 miles east to west and 13,368 miles north to south. The document details the system of pavilions every ten miles, townships every ten pavilions, and the roles of village elders and other officials. It notes that by the third year of a later reign, there were 10,677,960 households with 56,486,856 people, representing an era of increasing population.
