Three years later, he was moved to the position of chief and servant.
In the first year of Zhongdatong, he was transferred to the post of Taifuqing.
Three years later, he served as General Zhenwei and Internal History of Linchuan.
In the county, he was praised for his harmonious management of affairs, and all the officials liked him.
He returned to the capital and was appointed as a regular servant of casual cavalry, and soon he was appointed as a servant again.
In the second year of Datong, he moved to serve as a regular servant of Sanqi and a minister of state, and led the Dazhongzheng of Xuzhou in the south.
Immediately he was appointed as a waiter again, and his duties as a minister and official remained as before.
In the early years of the Liang Dynasty, all sacrifices to temples and temples in the suburbs were made with solid-colored whole animals without the fur removed. The music and lyrics for the sacrifices were all written by Shen Yue and are still in use today. Ziyun was the first to suggest the revision of the music and lyrics.
He started by saying: The Holy Lord respects the customs, and the sacrifices in the suburban temples are solemn and solemn, which is very popular among the people in the western neighboring countries. It can be compared with the deeds of Zhou Gong and Confucius. During the sacrifice, the processed and hairless animal skins are placed in the altar to communicate with the gods.
I have been working part-time as a Zhaiguan recently, and when I heard the songs sung by musicians during sacrifices, they were still old songs for sacrificial animals whose furs had not been removed.
The Shiliao official who worshiped the heaven in the circle hill also said "Shi prepares the animal bolt"; the northern suburbs performed "Jie Ya" to worship the heaven, and also sang "The sacrifice of the jade hole prepares"; the ancestral temple worshiped and sang, and said "I sacrifice to clean"; the food and celebration music played in the three dynasties still chanted "Red tail and green scales", the singing was accompanied by drums and bells, and the dispatch was not in line with the grand system.
The minister, who is in charge of Confucianism, thinks that singing this way is suspicious and is not sure whether the music should be changed?
The imperial edict said: This is because the supervisor sticks to narrow experience and does not know how to adapt and make emergency corrections.
Then he asked Ziyun to write some music poems.
The imperial edict said: The lyrics used for sacrificial rituals in suburban temples should be the elegant and ancient words in the imperial edicts, and should not be mixed with the simple words in the history books; and there are many errors in what Shen Yue wrote.
Ziyun replied to the edict: "To play grand music and songs to worship the ancestral temple of heaven and earth, and to use elegant names for music, we should adopt them from the Five Classics. The sage has become a religion."
However, the music poems compiled since the Han Dynasty are not all based on classics; those compiled by Shen Yue are even more crude and messy.
The minister changed the ten songs composed by Shen Yue, but he only knew that the animal pegs used for sacrifice had been replaced by leather, so the lyrics should be changed and the lyrics should still be continued, not avoiding the customs and deviating from the actual situation.
After obeying the order, I was able to broaden my horizons.
I have always been mediocre and stubborn, but now I suddenly understand. I respectfully follow Cheng's decree and completely correct Shen Yue's organization.
Only the Five Classics are used as the basis, followed by Erya, Zhouyi, Shangshu, and Dadaili. This is a category of classics and imperial edicts, and can also be used in foolish ways.
I also explored the books written by Yao and Shun in the Tang Dynasty, including "Song" of Yin Dynasty and "Ya" of Zhou Dynasty. They were mainly praising, but each described current events.
Daliang changed dynasties and the world obeyed, Yan Wu cultivated literature, made rituals and music, and promoted the Xia, Yin, and Zhou dynasties. However, the lyrics written by Shen Yue were only immersed in praising the beauty of holy virtues and did not describe the creation of the dynasty.
"Ya" and "Song" are precedents, and Shen Yue's arrangement is inconsistent with the style.
According to the music theory, rules and threads prescribed by the imperial edict, as soon as a person with profound and subtle literary thoughts and the ability to govern the world appears, it is like the sun and moon hanging in the sky, indelible classics, and the education of ritual and music was made in the peaceful and prosperous times.
I would like to collect them one by one and show their meaning according to the circumstances to show the appropriateness of the production.
I have thought deeply about it for many days, and now I have completed it and respectfully submit it.
Used together with the edict.
Ziyun was good at writing cursive official script and was regarded as a model by the world. He said that he was good at imitating Zhong Yao and Wang Xizhi and slightly changing his handwriting.
In reply to the edict: I used to have no ability to appreciate, so I decided it was precious according to the opinions of the world, so I imitated Wang Xianzhi's calligraphy for many years.
When he was twenty-six years old, he compiled the "Book of Jin" and wrote "The Biography of Two Kings". He wanted to write a comment on the writing style of cursive script, but it was not satisfactory and he failed to write it. He only briefly commented on Feibai style writing style.
It has been more than ten years since I first saw the imperial edict "On Calligraphy", a volume in which I commented on the calligraphy style and thoroughly understood the shape of the characters; I also thought that Wang Xizhi was inferior to Zhong Yao, just like Wang Xianzhi was inferior to Wang Xizhi.
After thinking about it, I realized that the rules of official script were first changed by Wang Xianzhi, and Zhong Yao was the one who standardized everything.
Since then, I feel that my writing skills have improved.
His calligraphy was highly praised by Emperor Gaozu. He once commented on Ziyun's calligraphy: "The pen is strong and straight, the heart and hand are in harmony, the skill is beyond Du Du, and the physical beauty is better than Cui Wei. He should compete with Zhong Yao."
He was appreciated like this.
In the seventh year, he served as General Renwei and Grand Administrator of Shuyang.
In the first year of Zhongdatong, he returned to the capital and was awarded Zong Zhengqing.
In the first year of Taiqing, he was again appointed as Shizhong and Guozi Jijiu, and led the Dazhongzheng of Xuzhou in the south.
In the second year, Hou Jing invaded the palace city, and Ziyun fled to the people.
In March of the third year, the palace city was lost. He fled eastward to Jinling and died of starvation in the monk's room of Xianling Temple. He was sixty-three years old.
His works include 110 volumes of "Book of Jin" and 20 volumes of "New Records of the East Palace".
The second son Xiaote was named Shida.
He became famous very early and was good at cursive calligraphy.
Emperor Gaozu once said to Xiao Te: Zijing's calligraphy is not as good as Wang Baozhi's.
Seeing Xiao Yi's handwriting recently made Qing feel threatened.
His official titles include Zuolang, Prince Sheren, Xuanhui, and the Zhongjun Records Office.
He took up the post of Haiyan Order, but was dismissed for some reasons.
At the age of twenty-five, he died in front of Wang Yun.
Zihui, whose courtesy name is Jingguang, is Ziyun's younger brother.
When he was young, he dabbled in book history and was also talented in literature.
He started as a member of the imperial family and served as a minister of Sanqi, and moved to the office of Nanzhonglang.
Served as Lin'an Order.
He has a quiet temperament and few hobbies. He once participated in the Chongyun Hall to listen to the "Three Wisdom Sutra" lectures, and came back to write "Lectures on Fu" as a memorial, which was highly praised.
He moved to Anxi to serve as a consultant to King Wuling of Anxi Province, and brought in new orders. He was transferred to Yitong to serve as a member of the imperial family, and to serve as the chief historian of Hussar. He died.
Chen Libu Shangshu Yao Chari: In the past, Aiqiao changed the fate of Lianqu by relying on his military power, and changed the calendar of the Wei Dynasty by relying on the Prime Minister. This is different from the ancient Zen teachings, which were passed down by virtue, so they suppressed the clans of the previous generation and cut off the popularity of the people.
However, Liu Ye and Cao Zhi were still prominent in the new dynasty; in the end, their surnames became obsolete in Saichi.
The Qi Dynasty was a relative of the Song Dynasty, but it wiped out all the Song Dynasty clans.
Its short-term national fortune may be caused by this reason.
The revolution of the Liang Dynasty did not adopt the practices of the previous dynasty, so the Zike brothers and their followers were given positions according to their talents. They were all nobles in the dynasty and did not abandon them because they were old people. Is it just that the Wei Dynasty was dim and the Jin Dynasty was obvious.
Therefore, a gentleman knows that the great ancestor is magnanimous and his magnanimity surpasses that of previous generations.
summary:
Xiao Zike, courtesy name Jingchong, was the second son of Xiao Yi, King Wen of Yuzhang in the Qi Dynasty. During the Yongming era, he was named Marquis of Nankang County. At age twelve, he co-wrote "Gaosong Fu" with his cousin, King Jingling of Situ, earning admiration from the guard Gongjian. He began his career as General Ningshuo and Grand Administrator of Jinduo, later moving to General Fuguo and Grand Administrator of Wujun during the Jiangan period. When Grand Sima Wang Jingze rebelled in Kuaiji, Zike fled to the capital, avoiding harm from Emperor Ming, who appointed him as the crown prince's concubine. Under Donghunhou, he became Secretary Supervisor, Right Army General, and Minister. In the second year of Zhongxing, he served as Auxiliary to Consult the Country. In the first year of Tianjian, he was demoted to Viscount, appointed as Regular Attendant of the Cavalry and Infantry Captain, but declined due to illness. He later held posts including Guanglu Doctor and Chief Historian of Situ Zuo.

Emperor Gaozu, in a conversation with Zike's disciples, emphasized that fame and fortune cannot be forced, citing historical examples like Xiang Ji's failure. He contrasted the jealous nature of Emperor Xiaowu of Song, who poisoned talented brothers, with the survival of Liu Ziye. Gaozu noted that those with destiny cannot be harmed, referencing his own rise. He advised against killing during dynastic changes, warning it damages harmony, and stressed the close clan relationship between Qi and Liang, urging loyalty. He also instructed Zhao Shuzu to reassure the princes of Beidi of his intentions.

Zike later served as Prefect of Yongjia, Guanglu Qing, Secretary Supervisor, General Mingwei, Prefect of Lingling, Regular Attendant of Sanqi, General of the Auxiliary Country, Zong Zhengqing, Du Guan Shangshu, Minister of Personnel, and Prince Zhan Shi. In the second year of Datong, he became General Ningyuan and Prefect of Yuxing, dying at age fifty-two in 536. He was posthumously given the titles Shi Zhong and Zhong Shu Ling, with the posthumous name Gong. His sixteen brothers all served in Liang, with five talented ones: Zike, Zizhi, Zixian, Ziyun, and Zihui. Wang Deng, another brother, praised their literary skills but abandoned his own writing.

Zifan, Zike's sixth younger brother, was named Marquis of Qiyang County in the tenth year of Yongming. In Tianjian, he was demoted to Viscount and held various posts, including Prince Xi Ma and Master Situ. Known for filial piety, he mourned excessively for his mother. He later served as Chief Secretary of Situ, Yan Yin Cheng, Prefect of Jian'an, and Grand Sima of the Imperial Household. He loved literary talents, favoring Wang Yan, and compiled the "Thousand-Character Essay." After Wang's death, Zifan moved to Xuanhui to consult and join the army. He felt undervalued compared to his brothers, often comparing himself to Du Xu's middle brother. He later became Sima, Zhongsan Doctor, Guanglu, Tingweiqing, General Rong Zhao, and Direct Internal History of Zhou. He returned to the capital as Taizhong Doctor and Secretary Supervisor. Under Taisai, he was appointed Guanglu Doctor but declined due to thieves. He died at sixty-four, posthumously given Jinzi Guanglu and the posthumous name Wen. His collected works totaled thirty volumes. His sons, Xiao Pang and Xiao Que, were early writers, with Xiao Pang serving as a lieutenant and Xiao Que as an official in Taiqing.

Xiao Ti, Zike's eighth younger brother, was intelligent and valued by his father. At seven, he was named Kongdu Tibao. In Tianjian, his title was reduced to Viscount. He held posts including Foreign Soldier in Anxi, Wei Jishi, and Taiwei Recorder. Tall and handsome, he wrote "Hongxu Fu," praised by Shen Yue, and compiled "Hou Mo" and "History of Qi." He later served as Prince Zhongsheren, Jianchenling, Shaoling Wangyou, Danyan Yincheng, Zhongshulang, and Zong Zhengqing. In the second year of Zhongdatong, he became Chief and Minister. Emperor Gaozu admired his talent and manner, once asking him about compiling "General History." In three years, he became a Doctor of Guozi, later moving to Guozi Jijiu and Minister of Civil Affairs. He was proud and solemn, often ignoring guests. He died at forty-nine in the third year of Datong, posthumously given Shizhong and Zhongshu Ling, with the posthumous name Mi. His works include "Houmo Shu," "Qi Shu," "Ordinary Northern Expedition," "Guijian Biography," and collected works. His sons, Xiao Xu and Xiao Kai, were early achievers, with Xiao Kai praised by Taizong for his poetry.

Ziyun, Zike's ninth younger brother, was named Marquis of Xinpu County at twelve in the fourth year of Jianwu. In Tianjian, his title was reduced to Viscount. Diligent in study, he began writing at twenty. Quiet and reluctant to serve, he was recruited as a secretary at thirty. He held posts including Prince Sheren, Beizhong Lang, and Danyang Yin Cheng. King Shu of Xiang appreciated him. He later served as Huang Menlang, General Qingche, and Minister of Civil Affairs. In the first year of Zhongdatong, he became Taifuqing, then General Zhenwei and Internal History of Linchuan. He returned as Regular Attendant of Sanqi and Minister of State. He proposed revising sacrificial music lyrics, replacing Shen Yue's works with classical references. Skilled in cursive calligraphy, he imitated Zhong Yao and Wang Xizhi, earning Emperor Gaozu's praise. In the seventh year, he served as General Renwei and Prefect of Shuyang. In the first year of Taiqing, he became Shizhong and Guozi Jijiu. In the second year, Hou Jing invaded, and Ziyun fled, dying of starvation at sixty-three in 549. His works include "Book of Jin" and "New Records of the East Palace." His son Xiao Te, skilled in calligraphy, died at twenty-five.

Zihui, Ziyun's younger brother, was talented in literature. He started as a member of the imperial family and served as Sanqi Minister and Lin'an Order. Quiet and reserved, he wrote "Lectures on Fu" after attending a lecture. He later served as Consultant to King Wuling and Chief Historian of Hussar, dying in office. Chen Libu Shangshu Yao Chari noted that the Liang Dynasty, unlike previous dynasties, did not suppress former clans, allowing Zike's brothers to hold positions, reflecting Emperor Gaozu's magnanimity.

translation:
Zhu Yi, whose courtesy name was Yanhe, was from Qiantang, Wu County.
His father, Zhu Xun, was well-known for his loyalty and righteousness. He served as an official in the Qi Dynasty until the king of Jiangxia joined the army and was ordered by Wu Ping.
When Zhu Yi was old, his grandfather stroked Zhu Yi's head happily and said to his grandfather Zhaozhi: "This son is not an ordinary person. He will become your family."
He is more than ten years old. He likes to gamble in groups and is extremely hated by the township party.
When he grew up, he forced himself to change his bad habits and studied as a teacher. He studied the Five Classics, especially "Li" and "Yi", dabbled in literature and history, and was proficient in miscellaneous arts. He was good at gambling, go, calligraphy, and arithmetic.
When he was twenty years old, he arrived in the capital. The Minister ordered Shen to interview him, so he joked with him: "You are young, why are you not honest?"
Zhu Yi hesitated and did not understand the meaning of these words.
Shen Yue then said: "The only skills in the world are literature, history, classics, Yi, chess, calligraphy and so on. If you take them all at once, you can call them dishonest."
In this year, a letter was written stating that it was appropriate for Jiankang to set up a prison department, and Yu Tingwei was of the same rank. The edict was submitted to Yu Shangshu for detailed discussion, and he agreed with his opinion.
Under the old system, one could only become an official at the age of twenty-five.
At this time, Zhu Yi was twenty-one years old, and the imperial court made an exception and ordered him to be promoted to the post of Yangzhou Councilor to engage in history.
Not long ago, Shaoling was looking for people with special talents. Doctor Mingshan of the Five Classics recommended Zhu Yi and said: I met Zhu Yi, a native of Qiantang. He was still young, but he had perfect moral character, was shrewd and sophisticated in his work, had no thoughts of distraction when he was alone, and when no one saw him, he still looked respectful as if he were facing guests. His mind was broad and deep, and his demeanor was extraordinary.
For example, a famous mountain is so high that it is difficult to climb to the top; a blue sea is so deep that it is difficult to peer into its depths.
Another example is that Guizhang has just been carved, and the brocade group he is wearing begins to weave. When touched, it will make a loud sound, and the decoration will appear in the world.
Observe his honest character, which is not only rare among ten families. If he is allowed to carry a heavy load and gallop on a long distance, he will definitely have the function of a thousand-mile horse.
Emperor Gaozu summoned him and asked him to explain the principles of "The Book of Filial Piety" and "The Book of Changes". He was very happy after hearing this and said to the people around him: "Zhu Yi is indeed special."
Later I met Ming Shanbin and said to him: The person you recommended is indeed a very qualified person.
So he called Zhu Yi to be on duty in the Western Province, and soon he became a doctor of Imperial College.
This year, Emperor Gaozu personally explained the "Book of Filial Piety" and asked Zhu Yi to read it.
He was moved to the post of Minister Yi Cao Lang, and concurrently served as Zhongshu Tongshi Shiren. After repeated promotions, he was promoted to Hongluqing, the prince's right guard, and soon he was appointed as a member of the imperial family.
In the fifth year of the Ordinary Period, a large-scale Northern Expedition was launched. Yuan Faseng, the governor of Xuzhou in the Northern Wei Dynasty, sent an envoy to ask for the surrender of the land and the people. Shao ordered a minister to discuss the truth of the matter.
Zhu Yi said: Since the king's army marched north and continued to win, the local forces in Xuzhou have weakened, and they all want to blame Fa Monk. Fa Monk is afraid of the impending disaster, so his surrender will not be false.
Emperor Gaozu sent Zhu Yi to report to the Dharma monk and ordered all the troops to respond, all under Zhu Yi's command.
After arriving, the monk followed the imperial decree, just as Zhu Yi predicted.
In the first year of Zhongdatong, he moved to serve as a regular attendant of Sanqi.
Since Zhou She's death, Zhu Yi took his place in charge of the court's affairs, the replacement of military commanders, court rituals and state codes, and the drafting of Shao's imperial edicts.
Whenever people from all over the world come in to submit their reports, the official records and detailed consultations are all piled up in front of him. Zhu Yi writes with his pen and makes decisions. He is talented and smart. He keeps writing in his hand, and everything is done in an instant.
In the fourth year of Datong, he was promoted to General Youwei.
In the sixth year, Zhu Yishou told the "Lao Zi Yi" written by Chan Dan in Jinshu Hall, and the imperial order allowed it.
When he sat down to speak, there were more than a thousand people from the imperial court and Taoists and laymen listening, which became a grand event at that time.
At that time, the Shilin Museum was opened in the west of the city to introduce scholars. Zhu Yiyu and Zuo Cheng He Chen took turns lecturing on the "Book of Rites" written by Gao Zu, and the crown prince summoned Zhu Yi to lect on "Yi" in Xuanpu.
In the eighth year, he was appointed as a servant.
In the first year of Taiqing, he was moved to the position of general of Zuowei and led the infantry.
In the second year, he was moved to the position of leader, but his family remained as usual.
Emperor Gaozu dreamed that he had pacified the Central Plains, and he praised and celebrated it. The next morning, he told Zhu Yi the dream, and Zhu Yi replied: This is a sign of the unification of the four directions in the universe.
When Hou Jing returned and surrendered, he summoned the ministers to discuss it. Shangshu Pu She Xie Li and others thought it was unacceptable to accept it. Emperor Gaozu wanted to take Zhu Yi over, but the matter was pending. Zeng came to Wu Shanyu at dawn and said to himself: Our country is so peaceful that I will accept the land now. If doing so will cause chaos to the country, it will be too late to regret it.
Zhu Yi sensed Gaozu's hidden thoughts and responded: The wise emperor rules the world and obeys the will of heaven. The people of the subjugated north do not admire you because they have no chance to express their wishes.
Now Hou Jing divides most of the land of Wei State, sincerely expresses his submission, and comes from afar to join the Holy Dynasty. Isn't it true that God enlightens his heart and everyone helps him realize his plan?
After deducing Hou Jing's original intention and examining this matter, it is highly commendable.
If we don't accept him today, I'm afraid it will make those who come after us despair.
This is obvious, may your Majesty have no doubts.
Emperor Gaozu wanted to adopt Zhu Yi's advice, but he thought of his previous dream, so he accepted Hou Jing's surrender.
The Marquis of Zhenyang was defeated and captured, and an envoy was sent back from Wei to tell him that Gao Cheng, the prime minister of Wei, wanted to live in harmony with the Liang Dynasty again.
In June of that year, Jiankang Ling Xie Ting and Tongzhi Lang Xu Ling were sent as envoys to Tonghao in the north.
At that time, Hou Jing was guarding Shouchun. He repeatedly warned Gaozu to sever peace with Wei and asked for the envoy to be recovered.
He also wrote to Zhu Yi with sincere words, but Zhu Yi just relayed the imperial edict in reply.
In August, Hou Jing raised his troops to rebel in the name of condemning Zhu Yi.
Zhu Yi recruited 3,000 troops. Hou Jing marched to Beijing and used these people to guard Da Sima Gate.
At the beginning, Hou Jing conspired to rebel, and the governor of Hezhou, Xiao Fan, the king of Poyang, and the governor of Sizhou, Yang Yaren, reported many times. Zhu Yi thought that Hou Jing would not do that if he was sent to the Liang Dynasty alone, so he said to the envoy: The king of Poyang does not allow the country to have a guest!
He also suppressed the report and did not report it, so the court did not take precautions against this matter.
When Hou Jing came to invade, the civil and military officials in the city blamed him.
The crown prince also wrote "Ode to the Siege of the City", the last chapter of which says: Wearing a high crown and thick-soled shoes, he sat on a fat horse, climbed to the palace where the emperor lived, opened the golden gate of the royal family, stated strategies to assist the king, and announced the power of political punishments. Many fortifications were built in the surrounding suburbs, and all nations were unrest.
May I ask the jackal who he is?
May I ask the gizzard who he is for?
This refers to Zhu Yi.
Zhu Yi was so angry that he fell ill and died at the age of sixty-seven.
Shaoling said: Zhu Yi, the leader of the old army, has a broad mind and outstanding talents. He has been discussing and planning strategies in the court for many years. I was supposed to be assisting the imperial government in its administration, and I had entrusted him with important responsibilities for a long time. He died suddenly, and my heart was filled with sadness.
You can posthumously give him a coffin as a posthumous gift from his attendant and minister, Youpu She.
The money needed for the funeral can be provided at will.
In the past, when ministers died, they did not give posthumous gifts to the chancellor. When Zhu Yi passed away, Emperor Gaozu felt sorry for him. When discussing the matter of posthumous gifts, some people who were friendly to Zhu Yi began to report: Although Zhu Yi held many officials, what he hoped for in his life was to be a law enforcement official.
According to his long-cherished ambition, Emperor Gaozu made this posthumous gift.
Zhu Yi had been in power for more than thirty years. He was good at peering into the innermost intentions of his lord, and he was able to flatter and obey the emperor's orders, so he was particularly favored.
Officials in the officialdom often serve from outside to the middle. All these four positions can wear mink tails on their hats, and lead from the right guard to the leader. These four positions all have retinues and honor guards when they travel. There has never been such a thing in modern times.
Zhu Yi and his disciples built houses from Chaogou all the way to Qingxi. The house was surrounded by terraces and ponds, where they could play with guests every spare time.
Gifts from all parties and wealth accumulated.
He has a stingy temperament and has never given anything to others.
The delicacies in the kitchen were delicious and rotten, and more than ten carts of them were often thrown away every month, even though his sons and relatives did not give them away.
He wrote more than 100 expositions, notes on rituals, and essays on "Li" and "Yi", many of which were lost during the war.
The eldest son was named Su, and he was a doctor of state; the second son was named Run, and he was appointed as Situ Tuo.
Both died in the war.
He Chen, named Guobao, was from Shanyin in Kuaiji.
His uncle He Chang was appointed as an infantry captain and was a great Confucianist of the time.
When He Chen was young, He Chang taught him Confucian classics, and he could understand the principles as soon as he listened.
He Yi felt very strange and often said: "This son should be distinguished by his understanding of the meaning of the scriptures."
After He Chang's death, He Chen's family was poor and he often traveled to and from Zhuji, selling millet to support himself.
In his spare time, he studied economics and was especially proficient in the "Three Rites".
At first, He Jiang gathered his disciples in the countryside to teach economics, but now they started to learn economics from He Chen.
In ordinary years, the governor of Linchuan called him to serve as a wine minister and engage in history.
He Ge began to show his talents in the capital. When Emperor Gaozu learned that he had knowledge, he summoned him in the Wende Hall and talked happily with him. He told Xu Mian, a servant of Xu Mian: "He Ge indeed has a scholarship that has been handed down from generation to generation."
So he was appointed as the minister of the kingdom, and soon he was concurrently appointed as the doctor of Taixue. Then he was moved to the position of Zhongwei to participate in military affairs, Shangshu general, Shiren, and ceremonial affairs.
After many years of promotion, he was promoted to Tongzhi Zhengyuanlang, but he remained the same.
He was also appointed to record the affairs of the king of Poyang in the west, and concurrently served as minister Zuo Cheng. Upon completion of his term, he was actually granted the title.
He Chen was ordered to compile the "New Mi Law", which is still in use today.
At that time, the crown prince suggested that at the end of the great career, the crown prince could marry the daughter.
He Chen retorted:
The decree holds that at the end of the great career, one can crown a son and marry a daughter, but one is not allowed to crown oneself and hold a wedding ceremony on one's own.
Looking at the literal meaning of "Book of Rites", I am still very confused about this explanation.
Looking at the etiquette of marrying a crown, it is originally presided over by the father. Only those without fathers can do the ceremony on their own, so it is called great merit and small merit, and it is a ritual system to marry a crown to a son;
At the end of Xiaogong, you can marry on your own, and it is also said that "a crown prince marries a wife", and its meaning becomes clearer.
Therefore, the two names for mourning are listed first, both of which state that the crown is married to the son, and they are placed in the next sentence, which clearly shows the meaning of marrying.
Since it is obvious that small meritorious deeds lead to self-marriage, it means that great meritorious deeds can lead to self-importance. This is to express the will in simple language.
If it is said that because the father is in mourning for a great service, the son is in mourning for a minor service, and the mourning for a minor service is light, he can marry his son with a crown, but the mourning for a major service is heavy, so he is not allowed to marry himself.
If it is said that the article of small merit has already stated that one can marry, the article of great merit does not say that one can be crowned. Therefore, knowing that one is in mourning for great merit, one is not allowed to give gifts on his own, but he can be crowned and married for his son.
I believe that rituals should not be performed when in mourning. The rituals of good and bad fortune should not interfere with each other.
Although the son is at the end of his life and can get married, his father still has to perform the wedding for them if necessary.
If the father can crown his son and marry his son at the end of his great work, it means that there is no obstacle between good and bad rites; there is no obstacle between good and bad rites, how can he not be allowed to marry by himself?
If one's crown and one's own marriage interferes with mourning, then is it possible for one's crown to marry one's own son alone?
He Chen was puzzled by the fact that he was allowed to be crowned his son but not allowed to crown himself.
He also decreed that if you have accomplished a small feat of sacrifice, you are not allowed to marry a wife, and if you have a great merit of surrendering, you are not allowed to marry a wife for your son.
I have studied this purpose and found out that if you have done a great job of surrender, you cannot marry someone else, and if you have done a small job in surrender, you cannot marry someone else. This means that anyone who has done a great job in surrender cannot be married.
In this case, the "Book of Rites" should say that if you surrender, you cannot marry, how can it only talk about mourning?
Today we don’t talk about surrender, but only mourning, which actually has its meaning.

Zhu Yi, courtesy name Yanhe, was from Qiantang, Wu County. His father, Zhu Xun, served as an official in the Qi Dynasty. As a child, Zhu Yi was fond of gambling and was disliked by his community. In his youth, he reformed his habits, studied the Five Classics—especially the "Li" and "Yi"—and became skilled in literature, history, chess, calligraphy, and arithmetic. At age twenty, he went to the capital, where Shen Yue interviewed him and remarked on his diverse talents. Despite the rule that officials must be at least twenty-five, Zhu Yi was appointed at twenty-one as Yangzhou Councilor due to an imperial exception. Doctor Mingshan of the Five Classics recommended him, praising his moral character and intellect. Emperor Gaozu summoned Zhu Yi to explain the "Book of Filial Piety" and the "Book of Changes," was pleased, and appointed him to the Western Province and later as a doctor of Imperial College. He rose through various posts, including Hongluqing and prince's right guard.

In the fifth year of the Ordinary Period, during a northern expedition, Yuan Faseng of the Northern Wei sought to surrender. Zhu Yi confirmed the sincerity of the surrender, and Emperor Gaozu placed him in command. After Zhou She's death, Zhu Yi managed court affairs, military appointments, and imperial edicts. He was known for his efficiency in handling documents. In the sixth year of Datong, he lectured on the "Laozi Yi" to over a thousand listeners. He later served as a servant and general. When Hou Jing surrendered, Zhu Yi advised Emperor Gaozu to accept him, citing a dream of unification. Despite warnings from officials like Xie Li, the emperor followed Zhu Yi's advice. Hou Jing later rebelled, blaming Zhu Yi, who raised troops to defend the capital. Zhu Yi had suppressed earlier reports of Hou Jing's conspiracy, leading to the city's siege. The crown prince's poem criticized Zhu Yi, who fell ill and died at sixty-seven. Emperor Gaozu mourned him deeply and granted posthumous honors. Zhu Yi held power for over thirty years, was skilled at flattering the emperor, and amassed wealth through gifts. He was stingy, never sharing with others, and wrote over 100 works, many lost in war.

He Chen, courtesy name Guobao, was from Shanyin. His uncle He Chang taught him Confucian classics, and he excelled in the "Three Rites." After He Chang's death, He Chen sold millet to support himself. He later taught economics and was summoned by the governor of Linchuan. Emperor Gaozu appointed him as a minister and doctor of Taixue. He Chen compiled the "New Mi Law" and debated ritual matters, such as whether one could marry during mourning. He argued that rituals should not interfere with mourning, and his views were accepted. He served as a regular attendant and censor, but was dismissed for buying the princess's house. He later held various posts, including Huangmen minister and Guozi doctor. He Chen was known for his elegant demeanor and was called "He Ya" in the palace. Zhang Mian, also known as Yuan Chang, was the son of General Hong Ce. As a child, his maternal grandfather Liu Zhongde recognized his exceptional nature, declaring him a noble person of the Zhang family. During the Qi Dynasty's Yongyuan period, when his father followed Gaozu to war, ten-year-old Zhang Mian was left in Xiangyang, where his emotions mirrored the army's victories and defeats. After his father was killed by demon thieves in the first year of Tianjian, Zhang Mian mourned excessively, beyond normal rituals. Upon completing mourning, he inherited the title of Marquis of Taoyang County. At eighteen, he was appointed governor of Huainan. Concerned about his youth, his superior sent a master to evaluate him but was impressed by his appropriate decisions. Returning to the capital, he served as Prince Sheren and later as a foreign soldier joining the army. Zhang Mian studied diligently, mastered required readings, and wrote extensively, clearly critiquing various academic schools. He answered guests' questions without omission. When a palace position became vacant, the chief minister recommended Zhang Mian for his literary talent. He later served as prefect of Wuling and Prince Xima. His mother Liu Ya, due to his father's poor burial, never lived as the main wife or in official residences. Zhang Mian did not use his salary for personal gain, giving it all to his mother, leaving his household as frugal as a poor family. He was promoted to Beizhonglang and served as internal history of Yuzhang, governing with favor and without suspicion, inspiring officials and people not to commit fraud. Elders noted no such governance in decades. In the first year of Datong, he was summoned as Situ Zuo Changshi but declined due to illness, later becoming the prince's concubine and Yulin Supervisor. He was moved to Yushi Zhongcheng but demoted for arresting people and fighting with foreign envoys. As imperial censor, he was fearless and upright, prompting Gaozu to have his portrait painted to encourage officials. In the third year of Zhongdatong, he was moved to serve as a minister but died at forty-two. Gaozu wept bitterly, and Prince Zhaoming mourned, praising Zhang Mian's knowledge and official skills in a letter to his brother. Zhang Mian loved classical books, collecting over 10,000 volumes, and compiled "Hou Han Ji" and "Jin Chao" along with "Jiangzuo Collection," though unfinished. His son Fu inherited his title.

Zhang Zan, courtesy name Boxu, was Zhang Mian's third brother, adopted by his uncle Hong Ji. At eleven, he married Princess Fuyang, Emperor Gaozu's fourth daughter, becoming Prince Consort Duwei. At seventeen, he was recruited as a secretary. Standing seven feet four inches tall with handsome features, Gaozu found him remarkable. Zhang Zan was eager to learn, reading his brother's vast collection day and night. As one of four Secretary Langs, he firmly requested not to move positions to read all books in the pavilion. He was later moved to Prince Sheren and then Xima and Zhongsheren, managing records. He was as famous as Wang Xi. In the early Tongren years, Northern Wei's Liu Shanming admired him greatly. Zhang Zan was promoted to Taiwei and Minister of Libu Lang, becoming commander and minister at a young age. Pei Ziye praised him as a mouthpiece but regretted his late appointment. After mourning, he became prefect of Wuxing, simplifying administration for the people's convenience. In the fifth year, Gaozu praised him as the leader of the imperial court. Zhang Zan had conflicts with He Jingrong, refusing to treat his guests. In office, he proposed suitable ancient and modern reforms for court uniforms. In the ninth year, he was transferred to General Xuanhui and Danyang Yin but was appointed as envoy Chijie and governor Yu Guasai. On his way, he wrote "Ode to the Southern Expedition," reflecting on his journey, governance, and historical reflections. He managed Xiangzhou effectively, increasing household registration by over 100,000 and bringing peace. In the second year of Taiqing, he was recruited as leader and later as governor of multiple regions. He had conflicts with Xiao Shu and Xiao Yu, leading to his arrest and forced shaving as a Taoist priest. He was killed at fifty-one. Emperor Yuan posthumously honored him as Jian Xian Gong. Zhang Zan wrote one hundred volumes of "Hongbao" and twenty volumes of collected works. His son Zhang Wang married Princess Haiyan.

Wang Mao, whose courtesy name is Xiuyuan, was born in Qi, Taiyuan.
Grandfather Wang Shen, Beizhonglang Sima.
His father was born in Tianjin. He served as a general in the late Song Dynasty. He defeated Situ Yuancan at Shitou. He became an official with military merit and became the prefect of Brazil and Zitong counties. He was a man in Huang County.
When Wang Mao was a few years old, he was valued by his grandfather Wang Shen. He often said to relatives and friends: This child is the horse of my family, and he must be the one who establishes the family.
When he grew up, he liked to read military books and explore the main ideas in them in general and brief terms.
She is calm and reserved by nature, not sociable, eight feet tall, and has a white and beautiful face.
When Emperor Wu of Qi was still a commoner, he sighed when he saw him: "Wang Mao is young and looks so majestic. He will definitely become a talent to assist the emperor."
At the end of the Song Dynasty and the Ming Dynasty, Wang Maoren was appointed from home to serve in the imperial court. He served successively as Houjunxing, Sikong Cavalry, and Taiwei Zhongbing.
Wei general Li Wunu invaded the desert, and Wang Mao was ordered by the emperor to march westward.
After the Wei army retreated, he returned and served as Sima of Zhennan, leading the Linxiang order.
He entered Beijing and served as the captain of the Yue Cavalry School.
When the Wei army invaded Yanzhou, Wang Mao was serving as General Shi of Ningshuo to guard and reinforce the northern border. He was transferred back to serve as the former general of Jiangxia, Wang Sima of Jiangxia.
He was also promoted to General Ningshuo and Internal History of Jiangxia.
In the early years of Jianwu's reign, the Wei army besieged Sizhou, and Wang Mao led the Yingzhou army to rescue him.
Gaozu led his troops to climb Xianshou Mountain first, and Wei generals Wang Su and Liu Chang came to fight. Wang Mao followed Gaozu to resist the enemy and defeated Wang Chong and others' army.
After the Wei army retreated, Wang Mao returned to Yingzhou and served as the chief minister of the auxiliary state and the governor of Xiangyang.
When Emperor Gaozu raised a righteous army, Wang Mao consulted privately with Zhang Hongce and persuaded Emperor Gaozu to welcome Emperor He, but Emperor Gaozu did not agree to do so. These words are recorded in "Gaozu Ji".
Emperor Gaozu sent the Yong army to advance, often sending Wang Mao as the vanguard.
The army was temporarily stationed in Yingcheng. Wang Mao attacked and pacified Jiahu, defeated Guangzijin, Wu Ziyang and others, beheaded and cut off the ears of tens of thousands of people, and returned to Hanchuan to report his victory.
After Ying and Lu were pacified, he followed the emperor's troops and became the vanguard of the army.
The army was stationed in Moling. Shuhunhou sent General Wang Zhenguo to assemble the army at Zhuque Gate. The number of soldiers was said to be 200,000, and they crossed the sea to fight.
Wang Mao, Cao Jingzong and others went to attack together and defeated the enemy.
The army was allowed to pursue the fleeing enemies, and the corpses of the enemy soldiers were piled up to the height of the fence. Those who died by jumping into the Huai River were incalculable.
Chase them all the way to Xuanyang Gate.
After Jiankang City was pacified, Wang Mao was appointed as the general guarding the army, and was soon promoted to the rank of Shizhong and leading general.
The thieves set fire to Shenhu Gate. Wang Mao led his army to Dongye Gate to respond to the rescue. The thieves fired arrows at them. Wang Mao whipped his horse and advanced, while the thieves fled back.
Wang Mao believed that he had failed to control the traitors, so he petitioned to be relieved of his duties, but the emperor's generous Shao Ling did not agree.
He was also given the title of general of the town army, and was granted the title of Duke of Wangcai County, with a settlement of 2,300 households.
In the first year of the Han Dynasty, Chen Bozhi, the governor of Jiangzhou, rebelled. Wang Mao was appointed as envoy Chijie, regular servant of Sanqi, governor of Jiangzhou's military affairs, general in the southern expedition, and governor of Jiangzhou. He was given a set of drums and drums and went to conquer Chen Bozhi in the south.
Bozhi defected to Wei.
At that time, Jiujiang had just suffered from military turmoil, and the people wanted to return to farming. Wang Mao focused on farming to reduce civil service, so the people were content with agricultural production.
In the fourth year, Wei invaded Mozhong again. Wang Mao was ordered by Emperor Shao to march westward, and Wei retreated.
In the sixth year, he was promoted to the right servant of Shangshu, and he still served as a regular attendant.
However, he refused to resign and took up the post, so he was appointed as a minister in charge and a general in charge of the Central Guards, leading Prince Zhan to serve.
In the seventh year, he was appointed as a general of chariots and cavalry, and he was still appointed as Prince Zhan Shi.
In the eighth year, he took his title as Kaifu Yitong Sansi and Danyang Yin, and continued to write poems.
At that time, the world was peaceful and Emperor Gaozu was trusting gentle people. Wang Mao was in a bad mood. After drinking and drinking with the emperor, it often showed in his words and expressions. Emperor Gaozu often forgave him but did not blame him.
In the eleventh year, he was promoted to Sikong, but the positions of Shizhong and Yin remained the same.
Wang Mao resigned from Beijing and became General Zhongquan.
Wang Mao has a generous temperament. Although he does not have a great reputation as an official, he still manages to calm down the lower-level officials and the people.
He is fair and upright in his daily life. Even when he is wearing clothes and hats indoors, he is very conscientious. Even his slaves and concubines cannot see his laziness.
His posture and appearance are unique and gorgeous, his beard and eyebrows are picturesque, and he often attracts the admiration and attention of everyone when he comes in and out of court meetings.
In the second year, he served as envoy Chijie, regular attendant of Sanqi, general of hussar, Kaifu Tongsansi Zhiyi, governor of all military affairs in Jiangzhou, and governor of Jiangzhou.
He worked for three years and died in the state at the age of sixty.
Emperor Gaozu felt sorry for him and gave him 300,000 yuan and 300 pieces of cloth for his funeral.
The imperial edict said: Commending virtue and recording meritorious deeds is the decree of the Ming Emperor; remembering the deceased and remembering the past is the clear mandate of the emperor in the previous dynasty.
The original envoy Chijie, the regular attendant of Sanqi, the general of hussar, the third division of Kaifu Yitong, and the governor of Jiangzhou Wang Mao had profound knowledge and magnanimity, and the style of his utensils was correct.
From the earliest days of creation, he has done his best to fulfill his responsibilities, and has shared my joys and sorrows with great affection, regardless of separation and separation, hardships and peace.
At first, I relied on him to provide advice and support, and entrusted the court to him for long-term prosperity; but he suddenly passed away, and my heart was really filled with sorrow.
The level of etiquette should be increased to highlight his great achievements.
He can be granted the posthumous title of Shizhong or Taiwei, plus twenty people wearing decorated wooden swords, and a set of drums and music.

When Wang Mao was in Jiangzhou, he dreamed that the bell was on a shelf. He fell down for no reason, and he felt disgusted with such things.
When he wakes up, he asks people to play music.
The musicians were already lined up, and the bell and chime were on the stand. Sure enough, the rope broke for no reason and fell to the ground.
Wang Mao said to Chang Shi Liao Quan: "Wole is a favor that the emperor bestows on his meritorious officials."
The joy has reached its extreme, how can there be no sorrow?
He soon fell ill and died within a few days.
His son Zhen Zhou succeeded him. Because he did not observe etiquette during the funeral, he was reported to the government and transferred to Yue. Later, the emperor ordered him to stay in Lu Ye's post. He secretly colluded with soldiers from the Renwei Prefecture to join the army and Du Jing, planning to attack the prefecture city.
