Kong Guang had often heard that Empress Dowager Fu was fierce and cruel in dealing with others, and was good at playing politics and strategies. She raised the emperor when he was still in his infancy and educated him until he became an adult. She also helped when the emperor ascended the throne.
Kong Guang was worried that Empress Dowager Fu would interfere in government affairs and did not want her to be close to the emperor day and night, so he expressed his opinion that Empress Dowager Dingtao should build another palace to live in.
Grand Sikong Hewu said: You can live in Beigong.
The emperor listened to He Wu's words.
There is a Purple Room in the North Palace and a pavilion in the air is connected to the Weiyang Palace. Mrs. Fu indeed went to the emperor's residence from the pavilion in the morning and evening and asked the emperor to grant her a title so that her relatives could be rich and favored, which prevented the emperor from acting impartially according to the principle of integrity.
Soon, Fu Qian, the son of the Queen Mother's cousin, displayed treacherous tricks around the emperor. The emperor dismissed him from his official position and sent him back to his hometown.
Empress Dowager Fu was angry, and the emperor had no choice but to keep Fu Qian again.
Kong Guang and the Grand Sikong Master Alchemy reported: The emperor issued an edict saying: Fu Qian, the prince-in-law of the imperial court, is a clever and evil person who leaked the secrets of the court and was disloyal to the emperor. He is a scourge to the country. He should be dismissed from his official position and sent home.
Later, an edict was issued to stop the operation. All officials were puzzled and felt that there was nothing worthy of trust. This was a great damage to the emperor's sanctity, and it was indeed not a small fault.
Due to the occurrence of disasters one after another, His Majesty once left the main hall and summoned all the officials of the court to think about the reasons for the disasters. Until now, those things that were not done well in the past have not been corrected.
We ask the emperor to still send Fu Qian back to his hometown to eliminate the traitors and obey God's warning.
But Fu Qian was not sent home in the end and became a servant again.
The emperor acted in a coercive manner and obeyed the Queen Mother Fu, which was the same situation.
In addition, Empress Dowager Fu wanted to receive a title together with Emperor Cheng's mother. Many ministers obeyed her will, saying that the mother was distinguished by her son and should be given a title to promote filial piety.
Only Shidan and Renmi thought it was impossible.
It was difficult for the emperor to go against the honest opinions of his ministers, and he was internally coerced by the Empress Dowager Fu, so the matter was delayed for several years without being resolved.
Shi Dan was dismissed from office for committing a crime, and Zhu Bo replaced him as chief minister.
When Kong Guang was the late emperor, he disagreed with the emperor when discussing the successor to the throne. Later, he seriously violated the will of Empress Dowager Fu. Therefore, Fu's reigning chief minister Kong Zhubo colluded to slander and frame Kong Guang. After a few months, the emperor dismissed Kong Guang and said: The prime minister is a minister who assists the monarch. He inherits the country with the monarch and is responsible for governing the country. He also assists the emperor's deficiencies so that the country can be governed.
The emperor is confused, disasters continue, the sun and moon lose their light, mountains collapse, the Yellow River bursts, and the five stars move abnormally, these all show that I am not moral enough, and that the ministers who assist the monarch are not virtuous enough.
When you were the imperial censor, you assisted the late emperor for eight years, but you never had any loyal words or good strategies. Now I have been serving as my prime minister for three years, and I have not yet heard your advice on caring for the country and the people.
Recently, the yin and yang qi between heaven and earth have been erroneous and inconsistent. There has been no harvest for many years. The country's granaries are empty. The people are starving. Fathers and sons are scattered and wandering around. In a few days, more than 100,000 people have been displaced.
However, the duties of all the officials in the imperial court were abolished, all kinds of evil spirits were rampant, and bandits were rampant. Some attacked the government and killed officials.
I asked you many times about these things, but you showed no sorrow or fear and replied that there was no harm.
Therefore, all the officials became lazy and neglected, and did not take these things to heart. This is all your responsibility.
You bear the important responsibility of governing the country and the officials, but you can't correct my mistakes when you are above me, and you can't appease the people when you are below.
The Book of Books does not say: Do not appoint incompetent officials.
Those who manage hundreds of officials on behalf of heaven must be competent, Daohu! You hand over the palace seal of Prime Minister Boshan Hou, dismiss from office and go home.
After Kong Guang retreated to his hometown, he stayed behind closed doors.
Zhu Bo replaced Kong Guang as prime minister. A few months later, he committed suicide by following the instructions of Empress Dowager Fu and mistaking political affairs.
Pingdang succeeded Zhu Bo as prime minister, but died a few months later.
Wang Jia then took over as prime minister and made several remonstrances, disobeying the emperor's will.
Three prime ministers were replaced frequently in a short period of time, and public opinion believed that none of these prime ministers could keep up with Kong Guang.
Therefore, the emperor often missed Kong Guang.
There happened to be a solar eclipse on the fifteenth day of the first lunar month of the first year of Yuanshou, and Empress Dowager Fu died more than ten days later.
This month the emperor summoned Kong Guang to the government office to inquire about the solar eclipse.
Kong Guang replied: I heard that the sun is the origin of all penises, the representative of the king, and the symbol of supreme dignity.
When the monarch's virtue declines and his ministers become prosperous and powerful, encroaching and blocking the light of the sun, then the phenomenon of eclipse will occur.
"Shu Jing" says to use the five things of appearance, speech, sight, hearing, and thinking to establish the broad and righteous way. If there are faults in the five aspects of appearance, speech, sight, hearing, and thinking, and the righteous way is not established, then the phenomenon of disaster will gradually occur, and the six kinds of punishments and disasters given by God, namely, evil, evil, illness, poverty, weakness, and sorrow, will occur frequently.
It is said that the sun and the moon will often move randomly at this time. The sun and the moon will either move faster or rotate slower, and even a solar eclipse will occur.
"Yi Zhuan" also said that six kinds of evil qi are blocked. The dynasty of the year, the dynasty of the month, and the dynasty of the day are called three dynasties, and their induction is very strong.
A solar eclipse occurred on the first day of Xinchou in the first lunar month, which was a disaster that occurred at the meeting of the three dynasties.
God is wise and discerning. If nothing happens in the country, the phenomenon of mutation will not happen for no reason.
"Book" says: First, use the name of the Supreme King to correct the matter, which means that the phenomenon of mutation occurs because something incorrect happens.
I heard the teacher say that in order to assist the monarch, God allows disasters and strange phenomena to occur many times to warn the monarch and ask him to change his mistakes.
If the monarch is not afraid, but still conceals and perverts, ignores God's warnings, and deceives God with street noise, then there is no doubt that punitive disaster will befall him. "The Book of Songs" says: Respect God, respect God, God is extremely discerning, how difficult it is to accept the destiny!
He also said: Only by fearing the power of God can you maintain peace. These all mean that if you don't fear God, you will suffer disaster, and if you fear God, you will have good luck.
His Majesty is wise and wise, conscientious in his work, respects and obeys the warnings of God, respects various phenomena of variation, is diligent, and is open-minded. He summons hundreds of officials and officials to reflect on the causes of variation, and then leads by example, self-disciplines, prime minister, corrects everything, and neglects everything. Staying away from villains who form factions for personal gain, accepting loyal and good people, removing greedy and cruel officials, appointing wise and loyal officials, fairly rewarding and punishing people, reducing taxes, and extending benefits to the people. This is truly the foundation of handling government affairs and the primary task of dealing with all kinds of disasters.
This is a great blessing for the country.
"Shu Jing" says: Since you have accepted the destiny, you should implement virtuous government, which means implementing virtuous government to comply with God.
He also said that God will assist him sincerely, which means that if he has a loyal heart, God will assist him.
Wisely accepting and obeying the way of heaven is to improve your moral character, extend your kindness widely, become more sincere and never slack off.
The little tricks used by the world to seek blessings and eliminate misfortunes are ultimately useless in complying with God, eliminating disasters, and eliminating misfortunes to seek blessings. It is clearly revealed, and there is no doubt about it.
When the memorial was handed in, the emperor was very happy after reading it. He rewarded Kong Guangguang with silk and worshiped him as Guanglu doctor. He was given a salary of two thousand dan, and his official position was second only to the prime minister.
The emperor issued an edict asking Kong Guang to recommend someone who could serve as minister. After he wrote it and sealed it, Kong Guang wrote a letter of thanks and said: As an old man, I have held various important positions in the past without any success. I was spared from being executed for no crime and saved my life. Now I have been promoted and appointed again. As a reserve minister of the imperial court, I participate in the affairs of the government.
I, Kong Guang, am very short-sighted in wisdom and strategy. Now that I am old, I am really worried that I will die suddenly one day and have nothing to repay the emperor.
I have seen privately that in national government affairs, the post of Minister has been constantly changing, and it is very difficult for someone without outstanding talents to be qualified.
The servant of the minister is open, fair, diligent in his duties, and quick-witted when dealing with problems, so he can serve as the minister.
Now solemnly write it down and seal it for memorial.
Because of Kong Guang's recommendation, Chang became the prefect of Shuping.
Chang's surname is Chenggong, and he is from Shuhai County.
Kong Guang served as doctor for a month. Prime Minister Wang Jia was imprisoned and died. The censor doctor bought an extension and was dismissed.
Kong Guang resumed his role as the imperial censor, and two months later he resumed his role as prime minister and was granted the title of Marquis of Boshan again.
Only then did the emperor realize that the reason why Kong Guang had been dismissed from his official position was not that Kong Guang had committed a crime, but that the ministers around him had slandered and framed him, so he dismissed Fu Jia from his official position, saying: When Fu Jia was serving as a minister, he slandered and framed people who were benevolent, righteous and virtuous, and falsely accused ministers, so that virtuous and handsome people could not be reused for a long time.
On the contrary, Fu Jia was clever and hypocritical, harbored treachery, deceived the emperor, formed cliques for personal gain, blocked the sky with one hand, slandered loyal ministers, and acted unscrupulously.
Didn't the "Book of Songs" say: The flattering villain was rampant in deception and caused chaos in the country, so Fu Jia was removed from his official position and became a civilian, and was sent back to his original county.
The next year, the official position of the three princes was evaluated, and Kong Guang was changed to the post of Grand Situ.
Coinciding with the death of Emperor Ai, the Empress Dowager took Wang Mang, the new capital lord, as the Grand Sima and elected King Zhongshan as the emperor, namely Emperor Ping of the Han Dynasty.
Emperor Ping was very young, so the Empress Dowager was in charge of the government, and the Empress Dowager entrusted political affairs to Wang Mang.
During the reign of Emperor Ai, the Wang family was deposed. Therefore, the Queen Mother and Wang Mang were very resentful towards Ding, Fu and Dong Xian.
Wang Mang believed that Kong Guang was the former prime minister, a famous Confucian, trusted and admired by the world, and the Queen Mother also respected him and always received him with courtesy.
Whenever it was necessary to attack political opponents, Li Guang was always asked to help draft documents. According to the Queen Mother's orders, Kong Guang was asked to write the memorial. Anyone who has enmity against the Queen Mother, even if it is a small amount of hatred, will be retaliated and no one will be killed.
Wang Mang's power became stronger day by day. Kong Guang was very frightened and worried. He didn't know what to do, so he wrote to the emperor to resign.
Wang Mang then said to the Queen Mother: The emperor is very young and should be given a teacher.
He appointed Kong Guang as the emperor's Taifu, with the official position of Fourth Assistant. He was responsible for providing food, clothing, carriages, horses and food.
In the second year, he was promoted to Taishi, and Wang Mang served as Taifu.
Kong Guang often complained of illness and did not dare to take the throne with Wang Mang in the court.
The emperor ordered Wang Mang to go to court on the first and fifteenth day of each month and asked Wang Mang to command the city gate guards.
Wang Mang also ordered his officials to submit a memorial praising Wang Mang's merits. Emperor Ping of the Han Dynasty gave Wang Mang the title of Prime Minister, ranking him above the princes and kings and commanding hundreds of officials.
Seeing this situation, Ziguang felt even more panicked and insisted on resigning due to illness.
The Queen Mother then issued an edict saying: Taishi Kong Guang is a descendant of a saint and the son of the late emperor's teacher. He is pure and upright in virtue, proficient in morality and academics, and serves as the fourth assistant to assist the emperor.
Now I am old and sick. But highly respected ministers like Kong Guang are important ministers of the country and are still indispensable. "Book of Zhou."
Zhao Gao said: "Never abandon mature people. If the country wants to prosper, it must respect and reuse teachers."
He ordered Grand Master Kong Guang not to go to court, but to reward him with a meal every ten days.
The Grand Master was given a longevity stick, and the Huangmen Order set up a place for the Grand Master to sit within the palace. The Grand Master could hold the staff when entering the palace, and was rewarded with seventeen kinds of food. Then he returned to the mansion to retire, while his subordinate officials continued to work as usual.
Kong Guang served as the imperial censor and prime minister twice, and once as the chief situ, Taifu and Taishi. He experienced three generations of emperors and held the high position of auxiliary minister for a total of seventeen years.
After becoming the minister, he stopped teaching activities, and later became the prime minister. Sometimes he would meet his disciples to discuss and raise difficult questions, and Kong Guang would often explain his principles to them.
Many of Kong Guang's disciples were successful in their studies and became doctors and doctors. When they saw their teacher holding important positions, they all wanted his help. However, Kong Guang never recommended them, so some people complained about him.
Kong Guang acted fairly, that's all.
Kong Guang was seventy years old and died in the fifth year of Yuanshi.
Wang Mang told the Queen Mother that he would give Jiu Qing's policy book to the Taishi Boshan Hou Yinshou, and give him a carriage, a coffin, money, and miscellaneous silk.
The Shaofu set up the curtains, and sent the admonishing doctor to hold the talisman and the visitor to receive the guests to take charge of the funeral. The doctor was responsible for the funeral ceremony.
The Queen Mother also sent visitors to come with talismans in hand to express their condolences.
All the ministers and officials paid their condolences and paid their respects together.
A funeral car and an auxiliary funeral car were used to carry the emperor's Habayashi guards and many Confucian scholars, a total of four hundred people.
There were more than 10,000 funeral vehicles. Everywhere they went, passers-by burst into tears. The crying stopped after the motorcade finished.
Five hundred soldiers were used to dig a hole and lower the coffin, and the tomb was raised, just like the funeral of General Wang Feng.
He was given the title of Jian Liehou.
At first, Kong Guang was granted the title of prime minister, and later he was granted additional titles, with a total of 11,000 households.
When Kong Guang was seriously ill, he wrote a letter to return 7,000 households and the first house given by the emperor.
Kong Guang's son Kong Fang inherited the title.
After Wang Mang usurped the throne, he appointed Kong Yong, the son of Kong Guang's brother, as the Grand Sima and a marquis.
Four or five of my brothers' sons became officials and reached the rank of minister.
At the beginning, Kong Guang's father Kong Ba was granted the title of Guannei Hou Shiyi in the first year of Chuyuan.
Kong Ba wrote a letter requesting that Confucius be enshrined and sacrificed. Emperor Yuan issued an edict saying: My respected master, I commend Kong Ba, the Marquis of Guan Nei, to sacrifice 800 households with the enfeoffed food town. son.
Therefore, Kong Ba moved his eldest son's household registration back to Lu to worship Confucius.
After Kong Ba's death, his son Kong Fu succeeded to the throne.
After Kong Fu died, his son Kong Fang succeeded to the throne.
After Kong Fang died, his son Kong Mang succeeded to the throne.
In the first year of the Yuan Dynasty, the emperor granted the descendants of Zhou Gong and Confucius the title of marquis, with 2,000 households each.
Kong Mang was later granted the title of Marquis of Baocheng, and was later renamed Kong Jun to avoid Wang Mang's taboo.
Ma Gong, courtesy name Youqing, was born in Qixian County, Shuhai.
After studying Yan's "Spring and Autumn Annals", he was selected as a member of the Jia Division in response to the examination, and served as a minister. He was later promoted to the chief historian of Chu, and was dismissed soon after.
Later he served as Prime Minister Shi Sizhi.
Shi Dan recommended that Ma Gong was of high moral character and was promoted to Ting Weiping. He served successively as the governor of Qingzhou and the prefect of Runan and Jiujiang. He was qualified for official positions and received praise everywhere he went.
Therefore, he was recruited by the emperor as Zhan Shi, Guang Luxun, and General You. He replaced Kong Guang as the chief disciple and was granted the title of Fudehou.
After Kong Guang's death as Grand Master, Ma Gong succeeded Kong Guang as Grand Master and concurrently served as Situ.
During the reign of Emperor Ai, Ma Gong discussed the issue of the title of the emperor's grandmother, the Empress Dowager Fu, with the prime minister and the imperial censor. During the Yuanshi period, Wang Mang moved the tomb of Empress Dowager Fu back to Dingtao, buried it according to common people's etiquette, and investigated the charges against those who had discussed the funeral.
Because Ma Gong had a close friendship with Wang Mang, he was the only one who was not forced to investigate. Ma Gong felt ashamed and frightened, so he wrote a letter to the emperor to confess his guilt and asked to retire.
Wang Mang issued an edict in the name of the Empress Dowager and gave Ma Gong a policy letter saying:
Taishi and Grand Situ Fudehou wrote a letter saying: When I was serving as Guangluxun, I discussed the nickname of the mother of the late Dingtao Gongwang. It was said that a woman should be honored by her husband's title, and the nickname should be Empress Xiaoyuan Fu, and she should be called Weiling Shuyuan.
I know that concubines cannot represent the king, and the lowly ones cannot be compared with the noble ones, but they cater to the will of the superiors, agree with them, go against the scriptures, and express heresy, causing the emperor to be confused and make mistakes.
As a minister, if you are disloyal to your superior, you should be put to death. Fortunately, the emperor asked me to repent and changed my ways, and I was able to save my life.
I have deeply reflected on myself. I served as the fourth minister in the court, enjoyed the treatment of the three princes when I came in and out, and was given the title of lord. I really have no face to enter the court again, no intention to hold an official position anymore, and I should no longer enjoy the food.
I respectfully hand over the great seal of Grand Master and Grand Situ Fudehou to make way for the virtuous people.
They all believe that the four auxiliary ministers are responsible for implementing the country's charter laws, and the three ministers shoulder the important task of assisting the monarch. Without outstanding moral character, they cannot hold this position.
What you said in your letter shows that you are loyal and heartwarming, but just because you made the mistake before you repented, no one dared to protect you. I respect you very much and will not deprive you of your title and land, in order to promote the great righteousness of people since ancient times.
You hand over the seal of Grand Master Situ to the envoy, and return home to take care of yourself in your old age.
After Wang Mang usurped the throne, he appointed Ma Gong as the crown prince's counselor and died in office.
His real surname is Ma Ya, and Ma Gong is the name of the academic officer he studied at, so he is called the Ma family.
Zan said: After Emperor Xiaowu attached great importance to Confucianism and appointed Gongsun Hong as his Confucian prime minister, Cai Yi, Wei Xian, Xuancheng, Kuang Heng, Zhang Yu, Zhai Fangjin, Kong Guang, Pingdang, Ma Gong and Pingdang's son Pingyan all regarded Confucianism as great Confucianism. He held the position of prime minister, wore Confucian clothes, preached the words of the previous kings, was erudite and tolerant, had good conduct, and was worthy of praise. However, in order to preserve his salary and official position, he suffered from flattery and ridicule.
They all act according to the ancient principles of straight conduct, how can they be qualified for their duties!
summary:
Kuang Heng, courtesy name Zhigui, was born in Haicheng County. His family had farmed for generations, and despite poverty, he loved studying and worked as a hired laborer to fund his education. His energy exceeded ordinary people, and many Confucian scholars praised him. He was awarded the title of "Jia Ke" but failed to pass its regulations, so he was appointed as Taichang's storyteller and later as Pingyuan County Literature. Scholars recommended him as unparalleled in classical studies, but Emperor Xuan did not favor Confucian scholars and sent him back. However, the crown prince secretly appreciated him.

When Emperor Yuan ascended the throne, Shi Gao appointed Kuang Heng as historian of Cao and recommended him to the emperor, who made him a doctor. During disasters like solar eclipses and earthquakes, Kuang Heng submitted a memorial stating that different times required different governance. He observed that amnesty did not reduce crime and argued that education should promote etiquette and humility. He criticized corrupt customs, greed, and luxury, urging the emperor to set an example through moral leadership. He cited classical texts to support his arguments and recommended reducing palace expenses, eliminating extravagance, promoting virtuous officials, and reforming education. The emperor was pleased and promoted him to Guanglu Doctor and Prince Shaofu.

Kuang Heng frequently advised the emperor on proper conduct, emphasizing that governing a country begins with governing one's family. He stressed the importance of distinguishing between the queen and concubines and establishing proper hierarchies. After Emperor Cheng ascended the throne, Kuang Heng warned about choosing a spouse according to Confucian etiquette. He later submitted a memorial to renovate suburban temples and cancel extravagant sacrifices. During Emperor Yuan's reign, Kuang Heng feared Zhongshu Ling Shi Xian and did not oppose him. When Emperor Cheng first ruled, Kuang Heng and Zhen Tan impeached Shi Xian, but were themselves impeached for not reporting Shi Xian's crimes earlier. The emperor did not punish Kuang Heng, but he felt ashamed and asked to resign. The emperor refused and encouraged him.

Kuang Heng's son Kuang Chang killed someone while drunk and was imprisoned. Kuang Heng's brother conspired to rescue him, and when discovered, Kuang Heng pleaded guilty. The emperor restored his position, but Kuang Heng was later impeached for land theft. His fiefdom in Le'an Township had mistakenly used incorrect boundaries for over ten years, gaining 400 extra hectares. Kuang Heng did not correct this and collected rent from the additional land. He was impeached, and although the emperor did not punish him severely, he was removed from the post of prime minister and demoted to a commoner. He died at home. His son Kuang Xian was also proficient in classics and held the position of Jiu Qing.

Zhang Yu, courtesy name Ziwen, was born in Ruan County. As a child, he liked watching fortune tellers and became skilled at divination. He studied the Book of Changes and the Analects of Confucius in Chang'an, then gathered disciples to teach. During Emperor Xuan's reign, Xiao Wangzhi praised his knowledge, but the emperor did not approve his appointment. Later, he became a doctor and taught the prince the Analects of Confucius. When Emperor Cheng ascended, Zhang Yu was appointed Guanglu Dafu and served as Shizhong. He felt uneasy serving alongside the authoritarian Wang Feng and repeatedly asked to resign, but the emperor refused and rewarded him generously. Zhang Yu eventually became prime minister and was granted the title of Marquis of Anchang. After six years, he resigned due to old age and illness.

Zhang Yu was cautious and kind, engaging in business and farming. He bought 400 hectares of fertile farmland and lived luxuriously, enjoying music. He treated his students differently: with Dai Chong, he shared wine and music in the back hall, while with Peng Xuan, he had simple meals in the main hall. When old, he built a tomb at Fei Niu Pavilion in Pingling, which was a royal ancestral worship site. Despite Wang Gen's objections, the emperor granted his request. Wang Gen slandered him, but the emperor respected Zhang Yu even more. When the emperor visited him during illness, Zhang Yu requested that his daughter be closer, and the emperor transferred her husband. The emperor also appointed Zhang Yu's youngest son as Huang Menlang. Zhang Yu served as the emperor's teacher even after resigning, and the emperor consulted him on major decisions. During solar eclipses and earthquakes, when officials blamed the Wang family, Zhang Yu advised the emperor not to trust such claims, dispelling doubts about Wang. He died in the second year of Jianping and was given the title of Marquis of Jie.

Kong Guang, courtesy name Zixia, was the fourteenth generation grandson of Confucius. His father Kong Ba was a doctor and teacher to the crown prince. Kong Guang was proficient in classics and was elected as Yilang before age twenty. Kuang Heng recommended him as an admonishing doctor, but he was demoted for disagreeing with the emperor. He later became a doctor and successfully completed missions, gaining fame. He was promoted to Guanglu Dafu and served as Shangshu for over ten years, maintaining laws and revising systems. He was cautious, never leaking court affairs, and avoided forcefully remonstrating. He recommended officials secretly and did not form factions. He became imperial censor and later prime minister, granted the title of Marquis of Boshan.

During the succession debate, Kong Guang argued for King Zhongshan based on blood relations, but the emperor chose King Dingtao. Kong Guang was demoted to Tingwei. Later, he argued that Chunyu Chang's concubines who left before his crime should not be implicated, and the emperor agreed. After Emperor Cheng's sudden death, Kong Guang was appointed prime minister. When Emperor Ai ruled, Kong Guang advised against Empress Dowager Fu living close to the emperor, but was overruled. He later opposed retaining the treacherous Fu Qian, but the emperor kept him. Kong Guang was eventually dismissed for failing to advise properly during disasters. After several prime ministers failed, the emperor recalled Kong Guang during a solar eclipse. Kong Guang explained that eclipses occurred when ministers became too powerful and advised the emperor to reform governance. The emperor reappointed him as prime minister.

Under Empress Dowager and Wang Mang's rule, Kong Guang was used to draft documents attacking political opponents. Fearing Wang Mang's growing power, Kong Guang tried to resign. Wang Mang appointed him as the emperor's Taifu, and later Taishi. Kong Guang often claimed illness to avoid attending court with Wang Mang. He served as imperial censor and prime minister twice, and as chief situ, Taifu, and Taishi, holding high positions for seventeen years. He died at age seventy in the fifth year of Yuanshi, receiving an elaborate funeral with thousands of mourners. His title was Jian Liehou. His descendants inherited his title, and Wang Mang later appointed his nephew as Grand Sima.

Ma Gong, courtesy name Youqing, studied Yan's Spring and Autumn Annals and served as a minister. He was promoted to Ting Weiping and served as governor of several provinces, gaining praise. He replaced Kong Guang as chief disciple and was granted the title of Fudehou. After Kong Guang's death, Ma Gong succeeded him as Grand Master and Situ. During the Yuanshi period, Wang Mang investigated those who discussed Empress Dowager Fu's funeral. Because Ma Gong was Wang Mang's friend, he was not investigated, but he felt ashamed and resigned. Wang Mang allowed him to return home. After Wang Mang usurped the throne, Ma Gong became the crown prince's counselor and died in office.

translation:
Wei Qing, courtesy name Zhongqing.
His father, Zheng Ji, was from Pingyang, Hedong Province. He served as a county official and worked as an errand in the Pingyang Hou family.
Pingyang Hou Cao Shou married Princess Yang Xinchang, the sister of Emperor Mowu.
Zheng Ji had an affair with his master's servant Wei Wei and gave birth to Wei Qing.
Wei Qing had an elder brother, Wei Changjun, and an elder sister, Wei Zifu. Wei Zifu was favored by Emperor Wu in Princess Pingyang's family, so Wei Qing assumed the surname Wei.
Wei's eldest daughter is Junru, her second daughter is Shaoer, and her third daughter is Wei Zifu.
Wei Zifu's younger brother Bu Guang took the surname Wei.
Wei Qing was considered a member of Pingyang Hou's family and returned to his father's home when he was a child.
His father made him herd sheep, and his aunt's sons treated him as a slave and were not counted among their brothers.
Wei Qing once followed someone to the prisoner's room in Ganquan Palace. A prisoner who was being tortured came to him and said, "You are a noble person. If you become an official, you can become a marquis."
Wei Qing smiled and said: "A son born from a slave would be very satisfied if he could not be beaten or scolded. How could there be such a good thing as becoming a prince?"
When Wei Qing grew up, he became a knight of the Pingyang Hou family and followed Princess Pingyang.
In the spring of the second year of Jianyuan, Wei Qing's sister Wei Zifu entered the palace and was favored by the emperor.
Queen Chen is the daughter of the eldest princess. She has no son and is jealous of others.
The eldest princess heard that Wei Zifu was favored and was pregnant. She was jealous of her and sent people to arrest Wei Qing.
Wei Qing was working as an errand in Jianzhang Palace at that time and was not yet famous.
The eldest princess caught Wei Qing, imprisoned him, and wanted to kill him.
Wei Qing's friend Qi Lang Gongsun Ao and the warriors went to snatch him out, and Wei Qing avoided death.
When the emperor heard about this, he summoned Wei Qing and asked him to be the eunuch of Jianzhang Palace and serve as a minister.
When his half-brothers became prominent, the rewards amounted to thousands of gold in a few days.
Jun Ru married Grand Servant Sun He as his wife.
Wei Shaoer originally had an affair with Chen Zhang, and the emperor summoned Chen Zhang to make him an official.
Gongsun Ao thus became more prominent.
Wei Zifu became the emperor's wife.
Wei Qing became a doctor in Taizhong.
In the sixth year of Yuanguang, Wei Qing served as the cavalry general and attacked the Xiongnu and sent troops to Shanggu County; Gongsun He served as the light chariot general and left Yunzhong County; Taizhong doctor Gongsun Ao served as the cavalry general and left Dai County; Wei Wei Li Guang served as the Xiaocai general and left Yanmen County.
Each army has one cavalry. Wei Qing marched to Longcheng and annihilated hundreds of enemy troops.
The cavalry general Gongsun Ao lost 7,000 cavalry, and the guard Li Guang was captured alive by the enemy, but fortunately escaped. Both of them were sentenced to death and made atonement by becoming commoners.
Gongsun He also had no military exploits.
Only Wei Qing conferred the title of Marquis of Guannei.
After that, the Huns continued to invade the borders.
The incident is recorded in "The Biography of the Huns".

Wei Qing, courtesy name Zhongqing, was the illegitimate son of Zheng Ji, a county official in Pingyang, and a servant named Wei. He assumed the surname Wei after his sister Wei Zifu gained favor with Emperor Wu. As a youth, Wei Qing herded sheep and was treated poorly by his relatives. A prisoner once prophesied he would become a marquis, but Wei Qing dismissed this, content to avoid beatings. He later became a knight for the Pingyang Hou family.

Wei Zifu's entry into the palace and pregnancy provoked jealousy from Empress Chen and her mother, the Grand Princess, who imprisoned Wei Qing. His friend Gongsun Ao rescued him, and the emperor subsequently appointed Wei Qing as a eunuch and minister. His rise brought wealth to his family. In 129 BC, Wei Qing led a cavalry attack on the Xiongnu, reaching Longcheng and killing hundreds. He was made Marquis of Guannei, while other generals faced punishment for failures.

In subsequent campaigns, Wei Qing defeated the Xiongnu, capturing livestock and driving out kings. He was granted the title of Marquis of Changping with 3,800 households. The emperor praised his victories, which included pacifying the Henan area and building Shuofang City. Despite continued Xiongnu raids, Wei Qing's successes led to additional rewards.

In 124 BC, Wei Qing led a surprise attack on the Xiongnu's Right King, capturing over 15,000 people and millions of livestock. He was promoted to General-in-Chief, and his sons were made marquises. Wei Qing declined the honors, crediting his officers. The emperor then rewarded several subordinates with marquisates.

In 123 BC, Wei Qing's campaign saw the defection of former Xiongnu marquis Zhao Xin and the destruction of Su Jian's force. Wei Qing spared Su Jian, sending him to the emperor for judgment. That year, Huo Qubing, Wei Qing's nephew, began his rise, leading a successful raid with 800 cavalry and being made Marquis of Champion.

Huo Qubing's subsequent campaigns were highly successful, including capturing the Xiongnu's golden statue and defeating the Hunxie King, who surrendered with 100,000 people. Huo Qubing was rewarded with additional households, and the surrendered Xiongnu were settled as vassal states.

In 119 BC, Wei Qing and Huo Qubing led a massive campaign. Wei Qing defeated the Xiongnu Chanyu but failed to capture him. Huo Qubing's forces killed over 70,000 enemies. Both were made Grand Sima, but Huo Qubing's star rose while Wei Qing's declined. Huo Qubing died in 117 BC, deeply mourned by the emperor.

Wei Qing died in 106 BC, having attacked the Xiongnu seven times and killing over 50,000 enemies. He recovered the Hetao region and established Shuofang County. His three sons were marquises, but all lost their titles. Huo Qubing's six campaigns killed over 110,000 enemies and opened the Hexi region. His subordinates also received honors. The text concludes with brief biographies of other generals and notes that Wei Qing and Huo Qubing refrained from recruiting scholars, following the emperor's wishes.

summary:
Ban Gu asserts that the Tang, Yao, Yu, Shun, Xia, Shang, and Zhou dynasties, along with the "Book of Songs" and "Shangshu," are foundational to the classics. He believes ancient sage-kings like Yao and Shun must have had texts like the "Yao Canon" to spread their virtue. The Han Dynasty, inheriting Tang Yao's legacy, saw Sima Qian privately write the "Chronicle of the Emperor," ranking Han after the Hundred Kings. Ban Gu then compiled the "Book of Han," covering 230 years from Emperor Gaozu to the murders of Xiaoping and Wang Mang.

The "Deshu" outlines the purpose of each chapter. It begins with Emperor Gaozu, who inherited Yao's virtues, overthrew the Qin, and established new systems. Subsequent chapters cover Emperors Huidi, Gaohou, Wen, Jing, Wu, Zhao, Xuan, Yuan, Cheng, Ai, and Ping, detailing their reigns, achievements, and failures. For instance, Emperor Wu expanded territory and promoted culture, while Emperor Yuan's reliance on eunuchs tarnished his virtue.

The text then lists various "Biao" (tables) covering princes, kings, marquises, meritorious officials, and foreign relatives. It also includes "Zhi" (treatises) on topics like music, punishment, food and goods, sacrifices, astronomy, five elements, geography, and waterways. These sections examine historical systems, natural phenomena, and cultural practices.

Biographies follow, detailing figures from Chen Sheng and Xiang Ji to Han Xin, Zhang Liang, and others. Each biography highlights key events and moral lessons. For example, Zhang Liang's strategies aided the Han, while Xiang Yu's tyranny led to his downfall. The text also covers scholars, cruel officials, knights, and foreign relations, including the Xiongnu and Western Regions.

The final sections address the rise and fall of imperial relatives, from Empress Gao to Wang Mang, who usurped the Han throne. Ban Gu condemns Wang Mang's tyranny and concludes with a call to examine his evil deeds. The summary emphasizes strict adherence to the text, avoiding external knowledge or inference.

Sima Xiangru, courtesy name Changqing, was born in Chengdu, Shu County. As a youth, he studied literature and practiced fencing. After completing his studies, he admired Lin Xiangru's character and changed his name accordingly. He purchased a government position serving Emperor Jing of Han, but found the role unsatisfying. Emperor Jing did not appreciate poetry, so when King Xiao of Liang visited the capital with scholars including Zou Yang and Meicheng, Xiangru associated with them. After King Xiao died, Xiangru returned home impoverished.

His friend Wang Ji, magistrate of Linyin County, invited Xiangru to stay. Xiangru lived outside the city, and though the magistrate visited daily, Xiangru eventually claimed illness and refused to see him, which only increased Wang Ji's respect. Wealthy locals Prince Zhuo and Cheng Yin, noticing the magistrate's distinguished guest, arranged a banquet. When invited, Xiangru initially declined, forcing the magistrate to personally fetch him. At the banquet, Xiangru's demeanor impressed everyone. When the magistrate brought out a zither, Xiangru played several tunes.

Zhuo Wangsun's daughter Wenjun, recently widowed, loved music. Xiangru used the zither to flirt with her. Wenjun secretly watched him from a doorway, admiring him. After the banquet, Xiangru sent gifts to Wenjun's servant to convey his feelings. Wenjun eloped with Xiangru that night, and they fled to Chengdu, where his home was bare except for four walls. Zhuo Wangsun was furious and refused to give them any money. Eventually, Wenjun persuaded Xiangru to return to Linyin, where they sold their possessions and opened a tavern, with Wenjun serving wine. Ashamed, Zhuo Wangsun was persuaded by relatives to give them a hundred slaves, a million in money, and wedding belongings. They returned to Chengdu, bought land, and became wealthy.

Later, Yang Deyi, a native of Shu serving as a dog keeper, praised "Zixu Fu" to Emperor Wu. When the emperor learned Xiangru wrote it, he summoned him. Xiangru confirmed this but offered to compose a hunting rhapsody for the emperor. He created three fictional characters—Zixu, Mr. Wuyou, and a deceased man—to discuss hunting. Zixu boasted of Chu's Yunmeng Marsh, describing its vast mountains, minerals, plants, animals, and the King of Chu's grand hunting expeditions. Mr. Wuyou criticized Zixu for boasting rather than praising virtue. The deceased man then described the emperor's Shanglin Garden, far surpassing anything in Qi or Chu, with its eight rivers, diverse terrain, abundant flora and fauna, and imperial hunts. He concluded by advocating frugality and virtue, warning against excessive luxury. The emperor was pleased and appointed Xiangru as a court gentleman.

Sima Xiangru served as a Langguan when Tang Meng was ordered to open Yelang and Fenzhong in the west, levying soldiers from Bajun and Shujun and executing leaders who disobeyed, causing great fear among the people. The emperor sent Xiangru to blame Tang Meng and inform the people that these actions were not the emperor's original intent. The message explained that the barbarians had long invaded the border, but the emperor had brought peace to China, attacked the Huns, and pacified Minyue and Nanyue. The recruitment of soldiers was meant to prevent war, not to cause fear. The emperor condemned those who committed suicide or fled from conscription, emphasizing the duty of subjects to serve their country. He also criticized the lack of moral education among the people and their fathers and brothers.

Xiangru returned to report. Tang Meng had opened Yelang and recruited tens of thousands of soldiers from Ba, Shu, and Guanghan to build a road, which took two years and cost hundreds of millions, with many soldiers dying. Many in Shu and the Han court opposed this. The commanders of Yinyi and Zha, seeing Nanyi's rewards, wished to become Han vassals. The emperor consulted Nuojia, who noted that the Yi tribes near Shu had been opened during Qin but abandoned after Han. The emperor agreed to reopen them, appointing Xiangru as Zhonglang General to pacify the southwestern barbarians. Xiangru used officials and property from Ba and Shu to bribe the barbarians, and the people of Shu were proud of his mission. Zhuo Wangsun, Xiangru's father-in-law, distributed property equally to his daughter. Xiangru pacified the barbarians, who submitted to Han, and the emperor was pleased.

However, many in Shu and some ministers opposed opening the southwestern barbarians. Xiangru wrote an article to admonish the emperor, using a conversation with the elders of Shu to question their views. He argued that the Han dynasty's virtues were vast, and the barbarians should be brought under control. He criticized the elders for their shortsightedness, comparing the emperor's efforts to those of Xia Yu in controlling floods. He emphasized that the emperor's goal was to extend benevolence and stop conquest, and that the people's labor was justified for such a grand cause. The elders eventually agreed with him.

Later, Xiangru was accused of accepting bribes and dismissed, but was reinstated as Langguan after a year. He suffered from diabetes and often stayed home due to illness. He once accompanied the emperor to hunt at Changyang Palace and advised against dangerous hunting, warning of potential disasters. The emperor appreciated his advice. Xiangru also wrote a eulogy for Qin II's mistakes and composed "Adult Fu" to express the emperor's desire for immortality. The emperor was delighted with the fu.

After Xiangru's death, the emperor sent for his writings but found none. His wife said he often wrote but had no books left. Xiangru had left a letter about Fengshan, which the emperor found strange. The letter discussed ancient monarchs and the importance of Fengshan rituals, arguing that the Han dynasty's virtues surpassed those of Zhou and that the emperor should perform the rituals. The emperor eventually performed the Fengshan ceremony eight years after Xiangru's death.

The historian praised Xiangru's works for their moral lessons, despite their exaggerations, comparing them to the satires in the Book of Songs. However, Yang Xiong criticized Xiangru for encouraging extravagance with his ornate language.

There is also the "Shiben", which records the ancestors and lineages of emperors, princes, and officials from the Yellow Emperor to the Spring and Autumn Period.
After the Spring and Autumn Period, seven kingdoms competed for supremacy, and finally the Qin State annexed all the vassal states. The history book that records this period of history is the Warring States Policy.
The rise of the Han Dynasty overthrew the Qin Dynasty and brought peace to the world. This period of history is recorded in the Chu-Han Spring and Autumn Annals.
Therefore, Sima Qian used some historical materials from "Zuo Shi Chun Qiu" and "Guo Yu" and "Shi Ben" and "Warring States Policy" to state the historical facts of "Chu Han Chun Qiu" and continued to record subsequent historical events, ending in the Tianhan period.
The history of the Qin and Han Dynasties is very detailed.
As for collecting and excerpting scriptures and biographies, and recording the historical events of several families, there are many places that are rough and concise, and some are contradictory.
In addition, he has covered a wide range of subjects, and has penetrated the classics and biographies, spanning thousands of years from ancient to modern times. This is the result of his diligent efforts.
In addition, his view of right and wrong is very different from that of the saints. When discussing the great road, he mainly focuses on Huang Lao's theory and supplements it with the Six Classics; when describing knights, he demotes hermits and promotes traitors; when describing economic activities, he advocates power and wealth and humiliates the poor. These are his shortcomings.
However, from Liu Xiang to Yang Xiong, these people were well-read, and they all praised Sima Qian for his talent as a good historian. They admired him for being good at explaining the truth of things in a preface, clear distinction but not gorgeous, simple but not vulgar. well!
Although Sima Qian was knowledgeable and well-informed, he could not rely on his wisdom to protect himself. He had already suffered the death penalty and was still writing vigorously in prison. What he stated in his letter to Ren An was also credible.
Investigate why he mourns himself, it belongs to the Book of Songs. People like Xiangbo in "Xiaoya".
Like the Book of Songs. As stated in "Daya", it is so difficult to be discerning and smart and still protect yourself!
summary:
The lineage of the Sima family, who were descendants of the ancient officials Zhong and Li, responsible for astronomy and geography during the reigns of Zhuanxu, Yao, Shun, and through the Xia and Shang dynasties. During the Western Zhou, their descendant Xiu Fu was named Cheng Bo. By King Xuan of Zhou, they lost their official positions and became the Sima clan, who then served as historians for the Zhou dynasty. During the reigns of King Hui and King Xiang of Zhou, the Sima family moved to Jin, and later scattered to Wei, Zhao, and Qin. In Wei, a descendant became prime minister of Zhongshan; in Zhao, they were known for sword theory; in Qin, Sima Cuo argued with Zhang Yi about conquering Shu, led the campaign, and became governor of Shu. His grandson Sima Qi served under Bai Qi and was involved in the Battle of Changping, after which both were ordered to die. Sima Qi's descendants served as iron officials in Qin, and later Sima Yan was made King of Yin by Xiang Yu. Sima Yan's son Sima Wutang served as mayor of Chang'an in Han, and his descendants included Sima Tan, who became Grand Historian.

Sima Tan studied astronomy, the Book of Changes, and Taoism, and served under Emperor Wu of Han. He worried that scholars misunderstood the six schools of thought—Yin-Yang, Confucianism, Mohism, Legalism, Mingjia, and Taoism—and discussed their principles. He noted that Yin-Yang had many taboos but its seasonal order was useful; Confucianism was broad but lacked essentials, though its rituals were important; Mohism was frugal but hard to follow, yet its emphasis on economy was valuable; Legalism was harsh but upheld the ruler-minister distinction; Mingjia was too formal but its name-reality dialectic was worth considering; and Taoism united spirit and action, absorbed strengths of other schools, and was concise and effective. He criticized Confucianism for tiring the ruler and praised Taoism for its simplicity and adaptability.

Sima Tan had a son, Sima Qian, who was born in Longmen, farmed and herded, and could read ancient texts at ten. At twenty, he traveled extensively, visiting historical sites and studying in Qi and Lu. He became a doctor and was sent on a mission to the southwest. Upon returning, he found his father ill in Luoyang. His father, unable to participate in the imperial Fengshan ceremony, urged Sima Qian to continue their ancestral work as historians, emphasizing the importance of recording history. Sima Qian promised to complete his father's plan. After his father's death, Sima Qian became Grand Historian and began compiling historical records. He later suffered the Li Ling disaster, was imprisoned, and castrated. Despite this, he continued his work, writing the "Records of the Grand Historian" from the Yellow Emperor to Emperor Wu. The text includes a detailed table of contents for the 130 chapters, covering annals, tables, treatises, hereditary houses, and biographies.

Sima Qian wrote a letter to his friend Ren An, explaining his reasons for enduring humiliation rather than committing suicide. He emphasized the importance of completing his historical work, comparing himself to ancient figures like King Wen, Confucius, Qu Yuan, and others who wrote under duress. He argued that death could be heavier than a mountain or lighter than a feather, and that his duty was to finish his book to express his thoughts and preserve history. After his death, his works gradually spread, and his grandson Yang Pang helped publish them. The text concludes with a commentary praising Sima Qian as a talented historian but noting his deviations from orthodox views, such as favoring Huang-Lao over the Six Classics and promoting knights and wealth.

In the fourth year of Emperor Gaozu's reign, Duke Lu, the Marquis of Linsi, passed away.

Mrs. Qi sang a song while pounding rice: The son is a king, the mother is a slave, pounding rice all day long, often accompanied by death!
Three thousand miles apart, who can tell you?
Queen Mother Lu was furious when she heard about it and said: Do you still want to rely on your son?
He summoned King Zhao to Chang'an and planned to kill him.
The envoy went back and forth three times, but Zhou Chang, the Prime Minister of Zhao, refused to let King Zhao go.
The Queen Mother summoned Prime Minister Zhao and summoned him to Chang'an.
Then he sent someone to summon King Zhao, and King Zhao came.
Emperor Hui was kind by nature and knew that the Queen Mother hated King Zhao, so he went to Ba Shang to greet King Zhao in person, and they entered the palace together, eating and living in the same place.
A few months later, Emperor Hui went out to hunt in the morning, but King Zhao did not get up early. The Queen Mother sent someone to give him poisoned wine while he was sleeping.
When Emperor Hui came back, King Zhao was already dead.
The Queen Mother cut off Mrs. Qi's hands and feet, gouged out her eyes, smoked her deaf ears, drank dumb medicine, and threw her in a cave to wrap her up, calling her a "human pig."
A few months later, Emperor Hui was called to see the pigs.
When Huitong saw and asked, he realized that this was Mrs. Qi, and he burst into tears. From then on, he became ill and did not recover for more than a year.
Emperor Hui sent someone to tell the Queen Mother: This is not something humans do.
As the Queen Mother's son, I will not be able to govern the world after all.
From then on, he drank and had fun every day and ignored political affairs at all. He died seven years later.
The Queen Mother mourned Emperor Hui and cried without tears.
Zhang Piqiang, the son of Liuhou, was a minister and was only fifteen years old. He said to the Prime Minister Chen Ping: The Queen Mother only has one son, the Emperor. Now she cries but does not feel sad. Do you know the reason for this?
Chen Ping said: What is the reason?
Zhang Piqiang said: The emperor has no eldest son, and the queen mother is afraid of you ministers.
Now, if the Queen Mother is asked to appoint Lu Tai and Lu Chan as generals, let them command the Southern Army and the Northern Army respectively, and give official positions to the Lu family members so that they can work in the court.
This will put the Queen Mother at ease, and you will be lucky enough to avoid death!
Chen Ping followed Zhang Piqiang's plan to invite the Queen Mother. The Queen Mother was overjoyed and began to cry sadly.

Now that the Lu family has been crowned king, the ministers are all aggrieved.
I am about to die, and I am afraid that the ministers will take the opportunity to cause chaos. You must lead the army to guard the palace, and do not go out to mourn, lest you be controlled by others.
After the death of the Empress Dowager, Taiwei Zhou Bo, Prime Minister Chen Ping, Zhu Xuhou Liu Zhang and others jointly executed Lu Chan and Lu Lu, and captured all the Lu family members, young and old, and killed them all.
So he welcomed Dai Wang and established him as emperor, that is, Emperor Xiaowen.
Empress Zhang of Emperor Xiaohui.

After the death of Empress Dowager Lu, the ministers brought order to the chaos and finally annihilated the Lu family.
The young emperor Hengshan King, Huainan King, and Jichuan King were all killed because they were not the biological sons of Emperor Xiaohui.

Bo Ji's father died in Shanyin and was buried there.
When the princes rebelled against the Qin Dynasty, Wei Bao proclaimed himself king, and Wei Yu sent her daughter to the Wei palace.
Xu Fu met Bo Ji and said that she could give birth to the emperor.

The king of Han asked about the reason, and the two men told him the truth.
The King of Han felt pity for Bo Ji, so he summoned her that day and planned to protect her.
Bo Ji said to the King of Han: Last night, I dreamed of a dragon coiled on my chest.
The King of Han said: This is a sign of your honor. I will help you achieve it.
Fortunately, Bo Ji became pregnant.
Emperor Wen was born in this year and was made king at the age of eight.
Since Bo Ji gave birth to her son, she rarely saw the emperor.
After the death of Emperor Gaozu, those favored concubines such as Mrs. Qi were hated by Empress Lu and were imprisoned and unable to leave the palace.
Because Bo Ji was rarely summoned by the emperor, she was able to follow her son to Dai and became the Queen Mother of Dai.
Bo Zhao, the younger brother of the Queen Mother Dai, also followed to the Kingdom of Dai.

Therefore, they welcomed King Dai as the emperor, honored the Queen Mother Dai as the Queen Mother, and named Bo Zhao, the Queen Mother's younger brother, Zhihou.

Liang Yang also set up a cemetery for Mrs. Lingwen, with the same specifications and rituals as the cemetery for Marquis Lingwen.
The Queen Mother lost her father in her early years and was raised by the Wei family of her grandmother's family. She summoned the Wei family and gave them preferential treatment, and rewarded them according to the distance of their relationship.
One member of the Bo family was granted the title of Marquis.

Because Empress Lu was a queen, she could not be buried with Emperor Gaozu in Changling, so a separate mausoleum was specially built close to Emperor Wen.
Empress Xiaowen Dou was the mother of Emperor Jing. When Empress Dowager Lu came to power, she was elected to the palace as a child of a good family.
After he was established, some maids were selected to leave the palace and be given to the princes and kings, five each. Concubine Dou was also selected from the palace.

However, the eunuch forgot her instructions and mistakenly put her name on the list of Dai Guo.
After the list was submitted, the emperor issued an edict to approve it.
When it was time to set off, Dou Ji burst into tears and resented the eunuch. She didn't want to go, so others persuaded her to leave reluctantly.
When he arrived in the Kingdom of Dai, King Dai only favored Shi Ji and gave birth to a daughter named Liu.

One evening at dusk, more than a hundred people were sleeping on the edge of the cliff. The cliff suddenly collapsed and everyone sleeping on the edge of the cliff was crushed to death. Only Shaojun survived.

He followed his master to Chang'an and heard that the newly canonized queen was originally from Guanjin and her surname was Bao.

Empress Dou told Emperor Wen these things, and then summoned Guang Guo for questioning. He told the whole story in detail, and it turned out to be true.
Asked about some past events he still remembered, he said: When my sister left me to go west, she said goodbye to me at the inn, asked for rice juice to wash my hair, and then gave me a meal before leaving.
So Queen Dou held his hand and cried loudly, and the waiters on the left and right also became sad.
He rewarded Guang Guo heavily and allowed him to live in Chang'an.
Jianghou Zhou Bo, General Guan Ying and others said: If we people do not die, our lives will be in the hands of these two people.
They were from a humble background and had to choose a good mentor for them, lest they follow the old example of the Lu family again.
Therefore, virtuous elders were selected to live with them.
From then on, Dou Changjun and Dou Shaojun became humble and courteous gentlemen, who did not dare to be arrogant because of their high status.
Queen Dou later became ill and became blind.
Emperor Wen also favored Mrs. Handan Shen and Yin Ji, but they had no sons.
After Emperor Wen passed away and Emperor Jing ascended the throne, Empress Bao became the Empress Dowager and granted Dou Guangguo the title of Marquis Zhangwu.
Dou Changjun died early and named his son Dou Pengzu the Marquis of Nanpi.
When Wu, Chu and other seven countries rebelled, Dou Ying, the cousin of the Queen Mother, was chivalrous and brave, and liked to make friends with scholars. He was appointed as a general. After the Wu and Chu rebellions were suppressed, he was named Wei Qihou.
There are three people in the Dou family who have been granted the title of Marquis.
Empress Dowager Dou liked the teachings of Huangdi and Laozi. Emperor Jing and the Dou family had to read "Laozi" and admire Huang and Laozi's techniques.
Empress Dowager Dou died six years after Emperor Jing's death, fifty-one years after she was established as queen, that is, in the sixth year of Yuanguang, and was buried in Ba Ling with Emperor Wen.
According to his instructions, Shao rewarded the eldest princess Liu Prostitute with all the gold and silver belongings in Shu Palace.

Empress Bo died in the fourth year after she was deposed and was buried south of Shupingwang Pavilion in Chang'an City.

The Jin family was furious and refused to give up, so Zang'er sent his daughter to the crown prince's womb.

When Mrs. Wang was pregnant with her son, she dreamed of a sun rising into her belly, so she told the prince about it. The prince said: This is a sign of noble status.
Before the child was born, Emperor Wen passed away and after Emperor Jing came to the throne, Mrs. Wang gave birth to a son.

Coupled with the auspicious news that the child was born in a dream, Emperor Jing thought about it over and over again and could not make up his mind.
Mrs. Wang secretly sent people to urge the ministers to propose canonizing Li Ji as queen.
Daxing wrote a letter to commemorate the matter, and one sentence said: A son is more valuable than his mother, and a mother is more valuable than his son. Now the title of the prince's mother should be the queen.
Emperor Jing was furious and said: Is this what you should say?
