summary:
The "Book of Xia" records Yu's thirteen-year flood control efforts, during which he passed his home without entering. He traveled by various means—car, boat, sled, or sedan—to delineate Kyushu's boundaries, dredge rivers, and assess land for taxation. Despite his work, the Yellow River continued to devastate the Central Plains. Yu prioritized managing it, guiding its waters from Jishi Mountain through Longmen and other locations, but its turbulent flow proved difficult to tame. He eventually split the river into two to reduce its force. After Kyushu's rivers and lakes were stabilized, the benefits extended to the Xia, Shang, and Zhou dynasties. The Yellow River was later diverted southeast, intersecting with several rivers and countries.

In various regions, canals were built for irrigation and transport. In Chu, ditches connected Moshui and Yunmeng; in Wu, canals linked three rivers and five lakes; in Qi, the Zi and Jishui rivers were joined. In Shu, Li Bing dug two rivers in Chengdu to prevent flooding. These canals facilitated boat travel and irrigation, bringing prosperity. During Wei Wenhou's reign, Ximen Bao governed Ye County with a good reputation, but his successor Shi Qi criticized him for not using the Zhangshui River for irrigation. Shi Qi then diverted the Zhangshui to irrigate Ye County, making the area fertile. Later, the Qin state employed Zheng Guo, a Han spy, to build a canal from the Jingshui River. Though initially suspected, Zheng Guo convinced Qin of the canal's long-term benefits. The canal irrigated over 40,000 hectares of salty land, enriching Qin and enabling it to conquer other states; it was named the Zheng Guo Canal.

During the Han dynasty, the Yellow River burst multiple times. In Emperor Xiaowen's reign, it broke at Suizao, and later during Yuanguang, it breached at Huzi, flowing into Juyeze and the Huai River. Attempts to block it failed, and Tian Ju advised against further efforts, citing divine will. Zheng Dangshi proposed a canal from Chang'an to divert the Wei River, reducing transport time and irrigating farmland. The emperor approved, and the canal was completed in three years, improving water transport and irrigation. Subsequent proposals included diverting Fen and Yellow River waters in Hedong, but the canals became useless after the river changed course. Other projects, like the Baoxie Road canal, faced challenges due to rocky waters. Yan Xiong's plan to irrigate salty land with Luoshui water led to the Longshou Canal, but it yielded little benefit after a decade.

After the Huzi breach, the emperor personally oversaw its blockage, composing songs about the struggle. The breach was finally sealed, and two canals were built to restore the river's old course. This success spurred widespread canal construction across Shuofang, Xihe, Hexi, and other regions, each irrigating over 10,000 hectares. Smaller canals were countless. By the sixth year of Yuanding, Ni Kuan proposed six auxiliary canals for the Zheng Guo Canal area. The emperor emphasized agriculture and reduced land taxes. Sixteen years later, Bai Gong opened the Baiqu Canal, diverting Jingshui water to irrigate 4,500 hectares. The people praised both canals for their fertility. During the Han-Xiongnu wars, Yannian proposed a massive canal to divert the Yellow River, but the emperor hesitated, citing Dayu's legacy. After the Xuanfang breach, the river broke again at Guantao, forming the Tunshi River, which was left unblocked.

During Emperor Xuan's Dijie period, Guo Chang straightened a meandering section of the Yellow River, benefiting the people. In Yongguang, the river burst at Lingmingdukou, causing the Tunshi River to disappear. Under Emperor Cheng, Feng Kui warned of flood risks and proposed dredging the Tunshi River. Despite initial inaction, a major breach in Guantao flooded 32 counties. Wang Yanshi successfully blocked it, earning rewards. Later breaches required further efforts, with Yang Yan and others involved. Debates over river management continued, with some advocating for relocating people and opening canals, while others favored minimal intervention. During Wang Mang's reign, various experts proposed strategies, but none were implemented. The text concludes by emphasizing the Yellow River's significance and the need for careful study of water management.

The principles mentioned in the "Six Classics" all achieve the same goal, and the functions of "Li" and "Yue" are particularly urgent.
Once those who cultivate themselves forget the propriety, they will suffer from evil and contempt; once those who govern the country lose the propriety, desolation and disorder will come.
Human beings contain the yin and yang of heaven and earth, and have emotions of joy, anger, sorrow and joy.
Heaven upholds its characteristics but cannot exercise restraint, but saints can use it restrainedly and without interruption. Therefore, rituals and music are made according to the laws of heaven and earth to communicate with gods, establish human ethics, correct human temperament, and regulate all things.
It is human nature to have differences between men and women and to be jealous of others, so we have formulated the etiquette of marriage; it is human nature to have the order of interaction between elders and younger generations, so we have formulated the drinking ceremony in the countryside;
Grief has the etiquette of crying and mourning, joy has the appearance of singing and dancing, which is enough for the upright person to be sincere, and it is enough for the evil person to prevent mistakes.
Therefore, if the marriage etiquette is abolished, then the etiquette between husband and wife will be coarse, and the sins of debauchery and lewdness between men and women will increase; if the country drinking ceremony is abolished, then the order of elders and younger generations will be confused, and there will be more lawsuits; If the etiquette is abolished, the kindness between flesh and blood will be weakened, and more and more people will abandon the dead and forget their ancestors; if the etiquette of meeting the emperor is abolished, then the positions of the monarch and his ministers will be wrong, and the phenomenon of aggression and bullying will gradually occur.
Therefore, Confucius said: There is no better way to stabilize a country and govern the people than propriety; to change the atmosphere and change customs, there is no better way than music.
Etiquette can control the thoughts of the people, music can harmonize the voices of the people, implement it with government decrees, and prevent it with criminal laws.
If etiquette, music, government orders, and criminal laws are all passed without hindrance, then the kingly way is complete.
If music is used to govern the interior, harmony is needed; if ritual is used to modify the exterior, diversity is needed; harmony can lead to harmony and mutual affection, and difference can produce fear and respect; harmony and mutual love will not cause resentment, and fear and admiration will not cause strife.
The world is governed well by doing nothing, the effects of etiquette and music.
The two are used together and become one.
Fear and respect are difficult to express, so they use wine and food, speeches, and kneeling to express it; the joy of harmonious love is difficult to describe, so they use poems, songs, chants, words, and bells and stones to express it.
This is to praise a person's respect without touching his property, and to praise a person's happy mood without touching his voice.
So Confucius said: "Etiquette, etiquette, can it be expressed in jade and silk?"
Joy, joy, how can we use bells and drums to express it?
This is the foundation of etiquette and joy.
Therefore, it is said: Those who understand the nature of ritual and music can innovate, and those who understand the system of ritual and music can inherit it; those who innovate are called saints, and those who inherit it are called Ming.
Mingsheng is all about innovation and inheritance.
The emperor must implement the rites of the previous emperors in accordance with the requirements of the times, add or delete them, and gradually make them according to the people's ideas, until the world is at peace and complete.
The Zhou Dynasty learned from the Xia and Yin Dynasties, and the etiquette system was particularly complete. Systems were established for major events and precautions were taken for minor matters. Therefore, there are 300 etiquette rituals and 3,000 etiquette details.
As a result, education was widespread, the people were harmonious, there were no disasters, no chaos, and the prisons were empty. This situation has been maintained for more than forty years.
Confucius praised it and said: The etiquette is so complete!
I want to learn from the Zhou Dynasty.
When the Zhou Dynasty declined, the princes exceeded the limits of the law and hated the etiquette system for harming their own interests, so they deleted the relevant books and documents.
Then the Qin Dynasty destroyed various schools of thought, and rituals and music were scattered and lost.
After the establishment of the Han Dynasty, he began to control the troubled times and restore normalcy and stability. Although he did not have a day to spare, Emperor Gaozu still ordered Shusun Tong to formulate etiquette to correct the status of the monarch and his ministers.
Emperor Gaozu happily exclaimed: "I just realized today that being the emperor is the most expensive thing!"
Shusun Tong was appointed as a regular official and etiquette laws were formulated, but Shusun Tong died before they were fully prepared.

The establishment of monarchs and ministers, the distinction between superiors and subordinates, the ordering of the country's system, and the harmony among relatives are not God's arrangements, but are established by man himself.
Since it is established by people themselves, it cannot be established if they are not practiced, and it will be destroyed if they are not cultivated.
The Han Dynasty has been established for more than 20 years now. It is necessary to formulate systems and promote rituals and music. Then the princes can get on the right track, the people can be simple and unpretentious, and lawsuits will gradually disappear.
So Jia Yi established etiquette, and Emperor Wen was very happy.
But ministers Zhou Bo and Guan Ying were jealous of him, so his suggestions were not adopted.
When Emperor Wu of the Han Dynasty came to the throne, he promoted and appointed people with outstanding talents, discussed the establishment of a bright hall to clarify politics and religion, and formulated etiquette and clothing colors to revitalize peace.
It happened that Empress Dowager Dou liked the Taoist teachings of Huangdi and Laozi, but did not like Confucianism, so the matter was dropped.

The angelic yang is always in the midsummer to nourish all things and make them grow, while the yin is always in the midwinter and accumulates in empty and unused places. From this we can see that heaven advocates virtue and not criminal law.

Yang Qi does not have the help of Yin Qi and cannot form the time sequence of the year alone.

The political and religious ethos has been clarified, habits and customs have been formed, and no one in the world will be in prison.

The principles of the "Six Classics" share a common goal, with the functions of "Li" (ritual) and "Yue" (music) being particularly urgent. For individuals, forgetting propriety leads to evil and contempt; for a state, losing it brings desolation and disorder. Ritual and music are made according to the laws of heaven and earth to communicate with gods, establish human ethics, and regulate all things. Specific rituals, such as those for marriage, drinking in the countryside, mourning, and meeting the emperor, are formulated to address human nature and prevent specific vices. Confucius stated that there is no better way to stabilize a country and govern the people than propriety, and no better way to change customs than music. When etiquette, music, government orders, and criminal laws all function smoothly, the kingly way is complete. The two are used together to create harmony and respect.

The Zhou Dynasty learned from the Xia and Yin Dynasties, creating a particularly complete etiquette system with 300 major rituals and 3,000 details. This led to widespread education, harmony, and a lack of disasters for over forty years. When the Zhou Dynasty declined, princes exceeded the law and deleted relevant documents. The Qin Dynasty then destroyed various schools, causing rituals and music to be scattered. After the Han Dynasty was established, Emperor Gaozu ordered Shusun Tong to formulate etiquette. Emperor Wen was pleased with Jia Yi's proposals to establish rituals, but ministers Zhou Bo and Guan Ying were jealous, so his suggestions were not adopted. Emperor Wu's plans were dropped due to Empress Dowager Dou's preference for Taoism. Dong Zhongshu argued that heaven advocates virtue over punishment, and that the Han Dynasty must change its education to reform the people. Emperor Xuan did not adopt Wang Ji's suggestion to select Confucian scholars and inherit old etiquette. Liu Xiang persuaded Emperor Cheng to build Piyong and arrange rituals and music, but the emperor died before the plan was completed. Wang Mang later built Piyong to confuse people and usurp the throne.

Emperor Guangwu established Mingtang and Biyong after thirty years of rule. However, moral education was not widespread because rituals and music were not in place. The rituals written by Shusun Tong were recorded with laws and collected by judges, but not passed down by Legalists. Music is loved by saints for its power to change people's minds. Since the death of Confucius, the subtle words of the classics have been discontinued, and after the passing of his Seventy Disciples, divergent interpretations emerged. The "Spring and Autumn Annals" was divided into five schools: Zuo Shi, Gong Yang, Gu Liang, Zou Shi, and Jia Shi. During the Warring States period, debates over authenticity proliferated, and various schools of thought became confused. Qin Shihuang, fearing this chaos, burned books to deceive the people. After the Han Dynasty was established, the shortcomings of the Qin were eliminated, and a large-scale collection of books was initiated, opening channels for donations. By the time of Emperor Xiaowu, texts were incomplete, bamboo slips had fallen apart, and rituals were destroyed. The emperor lamented this and established a repository for books, appointing officials to copy them, enriching the secret palace with the teachings of scholars. Under Emperor Cheng, the loss of books was severe, so emissaries were sent to collect scattered texts. Liu Xiang was ordered to collate classics and poems, while others studied military books, astronomy, and medicine. After each proofreading, Liu Xiang cataloged the books, summarized their main ideas, and presented them to the emperor. Upon Liu Xiang's death, Emperor Ai sent his son Liu Xin to complete the work, who then compiled the "Seven Strategies," including summaries of the Six Arts, various schools, poetry, military strategy, numerology, and prescriptions.

The "Book of Changes" has twelve chapters, with interpretations by Shi, Meng, and Liangqiu, among others. Thirteen schools of interpretation exist, totaling 294 chapters. The "Yi" states that Fuxi created the trigrams by observing heaven, earth, and all things. During the Yin and Zhou dynasties, King Wen, as a prince, followed heaven's will and wrote the judgments. Confucius added ten chapters, such as "Tuan" and "Xiang." The principles of "Yi" are profound, spanning three sages and three ancient eras. When Qin Shihuang burned books, the "Yi" survived due to its divinatory nature. After the Han, Tian He taught it, and by Emperor Xuan and Yuan, schools like Shi, Meng, and Liangqiu were officially taught, while Fei's version matched the ancient text.

The "Shangshu" has forty-six volumes of ancient classics and fifty-seven articles. It was compiled by Confucius, starting from Yao and ending with Qin, totaling a hundred chapters. During the Qin burning, Fu Sheng hid it in a wall, and only twenty-nine chapters survived. By Emperor Xuan, Ouyang and Xiahou schools were established. The "Guwen Shangshu" was found in the wall of Confucius's residence, with sixteen more chapters than the original. Kong Anguo dedicated it to the emperor, but it was not included in the official curriculum due to witchcraft incidents. Liu Xiang used the ancient text to correct the Ouyang and Xiahou versions, finding missing slips and over 700 variant characters.

The "Book of Songs" has twenty-eight volumes from Lu, Qi, and Han schools, with Mao's version adding thirty volumes. Confucius selected 305 poems from the Zhou dynasty, which survived the Qin burning due to their oral transmission. After the Han, Duke Shen of Lu, Yuan Gu of Qi, and Han Sheng of Yan provided explanations, but only Lu's version was closest to the original meaning. Mao Gong's teachings, claimed to be from Zixia, were favored by King Xian of Hejian but not officially taught.

The "Spring and Autumn" was used to record kings' actions, with left historians recording words and right historians recording deeds. After the Zhou decline, Confucius used Lu's records to compile the annals, and Zuo Qiuming explained the facts to preserve the true meaning.

summary:
The evolution of religious and sacrificial practices during the Han Dynasty, focusing on the reigns of Emperors Wu, Zhao, Xuan, Yuan, Cheng, Ai, and Ping, as well as the usurper Wang Mang. The belief in ghosts and gods in Guangdong, where King Shuou’s reverence for them allegedly extended his life to 160 years, while neglect shortened his descendants’ lives. This led to the construction of temples and divination using chicken bones. Emperor Wu, influenced by alchemists like Gongsun Qing, built pavilions and towers in Chang’an and Ganquan Palace to invite immortals, including the Feilian, Gui, Yishou, and Longshou Pavilions, and the Tongtian Tower. He conducted sacrifices, such as those to Taiyi and Houtu, and expanded palace rooms. After a drought, Gongsun Qing cited the Yellow Emperor’s precedent, leading to a decree for worldwide worship of the spiritual star. Emperor Wu performed numerous rituals, including suburban sacrifices at Yongcheng, worship at Mount Tai, and construction of a Mingtang based on a Yellow Emperor-era design. He also built Jianzhang Palace, Taiye Pool with artificial islands, and the Shenming Terrace, all to attract gods. The calendar was revised, and the year was renamed Taichu. Alchemists continued to advise, leading to the construction of five cities and twelve towers. Emperor Wu made five pilgrimages to Mount Tai for sealing ceremonies, and sacrifices were made to various mountains and rivers.

During Emperor Zhao’s reign, he was too young to participate in sacrifices. Emperor Xuan honored Emperor Wu as Shizong, building temples where divine signs like white cranes and five-colored geese appeared. Emperor Xuan personally performed suburban sacrifices at Ganquan and Jiese, changing the era name to Sujue. He ordered annual sacrifices to the Yangtze River, sea, and Luoshui, and regular worship of the Five Mountains and Four Rivers. Alchemists advised building temples for various gods, including Suihou and Zhoukangbaoding. Doctor Liu Gengsheng was punished for failed alchemy. Jingzhao Yin Zhang Chang advised against alchemists, and many were dismissed. A tripod found in Meiyang was debated; Zhang Chang argued it was a Zhou dynasty artifact, not suitable for the ancestral temple. Phoenixes and other auspicious signs led to the construction of Bushou Palace and Phoenix Hall. Emperor Xuan died after a reign marked by frequent sacrifices and omens.

Emperor Yuan followed old rituals, performing suburban sacrifices every other year, but favored Confucianism. Ministers like Gong Yu and Wei Xuancheng proposed abolishing many temples, but Emperor Yuan reversed this after dreaming of divine condemnation. Emperor Cheng’s reign saw a major reform: Prime Minister Kuang Heng and Imperial Censor Zhang Tan argued that sacrifices should be moved to Chang’an’s northern and southern suburbs, citing ancient practices and the hardships of traveling to Ganquan and Fenyin. After debate, the move was approved, and many temples were abolished. However, after Emperor Cheng had no heirs, the Empress Dowager ordered the restoration of the old temples at Ganquan, Fenyin, and Yongcheng, blaming the move for the lack of descendants. Emperor Cheng later became obsessed with alchemists, but Gu Yong warned against them, citing historical failures. Du Ye also criticized the distant sacrifices. After Emperor Cheng’s death, the Empress Dowager restored the northern and southern suburbs.

Emperor Ai, ill, revived many temples, but after his death, the Empress Dowager again restored the Ganquan and Fenyin temples. Under Emperor Ping, Wang Mang reported extensively on sacrificial history, arguing for a return to the northern and southern suburbs and proposing a system where heaven and earth were worshiped together with ancestors. He established altars for the Five Emperors and various gods in Chang’an’s suburbs, and later added an official shrine for the god of grain. After usurping the throne, Wang Mang built the Eight Winds Tower and engaged in alchemy, with over 1,700 temples by his death. The text concludes with a commentary on the Han Dynasty’s ritual evolution, noting debates over the five virtues and the influence of alchemists, with Gu Yong’s criticisms deemed correct.

Therefore, the "Poetry" says: Some pull weeds, some cultivate soil, millet and millet are already very lush.
Yun is weeding.
Taro is soil.
It means that when the seedlings get a little stronger, they often weed and cultivate the soil. In the hot summer, the ridges are gone and the roots are deep. They can withstand wind and drought, so they are very lush.
The instruments used for cultivating and sowing on behalf of the field are all convenient and flexible.
About twelve laborers had a field, a well and a house, so there were five hectares per acre. Two people worked together, two oxen and three people, and the harvest in a year was often more than one hu per acre of fields without furrow cultivation, and even twice as much for those who knew how to cultivate it.
Zhao Guo sent people to teach Taichang and Sanfu, and Da Si Nong appointed slaves who were good at making field tools to work and make farming tools.
Erqianshi sent the commander, Sanlao, Litian and Lifu Lao who were good at farming to receive farming equipment and learn the methods of farming and cultivating seedlings.
Some people suffered from the lack of cattle and the loss of the farming season when the soil was moist and timely for farming after the rain, so Guang Guang was ordered to teach Zhao Guo how to use people to pull the plow.
Zhao Yuzhuo asked Ren Guang to be the prime minister and teach the people to hire each other to pull plows.
Those with many people can plow about thirty acres a day, while those with few can plow thirteen acres, so most of the fields are cultivated.
Zhao Guo used the soldiers from the palace to cultivate the land between the inside and outside of the palace as an experiment, and the threshing of grain was more than one bush of dendrobium per mu than other fields.
He taught the family fields and the three auxiliary public fields, and also taught the border counties and Juyan City.
After that, the people in the border cities, Hedong, Hongnong, Sanfu, and Taichang all thought that Daitian was convenient and they could get more grain with less effort.
By the time of Emperor Zhao, the exiled people gradually returned to their hometowns. The opening of fields has increased, and there is a lot of savings.
After Emperor Xuan came to the throne, most of the officials appointed were virtuous people. The people were content with their own country, and their annual income was abundant. The price of grain reached five yuan per stone, and farmers had little benefit.
At that time, Geng Shouchang, the great minister of agriculture, was good at calculation and measurement, and could calculate the labor required for the project. He was favored by the emperor. During the Five Feng period, he reported: According to the old practice, four million dendrobium grains from Guandong were transported by water every year to supply the capital, and 60,000 soldiers were employed.
The grains in Sanfu, Hongnong, Hedong, Shangdang and Taiyuan counties should be purchased to be enough to supply the capital, which can save more than half of the soldiers needed for water transportation in Guandong.
He also asked for instructions to increase the sea rent three times, and the emperor followed his advice.
Xiao Wang, the imperial censor, said: "It turns out that the Xu Gong family of the imperial censor's subordinates lives in Shulai. He said that the sea rent was increased in previous years and the fish would not come out."
The elders all said that during the reign of Emperor Wu, the county magistrate personally fished, but no fish came out of the sea. Later, they returned it to the people, and the fish came out.
Yin and Yang interact with each other, and things of the same kind correspond to each other. This is the case for all things.
Now Geng Shouchang plans to purchase grain from the nearby water transport pass, build warehouses and ships, which will cost more than 200 million yuan. It involves the working people, fearing that a drought will occur and the people will suffer from it.
Geng Shouchang was accustomed to calculating things of one cent and one baht. His far-reaching calculations and thinking were really not up to the task. It would be better to remain as before.
The emperor did not listen.
Water transportation was indeed convenient, so Geng Shouchang asked for instructions and ordered the border counties to build warehouses. When the price of grain was low, the price was increased to buy in order to benefit farmers. When the price of grain was high, the price was sold at a reduced price, which was called Changping warehouse.
People feel convenient.
The emperor issued an edict and granted Geng Shouchang the title of Marquis of Guannei.
Because Cai Gui liked agriculture, he served as an envoy to encourage the country and became a high official.
Emperor Yuan ascended the throne and the world was flooded, especially in the eleven counties of Guandong.
In the second year of Emperor Yuan's reign, there was a famine in Qi. A grain of rice cost more than 300 yuan per stone. Many people starved to death. People in Langxie County were cannibals.
Most of the Confucian scholars in official positions said that Yantie Palace, Beijia Tianguan and Changpingcang could be dismissed, and they should not compete for interests with the people.
The emperor listened to their opinions and dismissed Yantieguan, Beijiatianguan and Changpingcang.
He also dismissed the palace guards of Jianzhang and Ganquan, Jiaodui, Qi San served as officials, reduced the number of forbidden gardens to provide for the poor, and reduced the number of guards in the princes' temples by half.
He also reduced the number of soldiers in Guanzhong by 500 and transferred grain to help the poor.
After that, due to insufficient funds, only Yantieguan was restored.
When he became emperor, there was no war in the world and it could be said to be peaceful. However, the people's customs were extravagant and they did not consider saving and hoarding.
In the second year of Yongshi, Liang State and Pingyuan County suffered from floods for consecutive years, and cannibalism occurred. The governor and county governor were dismissed from office for crimes.
Emperor Ai ascended the throne, and Shi Dan assisted in political affairs. He suggested: In ancient times, wise kings always established well fields and then managed them to achieve peace.
Emperor Xiaowen inherited the emptiness of the world after the collapse of the Zhou Dynasty and the violent wars of the Qin Dynasty, so he devoted himself to encouraging the people to engage in farming and mulberry farming, and set an example for the world with frugality.
The people had just begun to enrich themselves, and there was no danger of annexation, so there were no restrictions on people's land and slaves.
Nowadays, generations of peace have passed down, and the wealthy and officials have a lot of property, but the poor and weak are even poorer.
When a gentleman engages in politics, it is valuable to keep the old laws without changing them, so it is difficult to make changes and innovations. However, the reason why there are reforms is because they are used to save emergencies. However, it is not a complete change and should be roughly restricted.
The emperor conveyed his suggestions to his ministers.
Prime Minister Kong Guang and Grand Sikong Hewu submitted a petition requesting that all princes, kings and princes receive privately owned land in the country.
The land held by the princes in Chang'an, the princess in each county, and the land held by the princes and officials in Guannei in their private names should not exceed thirty hectares.
The number of slaves for the princes and kings is two hundred, the number of slaves for the princes and princesses is one hundred, and the number of slaves for the princes and officials in Guan Nei is thirty.
There is a three-year period, and any violation will be confiscated to the government.
At that time, the price of slaves in the fields and houses was reduced, Ding and Fu were in power, and Dong Xian was high-ranking, which was not good for them.
The emperor's order was postponed for the time being, but later it was stopped and not implemented.
There are already many collections in the palaces, gardens, and treasury. Although the wealth of the people is not as good as that of Emperor Wen and Emperor Jing, the population is the largest in the world.
After the death of Emperor Ping, Wang Mang became regent and he usurped the throne.
Wang Mang followed the Han Dynasty's achievements in peace and stability. The Huns became vassals and all barbarians obeyed. The places where boats and carriages passed were all subjects. The wealth of the treasury and hundreds of officials made the world comfortable.
Wang Mang took possession of it one day, but his heart was not satisfied. He despised the Han system and thought it was imprecise.
During the reign of Emperor Xuan, Shanyu began to be given seals, which were the same as those of the Emperor, and Yigou Town in the southwest became king.
Wang Mang sent an envoy to replace Shanyu's seal and demoted the king of Gouding to a marquis.
The two parties began to harbor resentments and invade the border.
Wang Mang then mobilized his army and sent three soldiers! The army of ten thousand planned to set out in ten groups at the same time to wipe out the Xiongnu in one fell swoop. Prisoners, adult men, and soldiers from all over the world were recruited to transport military supplies and weapons from the Jiang and Huaihe rivers backed by the sea to the north. Envoys drove vehicles to supervise, and the sea was disrupted.
They often imitated ancient times without considering the current situation, divided states and counties, changed the functions of officials, established official positions, and issued orders: In the Han Dynasty, land rents were reduced and one-thirtieth of the tax was collected. Money was often paid in lieu of military service taxes, and those who were disabled or sick had to pay. Moreover, powerful people invaded and divided the fields to seize tax revenue.
The nominal tax is one for thirty, but in reality it is a five-tenth tax. The rich are arrogant and evil, the poor are desperate and go astray, all are innocent, and the instruments of torture are not idle.
Now the Tianxia Tian is renamed Wang Tian, ​​and the slaves are called private servants, and they are not allowed to be sold or bought.
If there are less than eight men in the family and the field exceeds one well, the extra field will be distributed to the villagers of the Nine Nationalities.
Anyone who violates the law will be sentenced to death according to the law, but the system is not determined. Officials took this as an offense, and there was a lot of resentment in the world, and many people were punished.
Three years later, Wang Mang knew that the people were miserable and issued an edict to the kings! You can sell and buy your personal belongings without being arrested by law.
But the punishments were severe and the politics were chaotic.
There were more than 200,000 soldiers on the border who relied on the emperor for food and clothing. The expenses were insufficient, and several brutal taxes were imposed, making the people even poorer.
It often suffers from droughts and in unsafe years, grain prices soar.
In the last years of Wang Mang's life, thieves gathered in groups and he sent troops to attack them, but the generals left the soldiers alone.
The phenomenon of cannibalism appeared in the north and Qing and Xu areas. To the east of Luoyang, one meter per stone cost two thousand.
Wang Mang sent General Sangong to open various granaries in the east to help the poor people. He also sent doctors and envoys to teach the people how to cook grass and trees to make cheese. The cheese could not be eaten, which added to the trouble.
Hundreds of thousands of refugees entered Guanzhong, and support officials were set up to provide for them. The officials also stole their supplies, and eight out of ten people died of hunger.
Wang Mang felt shameful about his politics, so he went down to Shao and said: I have suffered from the hardships of Yangjiu, Bailiu, drought, frost, locusts, famines, barbarians disrupting China, bandits and bandits, and people displaced.
I am very sad and afraid that my life is about to end.
Say this every year until he dies.
summary:
Among the eight types of government officials in "Hong Fan," one oversees food and another property. Food refers to grain from farmers, while property includes cloth, silk, golden knives, and turtle shells, used to distribute wealth. These are the foundation of life, originating from Shennong's era, who taught farming and trade. Sufficient food and circulated property enrich the nation, forming political and religious culture. Huang Di adjusted for the people, Yao informed them of seasons, Shun appointed Houji to address starvation, and Dayu controlled floods, regulated fields, and encouraged trade. The Shang and Zhou dynasties prospered by stabilizing and enriching the people before educating them. The Book of Changes states that life is heaven and earth's great virtue, and a saint's most precious possession is the throne, held through benevolence and wealth accumulation.

Property is the basis for emperors to gather people, support the masses, and govern. Wise kings defined the people, built cities, houses, markets, and schools, dividing them into scholars, farmers, workers, and merchants. Officials were appointed by talent, and each group bore responsibility, ensuring no idleness. Land was measured in steps, acres, and wells, with eight families jointly owning a well, each receiving private and public land. People helped each other, fostering harmony. Land quality varied: good land yielded 100 acres, medium 200, poor 300. Farmers exchanged fields based on fallow periods. Taxes were one-tenth of public land and industry income, while labor provided military supplies. At age 20, fields were divided; at 60, returned. Grains were mixed to prevent disasters, and mulberry trees, vegetables, and livestock were cultivated. Houses in fields were huts; in communities, li. Neighborhoods, li, clans, parties, states, and townships were organized, with officials from corporal to qing. Education began at age eight, with university at 15. Outstanding students advanced, and princes recommended scholars to the emperor. Folk songs were collected to inform the ruler.

After the Zhou Dynasty declined, tyrants ignored boundaries, corvée was rampant, and public fields were neglected. Lu Xuangong's "first tax mu" was criticized. The Warring States period valued hypocrisy and violence over benevolence. Li Kui advised Wei Wenhou on land productivity, calculating that careful cultivation yielded extra grain. He noted that high grain prices hurt scholars, workers, and merchants, while low prices hurt farmers. A household of five with 100 acres produced 150 dan of millet, but after taxes, food, and expenses, they faced deficits, leading to poverty. Li Kui proposed buying grain at moderate prices during good harvests and selling during famines to stabilize prices, implemented in Wei, making it rich and strong. Qin Xiaogong appointed Shang Yang, who destroyed well fields and emphasized farming and warfare, dominating neighboring states. However, hierarchy was lost, the rich accumulated wealth, and the poor suffered. Qin Shihuang annexed the world, imposed heavy taxes, and conscripted labor, causing rebellion.

After the Han Dynasty, the Qin's shortcomings continued. Princes revolted, people lost jobs, and famine struck, with grain costing 5,000 yuan per stone and cannibalism. Emperor Gaozu ordered people to sell children and move to Shu and Han. After peace, the emperor restricted frugality, reduced land rents to one-fifteenth, and taxed based on official salaries. Emperor Wen practiced frugality and encouraged agriculture. Jia Yi advised that production must exceed consumption, warning of poverty and unrest. He urged returning people to agriculture to build savings. Emperor Wen was moved and began farming himself. Chao Cuo further advised that wise kings ensure people have savings, citing Yao, Yu, and Tang's success. He noted that poverty leads to evil, and farmers work hard but suffer from taxes and merchants' exploitation. He proposed valuing grain over gold and jade, and using grain for rewards and punishments. Emperor Wen allowed people to send grain to the border for titles, reducing taxes. Over 70 years, the country prospered, with full granaries and surplus property. However, wealth led to pride and land annexation. Dong Zhongshu advised planting more wheat and reforming taxes and labor, but after his death, prices rose and cannibalism returned.

Emperor Wu regretted his conquests and appointed Cheng Fu to promote agriculture. Zhao Guo introduced the Daitian method, with three furrows per acre, changing positions yearly. This method, using convenient tools, increased yields. Zhao Guo taught it widely, and it proved efficient. By Emperor Zhao's time, exiles returned, fields expanded, and savings grew. Emperor Xuan appointed virtuous officials, and grain prices fell to five yuan per stone. Geng Shouchang proposed purchasing grain from nearby counties to save on transport costs, building Changping warehouses to stabilize prices. Emperor Yuan faced floods and famine, with cannibalism in Langxie. Confucian officials advised dismissing salt, iron, and Changping offices, which the emperor did, but later restored salt and iron due to insufficient funds. Emperor Cheng's reign was peaceful but extravagant, with floods causing cannibalism. Emperor Ai considered land and slave restrictions, but they were not implemented. Wang Mang usurped the throne, despised Han systems, and provoked the Xiongnu, leading to war. He renamed land and slaves, prohibited sales, and imposed harsh punishments, causing chaos. Droughts and famines led to cannibalism, with grain prices soaring. Wang Mang opened granaries but officials stole supplies, and many died. He lamented his rule until his death.

translation:
As for the uses of property, money, cloth and silk, their details are not recorded before the Xia and Yin Dynasties.
Jiang Taigong established the method of currency circulation in the nine prefectures for the Zhou Dynasty: gold is one inch square and weighs one catty; coins are round and have square holes, and baht is used as the weight; cloth is two feet and two inches wide and is one piece, and four feet long is one piece.
Therefore, currency is more precious than gold, sharper than a knife, smoother than spring water, more dispersed than cloth, and more able to gather than silk.
After Jiang Taigong retreated to the feudal country, he implemented it in Qi.
When Guan Zhong assisted Duke Huan of Qi, he established the standard of measuring weight. He said: There are years of famine and years of harvest, so grains are expensive and cheap; orders are slow and urgent, so goods are light and heavy.
If the emperor does not govern, then the hoarding merchants will roam the market, and when the people cannot support themselves, they will raise the price to a hundred times the cost.
Therefore, a country with ten thousand cars must have merchants worth ten thousand gold to buy them, and a country with a thousand cars must have merchants worth ten thousand gold. This is because the profits are hidden.
If we consume what we produce, we will be able to meet our own expenses. However, if there are hungry people among the people, that is why the grain is hidden.
When the people have plenty, they despise grain, so the monarch levies a low price; when the people have a shortage, they value grain, so the monarch distributes it at a high price.
All low prices, high prices, collections, and distributions are all done at a certain time. Then supply and demand are adjusted, and prices will be stable.
Adhere to the measures of regulating supply and demand and stabilizing prices, so that a town with a population of ten thousand households must have a collection of ten thousand bells, and a string of money tied with millions of strings; a town with a population of only ten thousand households must have a collection of thousands of bells, and a string of money tied with millions of strings.
Farming is carried out in the spring, weeding is carried out in the summer, and the equipment and seeds must be abundant.
Therefore, big merchants and hoarding merchants cannot use their power to rob the people.
Duke Huan of Qi used the small state of Qi to unite the princes and promote his reputation as an overlord.
More than a hundred years later, when King Jing of Zhou Dynasty came to the throne, he was worried that the money was too light and planned to cast large coins instead. Duke Shan Mu said: "This won't work."
In ancient times, when disasters came from heaven, it was necessary to weigh property and currency to save the people.
The people think that money is light, so we create heavy money for them to use. In this way, big money and small money go hand in hand with heavy money being the main one, and the people can get convenience.
If heavy money cannot be used, make more light money for use, and do not abolish heavy money. Therefore, if the heavy money is insufficient, use light money to make up for it. Money and small money are mostly beneficial.
Now that the king has abolished light money and created heavy money, the people have lost their wealth. How can they not be in want?
If the people are in shortage, the king will have difficulty in spending money; if there is difficulty, he must collect more from the people; if the people cannot provide, they will flee. This is a way to separate the people.
Moreover, exhausting the people's wealth to enrich the palace is like blocking the water source to stop the flow of water. It will not take a few days for the water to dry up. Please make your decision, Your Majesty.
King Jing did not listen to his words, and finally made a large coin with "actual goods" engraved on it. The round edges and holes of the money had outlines, which were used to encourage farmers to make up for the shortage, and the people benefited.
When the Qin State annexed the world, its currency was divided into two classes: gold was measured in yi, which was the first-class currency; copper coins were shaped like the money of the Zhou Dynasty, with the inscription "ban liang" on the front and a weight of half a liang.
Pearls, jade, turtles, shells, silver and tin are used as decorations and treasures, not as currency, but they change at any time, and their weight has no rules.
After the rise of the Han Dynasty, they thought that the Qin Dynasty coins were heavy and difficult to use, so they ordered the people to mint pod coins instead.
The unit of gold returned to the weekly system of kilograms.
Those who did not abide by the law and pursued profits used their own surplus to accumulate goods, so that the goods on the market accumulated in their own hands, causing prices to skyrocket. The price of rice reached ten thousand gold per stone, and a horse was worth one hundred gold.
After the world was peaceful, Emperor Gaozu ordered merchants not to wear silk and ride in carriages, and increased taxes to frustrate them.
During the reign of Emperor Xiaohui and Queen Gao, considering that the world had just stabilized, the laws on merchants were relaxed again, but the descendants of people in the market could not become officials.
In the fifth year of Emperor Xiaowen's reign, because the money was more abundant and lighter, four baht coins were minted, with the characters "banliang" on the front.
Abolish the law on stealing money and let the people mint it at will.
Jia Yi remonstrated and said: The law allows the world to openly hire people to make coins with copper and tin. Anyone who dares to mix lead and iron to commit adultery will be punished by tattooing.
But the situation with coining money is that if there is no doping, there will be no benefits; and the more subtle the doping, the more generous the benefits will be.
Things can bring disaster, and laws can cause evil. Now the common people can mint money, and they mint it in hiding, intending to prevent their huge profits and cunning. Even if they are sentenced to tattoos every day, this situation cannot stop.
Recently, the people have paid their share of the crime, with as many as a hundred people in one county. As for the officials who suspected it, many people were whipped and tortured and fled.
There is nothing more than making laws to seduce the people and make them fall into a trap!
In the past, it was forbidden to mint coins, and the death penalty was accumulated at the bottom; now that coins are minted openly, the crimes of tattooing are accumulated at the bottom.
In enacting such a law, what would the emperor rely on?
In addition, the coins used by the people vary from county to county: some use light money, plus a hundred plus a few; some use heavy money, even if the weight is the same, it cannot be accepted.
There is no place for coins formulated according to law. If officials are anxious, they should unify them, but it is too cumbersome and not powerful enough. If they are allowed to flow without punishment, then the coins will be extremely confusing if they are used differently in the market.
If there is no way to deal with this situation, people will not know where to go!
Nowadays, more and more people are giving up farming and mining copper. They put down their farm tools and use furnace charcoal to smelt money molds. The illegal money is increasing day by day, but the grain is not increasing. If kind people are tempted and go astray, and cautious people fall into punishment, the punishment will be very unfair. How can we ignore this!
The country knows that the worries are like this, and the officials must have discussed that it is forbidden to mint money.
Forbidding coining money is illegal and will cause great harm.
If there is an order to prohibit the minting of coins, then the coins must be valuable; if they are valuable, the benefits will be great. Secretly minting coins is like a cloud, and the crime of abandoning the market is not enough to prohibit it.
The evil has never been exhausted and the law has prohibited the collapse. This is caused by copper.
Copper is scattered all over the world, so the harm it causes is great.
Now great disasters can be avoided and seven kinds of blessings can be obtained.
What are the seven blessings?
If the emperor collects copper and prevents it from being scattered, then the people will not mint money and the crime of tattooing will not increase. This is one kind.
There is not much fake money, and people do not doubt each other. This is the second type.
People who mine copper ore to mint money return to farming. This is the third type.
All copper is gathered in the emperor, and the emperor controls the weight by accumulating a lot of copper. If the coins are light, he will try to collect them. If the coins are heavy, he will try to distribute them. Money and things will definitely be balanced. This is the fourth.
It is used to make weapons, and it is used to give to noble ministers. There are some restrictions. Its use can distinguish the noble from the humble. This is the fifth.
It is used to monitor the market, adjust profits and losses, and collect surpluses. Then the government will be rich but the industrial and commercial people will be poor. This is the sixth type.
If we control our excess money and compete with the Xiongnu for its people, then the enemy will definitely surrender. This is the seventh way.
Therefore, those who are good at ruling the world can turn disaster into happiness and failure into success.
Now, the seven blessings have been suppressed for a long time and the great disaster has been allowed. I really feel sad for this.
The emperor did not listen to him.
At this time, Wu State relied on its status as a prince to mint coins in Shanhuo, and became richer than the emperor. Later, it finally became a rebellion.
Deng Tong was a great official. Because he minted coins, his wealth exceeded that of the king.
Therefore, the money of Wu and Deng Tong became popular all over the world.
Relying on the savings of Emperors Wen and Jing, Emperor Wu resented the harm caused by Hu and Guangdong. A few years after he ascended the throne, Yan Zhu, Zhu Maichen and others recovered Shuou and dealt with the two Guangdong. The Jianghuai issue was turbulent and cost a lot of money.
Tang Meng and Sima Xiangru began to open up the southwestern Yi. They dug mountains and opened more than a thousand miles of roads to expand Bashu. The people of Bashu were tired.
Peng Wu traveled through Huiqi and North Korea and established Canghai County. In this way, Yan and Qi successively launched catastrophes.
When Wang Hui set up a plan in Mayi, the Xiongnu broke off the peace and invaded the northern border. The war continued for many years, and the whole world was suffering from it.
The number of wars increased day by day. Those who traveled far away took their luggage with them, and those who did not leave went to see each other off. Internal and external harassments were connected, and the people were in decline. They had to resort to deception to avoid criminal laws, and the loss of property caused shortages.
Those who pay money can be replaced by official positions, and those who contribute money can be exempted from punishment. Elections are declining, integrity is ignored, force is used, and laws are strict.
This is where the profit-seeking ministers began.
After that, Wei Qing used tens of thousands of cavalry to attack the Xiongnu every year, and then captured the area south of Hetao and built Shuofang City.
At that time, the southwestern barbarian channel was opened, and tens of thousands of people were working. They carried the army's supplies thousands of miles. It took about ten minutes to send one stone. Coins were distributed in Gongkou and Jiaocheng to recruit people.
A few years later, the roads were still blocked, and the barbarians attacked several times. The officials sent troops to kill them.
After all the rents from Ba and Shu were insufficient to cover the expenses, they recruited wealthy people to farm in Nanyi, handed over millet to the local government, and received millet money from the capital.
Canghai County was established in Shumian, and the cost of personnel was comparable to that of Nanyi.
More than 100,000 people were mobilized to build a city to guard Shuofang. The water transportation was quite far. Starting from Shandong, the people had to suffer from fatigue, spending hundreds of thousands to tens of billions, and the treasury was even more empty.
The emperor called on the people who could provide slaves and maids to be exempted from taxes or labor for life, and those who were men could have their salaries increased. Accepting sheep to serve as Langguan began at this time.
For the next four years, Wei Qing led more than 100,000 people to attack the Xiongnu every year. The reward for killing and capturing the enemy soldiers was more than 200,000 catties of gold. However, more than 100,000 soldiers and horses of the Han Dynasty died, and the cost of weapons, boring armor, and transportation of grain was not included.
So Da Sinong reported that the usual money and taxes had been used up and were not enough to pay the soldiers.
Relevant officials asked for instructions so that people could buy titles and use money in exchange for exemption or reduction of the criminal penalties that prohibited industrial and commercial people from serving as officials; they also asked for the establishment of a rewarded official position, called Wugongjue, with each level worth 170,000 yuan, and a total value of more than 300,000 gold.
Anyone who buys a martial arts title will first try to confer it; the thousand-fu martial arts title is the same as the five great officers; if convicted, it will be reduced by two ranks; if you buy a title, you can go to the Leqing martial arts title to highlight military merit.
Most of the military merits are given by super-level awards, such as the title of marquis and minister for great achievements, and the title of Lang for minor achievements.
The official career is complicated and there are many clues, so the official position will be chaotic.
From the time when Gongsun Hong used the moral principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals to restrain his ministers and became the prime minister of the Han Dynasty, and when Zhang Tang judged lawsuits with harsh and stringent laws and became a court lieutenant, officials knew that others had committed crimes but did not report them.
A year later, signs of conspiracy by the kings of Huainan, Hengshan, and Jiangdu were discovered. The ministers looked for Mansuo to review the case and pursue their accomplices. Tens of thousands of people were sentenced to death. The officials used more ruthless methods and the laws became stricter.
At this time, scholars who respected the upright, virtuous, and literary were recruited, and some of them became ministers and officials.
Gongsun Hong used his position as prime minister, covered himself with cloth quilts, and did not eat many kinds of dishes as an example for the world. However, it did not benefit the folk customs and was only slightly beneficial to utilitarianism.
Another year passed, and the hussar general sent troops to attack the Huns again and won a great victory.
King Hunxie led tens of thousands of people to surrender, so the Han Dynasty sent 30,000 chariots to meet them.
After arriving, they were given rewards, including those who had meritorious service.
A total of more than 10 billion was spent this year.
More than ten years before this, the Yellow River burst and flooded the Liang and Chu regions. It had been in trouble several times, and the counties and counties next to the Yellow River built embankments to block the Yellow River breach, but it soon collapsed again, costing countless people.
After that, Fan Xi planned to save the water in the bottom pillar and use the canal connecting Fenshui and Yellow River to irrigate the fields. Zheng Zheng believed that the water transportation of Wei River was long and winding, so he dug a straight canal from Chang'an to Huayin; and Shuofang was also opening irrigation canals.
There were tens of thousands of people working on each project, and it took two or three years without success, and each cost billions of dollars.
Because of the attack on the Xiongnu, the emperor raised a large number of horses. Tens of thousands of horses traveled to Chang'an to obtain feed. The horse herders saw that Guanzhong was insufficient, so they transferred to the counties nearby Chang'an.
The tens of thousands of people who surrendered to the Xiongnu received generous rewards, and relied on government supplies for food and clothing. When the government's supplies were insufficient, the emperor reduced the meals, untied the horses from the carriages, and provided them with the property collected by the imperial palace.

summary:
The uses of property, money, cloth, and silk were not recorded before the Xia and Yin dynasties. Jiang Taigong established currency circulation for the Zhou Dynasty: gold was one inch square and weighed one catty; coins were round with square holes, using baht as weight; cloth was two feet two inches wide and four feet long per piece. Currency was considered more precious than gold, sharper than a knife, smoother than spring water, more dispersed than cloth, and more able to gather than silk. After Jiang Taigong retreated to Qi, he implemented this system. Guan Zhong assisted Duke Huan of Qi by establishing standards for measuring weight, noting that grain prices fluctuated with harvests and that goods varied in value based on demand. He warned that without governance, hoarding merchants would exploit the people, raising prices a hundredfold. A country with ten thousand cars needed merchants worth ten thousand gold to buy them, as profits were hidden. By consuming what was produced, expenses could be met, but hunger arose when grain was hoarded. The monarch should levy low prices when grain was abundant and distribute at high prices when scarce, adjusting supply and demand to stabilize prices. A town of ten thousand households should have a collection of ten thousand bells and millions of strings of money. Farming required abundant equipment and seeds in spring and summer, preventing big merchants from robbing the people. Duke Huan used Qi to unite the princes and become an overlord.

More than a hundred years later, King Jing of Zhou worried that money was too light and planned to cast large coins. Duke Shan Mu advised against it, arguing that when disasters came, property and currency should be weighed to save the people. If money was light, heavy money should be created for use, with both types circulating together. Abolishing light money for heavy money would cause the people to lose wealth, leading to shortages and flight. King Jing ignored this and made large coins with "actual goods" engraved, which benefited the people. When Qin annexed the world, currency was divided into two classes: gold measured in yi, and copper coins shaped like Zhou money with "ban liang" inscribed, weighing half a liang. Pearls, jade, turtles, shells, silver, and tin were decorations, not currency, and changed value arbitrarily. After the Han rose, they found Qin coins heavy and ordered pod coins instead, with gold returning to the weekly system of kilograms. Those who pursued profits hoarded goods, causing prices to skyrocket—rice reached ten thousand gold per stone, and a horse was worth one hundred gold. Emperor Gaozu ordered merchants not to wear silk or ride carriages and increased taxes to frustrate them. During Emperor Xiaohui and Queen Gao's reign, laws on merchants were relaxed, but their descendants could not become officials.

In the fifth year of Emperor Xiaowen's reign, four baht coins were minted with "banliang" on the front, and the law on stealing money was abolished, allowing people to mint coins freely. Jia Yi remonstrated, arguing that coining money with copper and tin led to doping for profit, and even daily tattooing could not stop it. He noted that coins varied by county—some light, some heavy—causing confusion. People abandoned farming to mine copper, increasing illegal money without increasing grain. He proposed collecting copper to prevent scattering, which would bring seven blessings: reducing tattooing crimes, eliminating fake money, returning miners to farming, balancing money and goods, distinguishing noble from humble, enriching the government while impoverishing merchants, and competing with the Xiongnu. The emperor did not listen. Wu State minted coins in Shanhuo, becoming richer than the emperor, and later rebelled. Deng Tong, a great official, minted coins and became wealthier than kings. Their money spread worldwide.

During Emperor Wu's reign, wars with the Xiongnu and campaigns in the southwest and Guangdong drained resources. The government used money to buy titles and exempt people from punishment, leading to official chaos. Gongsun Hong, as prime minister, used moral principles to restrain ministers, while Zhang Tang used harsh laws. The Yellow River flooded, costing billions. The emperor discussed changing coins to supplement expenses, using white deer skin for leather coins worth 400,000 yuan and silver-tin platinum coins. The government destroyed half-liang coins and recast three baht coins, punishing secret minting with death. Shu Guo Xianyang and Kong Wei were appointed as great agricultural ministers to manage salt and iron, while Sang Hongyang, a merchant's son, became favored. The government set up salt and iron officials, taxed merchants, and confiscated hidden property. The rich went bankrupt, and the government grew richer through salt and iron. The emperor built Kunming Pool and Bailiang Fortress, expanding palaces. The government used confiscated land and slaves for farming, and the grain transported to the capital reached four million shi.

After Wang Mang became regent, he changed the Han system, creating various coins like big coins, deed-knife coins, and wrong-knife coins. He later abolished these and introduced treasure goods, including gold, silver, turtle, shell, money, and cloth coins. He established six types of coins, each with different values, and implemented credit and five equalizations to control prices. He set up officials in Chang'an and five capitals to manage trade, taxing craftsmen and merchants. He also regulated wine production, with the government making wine and taking seven-tenths of the profit. Despite these measures, the people suffered, and many broke the law. Wang Mang executed those who made private coins and moved critics to remote areas. The corvee was heavy, and droughts and locusts caused trouble. Officials collected taxes privately, and the rich could not protect themselves, leading to widespread banditry. The Han army killed Wang Mang four years after the conquest of Zhutu Xiyong. Two years later, Shizu restored the five-baht coin and eliminated harsh laws. The text praises ancient methods of regulating commodities and prices, noting that during Emperor Xiaowu's time, expenses were met without increasing taxes, but under Wang Mang, the system failed, and the people suffered.

summary:
Emperor Yuan of Han, son of Emperor Xuan, was made prince at age eight. He was generous and respected Confucianism, often criticizing his father's reliance on legal officials and harsh punishments. Emperor Xuan warned that Confucian scholars would disrupt the Han dynasty's system, which blended kingly and hegemonic rule. Though Emperor Xuan favored another son, he ultimately kept Emperor Yuan as heir due to loyalty to his mother.

Upon ascending the throne in 48 BCE, Emperor Yuan honored his mother and wife as empresses, granted amnesty, and distributed rewards. He issued edicts addressing natural disasters, earthquakes, and famines, ordering relief efforts, tax exemptions, and land grants to the poor. He reduced palace expenses, dismissed entertainers, and lent public lands to farmers. He also sent officials to inspect local governance and seek wise men.

In subsequent years, Emperor Yuan continued responding to crises: earthquakes, floods, plagues, and famines led to further tax exemptions, amnesties, and relief measures. He abolished certain laws, reduced palace staff, and encouraged remonstrance. He appointed Confucian scholars like Gong Yu and Kuang Heng as officials, but his indecisiveness weakened the state. He also dealt with rebellions, such as the Xiqiang uprising, and military campaigns against the Xiongnu, including the execution of Zhizhi Chanyu.

Emperor Yuan's reign saw numerous natural disasters and social unrest. He repeatedly issued edicts blaming himself for poor governance and seeking advice. He reformed policies, including abolishing the death penalty for certain family crimes and reducing corvée labor. He also established his own mausoleum, Weiling, and ordered that no new migrants be forced to settle there.

Emperor Yuan died in 33 BCE after 16 years of rule. Ban Gu's commentary notes that Emperor Yuan was talented in music and calligraphy, respected Confucianism, and appointed many Confucian scholars as officials. However, his indecisiveness and adherence to literary principles led to the decline of Emperor Xuan's achievements. Despite this, his generosity, thrift, and gentle edicts reflected the legacy of ancient wise kings.

He is not sensual by nature, and sometimes watches martial arts dramas involving hand-held wrestling.
When he came to the throne, he suffered from fistula, which gradually worsened. He died after being emperor for six years at the age of 20. What a pity!
summary: Emperor Xiaoai, grandson of Emperor Yuan and son of Prince Dingtao Gong, became king at age three and developed an interest in literature and law. In the fourth year of Yuanyan's reign, he visited Emperor Cheng with his officials, while Prince Xiao of Zhongshan came with only one attendant. Emperor Cheng, impressed by King Dingtao's knowledge of the "Poetry" and his explanations, favored him over the incompetent King Zhongshan. Queen Mother Fu, King Dingtao's grandmother, bribed Emperor Cheng's favorites Zhao Zhaoyi and Wang Gen, who, seeing the emperor had no heirs, praised King Dingtao. Emperor Cheng crowned him at seventeen and later made him crown prince. King Dingtao humbly declined but accepted. After Emperor Cheng's death in the second year of Suihe, the prince became emperor, honoring the Queen Mother and issuing amnesties. He honored his grandmother and mother, granted titles to relatives, and dismissed Yuefu for lewd music. He rewarded Wang Gen and others for supporting his succession and granted lands to Wang Liang for mourning. He issued edicts to curb extravagance, limiting land and slave ownership, banning merchants from land and office, and stopping complex embroidery. He revoked certain laws, allowed inner palace residents under thirty to marry, freed slaves over fifty, and banned rare animal tributes. He increased salaries for low-ranking officials and punished corrupt officials. After disasters like earthquakes and floods, he sent officials to aid victims and exempted taxes for the poor. In the first year of Jianping, he pardoned the world, deposed guilty marquises, and gave Wang family lands to the poor. He sought talent, granted money and cloth to officials, and saw the suicide of Empress Dowager Feng and her brother. In the second year, he dismissed the chief minister, restored the imperial censor, and honored his ancestors with new titles and temples. After Empress Dowager Ding's death, he followed Zhou rites for burial, recruiting 50,000 workers. He initially accepted prophecies to change the era name but later revoked them, punishing the prophets and officials. He faced droughts, fires, and comets, restored sacrifices, and dealt with rebellions. He granted titles for reporting crimes, honored his wife, and sought military talent. In the first year of Yuanshou, a solar eclipse led to an edict blaming himself and seeking virtuous officials. After Empress Dowager Fu's death, he dismissed officials and saw portents. In the second year, Xiongnu envoys visited, and he divided official duties. Emperor Ai died in Weiyang Palace at age 20 after six years as emperor, buried in Yiling. Ban Gu noted his early talent and efforts to strengthen authority but lamented his short reign.

translation:
Emperor Xuan of the Han Dynasty, great-grandson of Emperor Wu, and grandson of Prince Ru.
Prince Ru took in Shi Liangdi and gave birth to Emperor Shi's grandson. His grandson took in Mrs. Wang and gave birth to Emperor Xuan, who was named Zenghuang's grandson.
A few months after giving birth, a "witchcraft incident" occurred. The prince, Liang Di, the emperor's grandson, and Mrs. Wang were all killed.
The facts are all recorded in "The Legend of the Prince".
Even though his great-grandson was still an infant, he was imprisoned.
At that time, Bingji was an official of Tingwei and was responsible for handling witchcraft incidents. He was extremely sympathetic to his great-grandson's innocent misfortune, so he ordered the female convicts Zhao Zhengqing from Huaiyang and Hu Zu from Weicheng to exchange breast-feeding and provide them with food and clothing privately. They treated him very kindly.
The witchcraft incident could not be concluded for several years.
In the second year of the Yuan Dynasty, Emperor Wu was ill and traveled back and forth between Changyang and Wuzha palaces. The astrologers who were watching the clouds said that there was the emperor's energy in Chang'an prison. Emperor Wu sent envoys to inform the various officials in the capital that criminals imprisoned due to witchcraft incidents would be executed regardless of their severity.
The emissary ordered Guo Rang to go to the county prison at night for inspection. Bingji closed the prison door so that the envoys could not enter, but his great-grandson Lai Bingji was saved.
Later, when there was a general amnesty, Bingji drove his great-grandson to his grandmother Shi Liangdi's home.
This incident is recorded in "Biography of Bingji" and "Biography of Foreign Relatives".
Later, there was an edict, sending officials from Yeting to visit the great-grandson at the historian's home, and ordered Zongzheng to record him in the royal genealogy.
At this time, Zhang He, the order of Yeting, was Prince Li's former attendant. He missed Prince Li's old kindness and sympathized with his great-grandson, so he treated his great-grandson considerately and used his personal money to support his great-grandson's education.
When he was older, he married the daughter of Xu Guanghan, a court dyer, for his great-grandson. Therefore, his great-grandson relied on the Guanghan brothers and the Shi family of his grandmother's family.
He returned from the East China Sea to learn "Poetry" from Zhong Weng. He was talented and never tired of learning. He also had the character of drawing a sword to help when the road was rough. He fought chickens and horses and made many friends. He was familiar with the evil in the alleys and the gains and losses of official governance.
He visited the tombs of his ancestors many times to pay his respects, and went to the Sanfu District of Kyoto to understand the people's sentiments. He was once trapped and humiliated in the salt pond of Lianshao County, especially in Du County?
He traveled between counties, mostly in Xiadu.
He went to the imperial court to attend court invitations and lived in Shangguanli, Chang'an. He had hair all over his body and on his feet. He always glowed when sleeping. Every time he went to a bakery to buy cakes, the business of the bakery prospered. People were surprised by this.

This incident is recorded in "The Biography of King He of Changyi" and "The Biography of Huo Guang".
In the seventh month of autumn, Huo Guang made a memorial and said: In the system of etiquette, people value blood relations, so they respect their ancestors, and if they respect their ancestors, they will respect their ancestors' cause.
Emperor Zhao has no heirs, so he should choose a virtuous descendant as his successor.
Emperor Wu's great-grandson Ming was ill and was ordered to be taken care of by Yeting. He is now eighteen years old. Study "Poetry", "The Analects of Confucius" and "The Classic of Filial Piety" as a teacher, be thrifty, benevolent and love others, and you can be the successor of Emperor Zhao.

The imperial servants used Lanyu light carriages to greet his great-grandson. He first went to Zongzheng's mansion to fast and salute. On July 25, he entered Weiyang Palace and met with the Empress Dowager. He was first granted the title of Marquis of Yangwu.

summary:
Emperor Xuan, great-grandson of Emperor Wu, was born into tragedy. His grandfather Prince Ru, grandmother Shi Liangdi, and parents were all killed in the "witchcraft incident" when he was an infant. Imprisoned, he was saved by official Bingji, who arranged for female convicts to nurse him. After a general amnesty, Bingji took him to his grandmother's home. Later, Yeting official Zhang He, remembering his loyalty to Prince Li, supported the boy's education and arranged his marriage to Xu Guanghan's daughter.

As he grew, Emperor Xuan studied poetry under Zhong Weng, showed talent, and became familiar with both common people's lives and official governance. He traveled extensively, visited ancestral tombs, and experienced hardship in Lianshao County. Strange phenomena surrounded him—his body glowed during sleep, and bakeries prospered when he visited.

When Emperor Zhao died without heirs, General Huo Guang initially appointed the King of Changyi, but soon deposed him for lewd behavior. Huo Guang then recommended Emperor Xuan, then eighteen, citing his virtue, education, and suitability. The Empress Dowager agreed, and after proper ceremonies, he ascended the throne.

Emperor Xuan's reign was marked by careful governance. He initially declined Huo Guang's offer to return power, entrusting him with major responsibilities. He rewarded meritorious officials generously, including Huo Guang, Yang Chang, and others. He issued edicts promoting agriculture, reducing waste, and caring for the poor. When earthquakes struck, he wore plain clothes, avoided the main hall, and sought advice from officials.

After Huo Guang's death, Emperor Xuan took personal control of government. He established regular reporting systems and tested officials' abilities. He promoted virtuous officials like Wang Cheng, who resettled refugees. He established the Crown Prince and granted amnesties. He reformed laws to protect filial piety, allowing parents to hide children's crimes and exempting mourners from corvée labor.

The Huo family later rebelled, and Queen Huo was deposed after being implicated in poisoning plots. Emperor Xuan continued his reforms, lowering salt prices, improving prison conditions, and requiring annual reports of deaths in custody. He built tombs, established temples, and rewarded those who had helped him in his youth, including Bingji, Zhang He, and the female convicts who nursed him.

Under his rule, the Xiongnu were pacified. Huhanxie Chanyu submitted as a vassal, visiting the court with great ceremony. Emperor Xuan treated him as a guest, rewarding him generously and establishing protectorates for surrendered tribes. The Western Qiang were subdued through military campaigns and farming strategies proposed by General Zhao Chongguo.

Emperor Xuan died in Weiyang Palace after a reign marked by competent administration, military success, and cultural achievements. Ban Gu commented that he rewarded merit, punished guilt, and examined names and facts thoroughly, making officials proficient in their duties and people content in their work. His reign was considered a restoration, with virtues comparable to those of King Xuan of Zhou.

summary:
Emperor Hui of the Han Dynasty, son of Emperor Gaozu and Empress Lu, became crown prince in the second year of Gaozu's reign. After Gaozu's death in April of the twelfth year, Hui ascended the throne on May 17, with his mother becoming empress dowager. He issued decrees rewarding subjects with titles and promoting officials based on service length: Zhonglang and Langzhong officials serving six years received third-level promotions, those serving four years received second-level promotions, and various other officials received specific rewards. Those who organized Gaozu's funeral received monetary rewards based on salary, and those who built his mausoleum received gold. Land rent was reduced to one tax per fifteen people. Certain officials and their families were exempted from corvée labor except military tax. Princes were ordered to build Gaozu's ancestral temple.

In the first year of his reign, King Liu Ruyi of Zhao died. Subjects could atone for capital crimes with money. Commoners received title promotions. Chang'an city construction began. In the second year, King Hui of Qi presented Chengyang County to increase Princess Lu Yuan's territory. Two dragons appeared in Lanling, an earthquake struck Longxi, drought occurred, and Yanghou Liu Zhong and Prime Minister Xiao He died. In the third year, 146,000 workers built Chang'an for thirty days. A Liu family princess married the Xiongnu Shanyu. The King of Minyue was titled King of East China Sea, and 20,000 princes and slaves built Chang'an. A fire broke out in royal stables, and Zhao Tuo of South Vietnam paid tribute. In the fourth year, Zhang Ao's daughter became queen. Filial and loyal sages were exempted from corvée. The emperor held a crown ceremony with amnesty, abolished restrictive Qin laws, and fires occurred in Changle and Weiyang Palaces. In the fifth year, unusual weather included thunder and fruit blossoming in winter. Another 145,000 workers built Chang'an. Severe drought struck, Prime Minister Cao Shen died, and Chang'an city was completed. In the sixth year, King Fei of Qi died. Titles could be bought, and unmarried women aged fifteen to thirty were fined. Fan Kuai died, and the west city and Aocang were built. In the seventh year, chariot officers were sent to Xingyang. Solar eclipses occurred, and Emperor Hui died in Weiyang Palace on August 12, buried in Anling on September 5. Ban Gu commented that Hui was kind and respectful but fell short of saintliness due to Empress Lu's actions.

The dew fell on the capital, and the people of Chang'an were rewarded with cattle and wine.
In the first month of spring in the first year of Suihe, a general amnesty was granted to the whole world.

Wang Xin of Dingtao is my heir. He is kind and filial. He can inherit the order of heaven and continue the sacrifice.
